concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 4 (Primary Adam Literature (Life of Adam and Eve))

details.intro: The Life of Adam and Eve narrates the lives of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from Paradise: their penitence, Seth's journey to Paradise for oil from the tree of mercy, Adam's death and burial, and Eve's account of the fall.
details.provenance: The Greek version (often called the Apocalypse of Moses) and the Latin, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic versions differ widely. The date and origin of the primary Adam literature remain debated: M.D. Johnson (OTP 2) argued for a Jewish original of c. 100 BCE–200 CE, while others regard the work as Christian, of the 2nd–4th c. CE.

Greek Text

  • ** Now the best available text.

  • G. A. Anderson and M. E. Stone, A Synopsis of the Books of Adam and Eve (Rev. ed.; SBLEJL 5; Atlanta: Society of Biblical Literature, 1999).

  • ** A true critical edition of the Greek text. Intensively eclectic, geared largely toward producing a smooth, translatable text.

details.intro:
The Testament of Adam (TAdam) is a short Christian pseudepigraphon from late antiquity. It was likely composed in Syriac, though it now survives in numerous languages and recensions. In many manuscripts the text is titled ”The testament of our father Adam” or something similar. The document is comprised of two main parts, usually called the Horarium and the Prophecy by modern scholars. The document is conventionally divided into four chapters, with the Horarium comprising the first two chapters and the Prophecy as chapter three. What we often call the fourth chapter is an additional section, the Hierarchy, which only appears in one manuscript and was almost certainly not part of the original document.

The Horarium

In the first main part, the Horarium, Adam lists the hours of the night and/or day in which the various creatures of the creation give praise to God, each in its appointed hour. In most manuscripts this list is divided into two sections, the "Hours of the Night" and the "Hours of the Day," each of which is allotted a chapter in the document's conventional organization. In a few manuscripts, however, one or the other of these sections is missing.

The Greek version of the Horarium seems to have a complex history. The six Greek manuscripts of TAdam contain a modified version of the Horarium that has no connection with Adam. This version is also extant in an Armenian recension. A third, simpler form of the Horarium is found in the work of George Cedrenus (11th century C.E.) where that chronicler describes revelations that Adam received from God. Cedrenus does not provide any other parts of TAdam, though his discussion of Adam's revelations may have been influenced by the Prophecy as well (see below). In any case, the relationship between these three versions of the Horarium (Syriac, Greek, and Cedrenus) is unclear.

The Prophecy

The second part of TAdam, the Prophecy, is a testament with apocalyptic features, presented as the final words of Adam recorded by his son Seth. In it Adam passes on revelations he received from God concerning the future. Some of these revelations concern the relatively near future, focusing on the Flood and Adam's own fate after death. More broadly, Adam describe the eschatological fate his posterity and the world. The Christian nature of the document is most visible when Adam predicts the divine incarnation. 

The Hierarchy

One late manuscript (Vatican Syr 164, 1702 C.E.) appends a unique section concerning the heavenly orders, with the heading ”Also from the testament of our father Adam." This section, usually designated the Hierarchy, is an angelology which lists the nine orders of the heavenly beings and their functions. Since it only appears in one manuscript, and since its content is incompatible with the narrative fiction of the two other parts, the Hierarchy was probably not part of the original TAdam. Nevertheless, modern scholars often include it as a fourth chapter of the document.
details.provenance:
A Syriac Christian Document

Beginning with M. E. Renan, the Testament of Adam was long regarded by modern scholars as a Gnostic work, but both Reinink and Robinson have shown this view to be wrong. Robinson has argued that the Syriac recension 1 is likely the most ancient form of TAdam known to us, and he has furnished good evidence that the original language of both the Horarium and the Prophecy was Syriac (Robinson, 137-42). If Robinson is correct, the work in its present form most likely originated within the Christian communities of Syria in late antiquity.

Earlier Jewish Sources?

The question of earlier sources is closely related to the question of unity. In all its extant forms the Horarium and the Prophecy are presented together as a unified composition, and their redactional and compositional history is difficult to untangle with any certainty. Still, the two parts are strikingly different in form and genre. Various literary elements also strongly suggest that the Horarium and the Prophecy were once two separate documents, combined and adapted at some point by a redactor to produce the Christian work we know.

The original Horarium would then likely have been a Jewish work, not necessarily related to Adam at all. The Prophecy could very well have been a Christian work from the beginning, but it could also be a heavily redacted Jewish composition. On the basis of a passage from the Apocalypse of Elijah (???), Robinson tentatively suggests that this earlier version of the Prophecy was composed in the third century C.E. and the earlier independent Horarium no later than that (Robinson, 150–3). Richard Bauckham has since made the case that the Horarium originated as a Jewish work from the second temple period (Bauckham, 2002).

The Provenance of the Hierarchy

The Hierarchy has only been superficially adapted to fit TAdam. The speaker, supposed to be Adam, refers to biblical events in past time and addresses ”my beloved” (plural; 4:1). The Hierarchy might well be a lightly redacted version of a Jewish angelology, possibly dating from the Second Temple period. The Christian additions may have involved nothing more than the interpolation of ”Jesus Christ” into 4:1 and 4:8 (see Robinson, 146-48; 159-60).
details.manuscripts:
Syriac Text

The earliest form of the Testament of Adam is witnessed in eight manuscripts dating between the 9th and the 18th centuries C.E.  The Syriac manuscripts are divided into three recensions based on content, chronology, writing system and arrangement of the four sections. (Note that the dating and alphabetic names for these manuscripts are all taken from S.E. Robinson's The Testament of Adam: An Examination of the Syriac and Greek Traditions. SBLDS 52; Chico, Ca.: Scholars Press, 1982.)

Recension 1

Recension 1 consists of the aforementioned Manuscript A (BM Add. 14,624 [folios 8b-10a]), dating to the early 9th century B.C.E., in addition to Manuscript B (Vat. Syr. 58), which is and dated to the late 16th century. Manuscript A is written in the Estrangela script with some letters in Serta, while Manuscript B is written entirely in Serta. Both manuscripts contain the Horarium (Hours of the Night and Hours of the Day) and the Prophecy in that order. In spite of the chronological differences, these two mss are nearly identical in content.

Recension 2

Recension 2 consists of Manuscript C (Vat. Syr. 164), written in Nestorian and dated to the early 18th century, and Manuscript D (BM Add 25,875), also written in Nestorian and dated to the early 18th century. Manuscript C contains the Horarium (only the Hours of the Night), the Prophecy and – as the sole witness – the Hierarchy. Manuscript D contains only the Prophecy.

Recension 3

Recension 3 consists of the following manuscripts: Manuscript E (Arund. Or. 53), written in Serta and dated to the 16th century, Manuscript F (Vat. Syr 159) written in Serta and dated to the 17th century, Manuscript G (Rylands 44) written in Nestorian and dated to the 15th century and Manuscript H (BM Add 14,577), written in Estrangela and dated to the late 9th century. All manuscripts in Recension 3 contain the Horarium except in the same order as the Greek versions, with the Hours of the Day first, followed by the Hours of the Night. Manuscripts E and H merely contain the Horarium. Manuscript F is the only one in Recension 3 that contains the Prophecy. Manuscript G also contains the so-called Treatise of Shem.

Greek Text

The Greek version of TAdam comes to us in two independent forms. Both contain only the Horarium. One recension is witnessed in six Greek manuscripts from the 15th to the 17th centuries C.E. This modified version of the Horarium bears no connection with Adam or with a testamentary context. It seems to be a late reworking of the Syriac recension 3, in part because it reverses the order of the Hours of the Night and Hours of the Day in the same way. This Greek recension bears some resemblance to late Byzantine magical texts and in most cases appears as part of a larger work on astrology and magic called Apotelesmata, attributed in some of the manuscripts to Apollonius of Tyana. This peculiar magic-Apollonius version of the Horarium is also extant in Armenian (published in Stone, pp. 39-77).

The other form of the Greek Horarium appears in one passage from Cedrenus. Here the 11th century chronicler lists the hours of the day in which prayers are sent up to heaven. Again this list is not attached to a version of the Prophecy, and it does not appear in a testamentary context. Unlike the other Greek witnesses, however, Cedrenus does connect this modified Horarium with Adam, presenting it among the revelations Adam received from God. Although Cedrenus only lists the hours of the day, the chronicler tells us that both the hours of the day and the hours of the night had been revealed to Adam. An almost verbatim passage in George Syncellus (9th century) is likely the Vorlage for Cedrenus' Horarium. Unfortunately the text of Syncellus is damaged from the point where the listing of the hours would begin.

details.intro:
The Primary Adam Literature encompasses a multifaceted cycle of closely related Jewish and Christian narratives recounting the creation, fall, penance, death, and burial of the protoplasts Adam and Eve. The literature is extant in six principal ancient and medieval versions:

A. Greek Apocalypse of Moses (Apocalypsis Mosis / Greek Life of Adam and Eve [GLAE])

  • Primary Witnesses:
  • A₁: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Marcianus gr. VII 22 (11th c.).
  • B: Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. theol. gr. 237 (13th/14th c.).
  • C: Vienna, ÖNB, cod. theol. gr. 247 (14th c.).
  • D: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, cod. C 210 inf. (13th c.) — ed. A. M. Ceriani (1868).
  • Additional witnesses: Paris gr. 1313, Paris Suppl. gr. 162.

B. Latin Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae)

  • Classification: Divided by Wilhelm Meyer (1878) into four manuscript classes spanning the 9th to 15th centuries across Continental Europe (especially Munich Bayerische Staatsbibliothek: Clm 4807, Clm 5601, Clm 8470, Clm 13002) and England (12 Insular MSS classified by J. H. Mozley 1928–1929; analyzed by J.-P. Pettorelli 1999).
  • Notable for interpolations such as the Fall of Satan (chs. 12–16) and the quest of Seth for the Oil of Mercy.

C. Armenian Version (The Penitence of Adam / Book of Adam)

  • Discovered in the Library of the Mechitharist Congregation of San Lazzaro (Venice) and the Matenadaran (Yerevan), edited critically by Michael E. Stone (CSCO 429–430, 1981). Closer than the Greek or Latin to the lost archetype in its preservation of the penance in the rivers.

D. Georgian Book of Adam (K‘art‘uli versia)

  • Preserved in 16th/17th-century manuscripts (Tbilisi S-354 and H-1691), critically studied and translated by J.-P. Mahé (1981) and C. Kurtsikidze (1964). Parallels the Armenian text very closely.

E. Slavonic Life of Adam and Eve (Slovo o Adame i Eve)

  • Transmitted in Serbian, Russian, and Bulgarian redactions embedded in Palea collections, edited by V. Jagić (1893), N. S. Tikhonravov (1863), and I. Franko (1896–1910). Includes the related Bohemian (Old Czech) vernacular fragment.

F. Coptic Fragments

  • Sahidic and Fayyumic papyri preserving portions of the Vita and Apocalypse of Moses (Manchester John Rylands Coptic MS 84, ed. W. E. Crum 1909; Berlin Papyrus 181, ed. J. Leipoldt 1904).

details.intro:
The Primary Adam Literature encompasses a multifaceted cycle of closely related Jewish and Christian narratives recounting the creation, fall, penance, death, and burial of the protoplasts Adam and Eve. The literature is extant in six principal ancient and medieval versions:

A. Greek Apocalypse of Moses (Apocalypsis Mosis / Greek Life of Adam and Eve [GLAE])

  • Primary Witnesses:
  • A₁: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Marcianus gr. VII 22 (11th c.).
  • B: Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. theol. gr. 237 (13th/14th c.).
  • C: Vienna, ÖNB, cod. theol. gr. 247 (14th c.).
  • D: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, cod. C 210 inf. (13th c.) — ed. A. M. Ceriani (1868).
  • Additional witnesses: Paris gr. 1313, Paris Suppl. gr. 162.

B. Latin Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae)

  • Classification: Divided by Wilhelm Meyer (1878) into four manuscript classes spanning the 9th to 15th centuries across Continental Europe (especially Munich Bayerische Staatsbibliothek: Clm 4807, Clm 5601, Clm 8470, Clm 13002) and England (12 Insular MSS classified by J. H. Mozley 1928–1929; analyzed by J.-P. Pettorelli 1999).
  • Notable for interpolations such as the Fall of Satan (chs. 12–16) and the quest of Seth for the Oil of Mercy.

C. Armenian Version (The Penitence of Adam / Book of Adam)

  • Discovered in the Library of the Mechitharist Congregation of San Lazzaro (Venice) and the Matenadaran (Yerevan), edited critically by Michael E. Stone (CSCO 429–430, 1981). Closer than the Greek or Latin to the lost archetype in its preservation of the penance in the rivers.

  • Preserved in 16th/17th-century manuscripts (Tbilisi S-354 and H-1691), critically studied and translated by J.-P. Mahé (1981) and C. Kurtsikidze (1964). Parallels the Armenian text very closely.

  • Transmitted in Serbian, Russian, and Bulgarian redactions embedded in Palea collections, edited by V. Jagić (1893), N. S. Tikhonravov (1863), and I. Franko (1896–1910). Includes the related Bohemian (Old Czech) vernacular fragment.

  • Sahidic and Fayyumic papyri preserving portions of the Vita and Apocalypse of Moses (Manchester John Rylands Coptic MS 84, ed. W. E. Crum 1909; Berlin Papyrus 181, ed. J. Leipoldt 1904).

details.intro:
The Apocalypse of Adam is preserved in a unique Sahidic Coptic manuscript discovered at Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945:

  • Codex: Cairo, Coptic Museum, Nag Hammadi Codex V, tractate 5 (pp. 64, line 1 – 85, line 32).
  • Facsimile Edition: Robinson, James M., ed. The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices: Codex V. Leiden: Brill, 1975, pls. 74–96.
  • Date and Context: Copied ca. mid-4th century CE; the Greek original is widely dated between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. Strikingly, the work lacks explicit Christian terminology or overt references to Jesus Christ, making it central to debates over non-Christian Jewish-Gnostic apocalypticism and Sethian origins.

A. Greek Apocalypse of Moses (Apocalypsis Mosis / Greek Life of Adam and Eve [GLAE])

  • Primary Witnesses:
  • A₁: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Marcianus gr. VII 22 (11th c.).

details.intro:
The Apocalypse of Adam is preserved in a unique Sahidic Coptic manuscript discovered at Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945:

  • Codex: Cairo, Coptic Museum, Nag Hammadi Codex V, tractate 5 (pp. 64, line 1 – 85, line 32).
  • Facsimile Edition: Robinson, James M., ed. The Facsimile Edition of the Nag Hammadi Codices: Codex V. Leiden: Brill, 1975, pls. 74–96.
  • Date and Context: Copied ca. mid-4th century CE; the Greek original is widely dated between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. Strikingly, the work lacks explicit Christian terminology or overt references to Jesus Christ, making it central to debates over non-Christian Jewish-Gnostic apocalypticism and Sethian origins.

details.intro:
The Primary Adam Literature encompasses a multifaceted cycle of closely related Jewish and Christian narratives recounting the creation, fall, penance, death, and burial of the protoplasts Adam and Eve. The literature is extant in six principal ancient and medieval versions:

A. Greek Apocalypse of Moses (Apocalypsis Mosis / Greek Life of Adam and Eve [GLAE])

  • Primary Witnesses:
  • A₁: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Marcianus gr. VII 22 (11th c.).
  • B: Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. theol. gr. 237 (13th/14th c.).
  • C: Vienna, ÖNB, cod. theol. gr. 247 (14th c.).
  • D: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, cod. C 210 inf. (13th c.) — ed. A. M. Ceriani (1868).
  • Additional witnesses: Paris gr. 1313, Paris Suppl. gr. 162.

B. Latin Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae)

  • Classification: Divided by Wilhelm Meyer (1878) into four manuscript classes spanning the 9th to 15th centuries across Continental Europe (especially Munich Bayerische Staatsbibliothek: Clm 4807, Clm 5601, Clm 8470, Clm 13002) and England (12 Insular MSS classified by J. H. Mozley 1928–1929; analyzed by J.-P. Pettorelli 1999).
  • Notable for interpolations such as the Fall of Satan (chs. 12–16) and the quest of Seth for the Oil of Mercy.

C. Armenian Version (The Penitence of Adam / Book of Adam)

  • Discovered in the Library of the Mechitharist Congregation of San Lazzaro (Venice) and the Matenadaran (Yerevan), edited critically by Michael E. Stone (CSCO 429–430, 1981). Closer than the Greek or Latin to the lost archetype in its preservation of the penance in the rivers.

D. Georgian Book of Adam (K‘art‘uli versia)

  • Preserved in 16th/17th-century manuscripts (Tbilisi S-354 and H-1691), critically studied and translated by J.-P. Mahé (1981) and C. Kurtsikidze (1964). Parallels the Armenian text very closely.

E. Slavonic Life of Adam and Eve (Slovo o Adame i Eve)

  • Transmitted in Serbian, Russian, and Bulgarian redactions embedded in Palea collections, edited by V. Jagić (1893), N. S. Tikhonravov (1863), and I. Franko (1896–1910). Includes the related Bohemian (Old Czech) vernacular fragment.

F. Coptic Fragments

  • Sahidic and Fayyumic papyri preserving portions of the Vita and Apocalypse of Moses (Manchester John Rylands Coptic MS 84, ed. W. E. Crum 1909; Berlin Papyrus 181, ed. J. Leipoldt 1904).

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 15 (1 Enoch / Qumran (4Q369 Prayer of Enosh))

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

1. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36): Early Hellenistic period (3rd cent. BCE). Relates the rebellion of the Watchers (the angels led by Shemihazah and Asael, Gen 6:1–4), Enoch's intercession, and his cosmic journeys through the earth and heavens.

2. The Book of Parables / Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71): Late 1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE. Contains three parables centering on the eschatological figures of the Righteous One, Chosen One, and "Son of Man" (identified with Enoch in ch. 71). Absent from the Qumran Aramaic corpus.

3. The Astronomical Book / Book of the Heavenly Luminaries (1 Enoch 72–82): The oldest Enochic composition (late 3rd cent. BCE or earlier). Details the 364-day solar calendar, lunar phases, and cosmic gates revealed by the angel Uriel.

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).
details.manuscripts:
A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q201 (4QEn$^a$ ar): 4Q Enoch$^a$ (early 2nd cent. BCE; Watchers).
  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr$^c$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • Crucial Finding: No manuscript traces of the Parables of Enoch (chs. 37–71) have been found at Qumran; instead, the Cave 4 library preserved multiple copies of the Book of Giants (see §7 below).

B. Greek Tradition

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

  • 6th-century CE codex discovered in a Christian monk's tomb at Akhmim in 1886–1887.
  • Contains two distinct copies: GrP$^1$ (1 Enoch 1:1–32:6) and GrP$^2$ (1 Enoch 19:3–21:9).

2. Chester Beatty Papyrus 185 (Chester Beatty XII + Michigan Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE papyrus codex leaves.
  • Preserves 1 Enoch 97:6–104:13 and 106:1–107:3 (lacking ch. 105 and 108), followed directly by Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha.

3. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus XVII 2069:

  • Late 4th-century CE papyrus fragments containing 1 Enoch 77:7–78:1, 78:8, 85:10–86:2, 87:1–3.

4. Vatican Greek 1809:

  • 11th-century CE tachygraphic parchment manuscript containing 1 Enoch 89:42–49.

5. Georgius Syncellus, Chronographia (ed. Mosshammer 1984):

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

6. Qumran Cave 7 Greek Fragments (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12):

  • Proposed by E. A. Muro Jr. (1997) and É. Puech (1997) as fragments of Greek 1 Enoch 103:3–4, 7–8, refuting J. O'Callaghan's 1 Timothy hypothesis.

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

Preserved in over 40 known manuscripts cataloged from the 15th through 19th centuries, classified into two genealogical families:

1. Family $G^1$ (Eth I): The older, unrevised textual recension (15th–16th cent.), exhibiting closest affinity to the Greek Vorlage:

  • Tānāsee 9 (TS): Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9 (15th cent.; complete 1–108).
  • London, BL MS Or. 485 (Lo4 / g): 16th century (base text for Knibb).
  • Berlin, Staatsbibliothek Petermann II, Nachtrag 29 (Be / q): 16th century.
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.
  • EMML 2080 (Co2): Project of Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (15th/16th cent.).
  • Cambridge, University Library Add. 1570 (Ca): Dated 1588–1589.

2. Family $G^2$ (Eth II): The vulgate / learned secondary recension (17th–18th cent.), smoothed and harmonized by Ethiopian scribes:

  • Oxford, Bodleian Bruce 74 (Ox2 / b) and Bodleian Or. 531 (Ox1 / a): 18th century.
  • London, BL MS Or. 8822 (Lo1 / d, olim Curzon 55) and BL Add. 24185 (Lo3 / f).
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

D. Latin, Syriac, and Coptic Fragments

1. Latin:

  • London, BL MS Royal 5 E XIII, fols. 79v–80r (8th cent. CE): Contains 1 Enoch 106:1–18 (the miraculous birth of Noah, discovered and edited by M. R. James, 1893).
  • Pseudo-Cyprian, Ad Novatianum 16.5 (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9).
  • Tertullian (De idololatria 4.2–3, 15.6; De cultu feminarum 1.3, 2.10).

2. Syriac:

  • Chronicle of Michael the Syrian I.4 (ed. Chabot 1899; Brock 1968), preserving an excerpt of 1 Enoch 6:1–7.

3. Coptic:

  • Papyrus fragment from Antinoë (discovered 1937, ed. Donadoni 1960), preserving 1 Enoch 93:3–8 in Sahidic.
  • Related Coptic Enochic fragments (ed. Pearson 1976).

title: Henoch aethiopicus
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro: 1 Enoch is a collection of five Enochic works: the Book of the Watchers (1–36), the Similitudes (37–71), the Astronomical Book (72–82), the Book of Dreams (83–90) and the Epistle of Enoch (91–108). It deals with the fall of the watchers, cosmic geography and the calendar, and the final judgment.
details.provenance: The oldest parts date from the 3rd–2nd c. BCE; the Similitudes are probably from the 1st c. CE. Aramaic fragments of every part except the Similitudes were found at Qumran. The complete work survives only in Ge'ez; substantial portions survive in Greek.

title: Liber gigantum
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

1. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36): Early Hellenistic period (3rd cent. BCE). Relates the rebellion of the Watchers (the angels led by Shemihazah and Asael, Gen 6:1–4), Enoch's intercession, and his cosmic journeys through the earth and heavens.

2. The Book of Parables / Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71): Late 1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE. Contains three parables centering on the eschatological figures of the Righteous One, Chosen One, and "Son of Man" (identified with Enoch in ch. 71). Absent from the Qumran Aramaic corpus.

3. The Astronomical Book / Book of the Heavenly Luminaries (1 Enoch 72–82): The oldest Enochic composition (late 3rd cent. BCE or earlier). Details the 364-day solar calendar, lunar phases, and cosmic gates revealed by the angel Uriel.

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).
details.manuscripts:
A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q201 (4QEn$^a$ ar): 4Q Enoch$^a$ (early 2nd cent. BCE; Watchers).
  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr$^c$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • Crucial Finding: No manuscript traces of the Parables of Enoch (chs. 37–71) have been found at Qumran; instead, the Cave 4 library preserved multiple copies of the Book of Giants (see §7 below).

B. Greek Tradition

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

  • 6th-century CE codex discovered in a Christian monk's tomb at Akhmim in 1886–1887.
  • Contains two distinct copies: GrP$^1$ (1 Enoch 1:1–32:6) and GrP$^2$ (1 Enoch 19:3–21:9).

2. Chester Beatty Papyrus 185 (Chester Beatty XII + Michigan Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE papyrus codex leaves.
  • Preserves 1 Enoch 97:6–104:13 and 106:1–107:3 (lacking ch. 105 and 108), followed directly by Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha.

3. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus XVII 2069:

  • Late 4th-century CE papyrus fragments containing 1 Enoch 77:7–78:1, 78:8, 85:10–86:2, 87:1–3.

4. Vatican Greek 1809:

  • 11th-century CE tachygraphic parchment manuscript containing 1 Enoch 89:42–49.

5. Georgius Syncellus, Chronographia (ed. Mosshammer 1984):

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

6. Qumran Cave 7 Greek Fragments (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12):

  • Proposed by E. A. Muro Jr. (1997) and É. Puech (1997) as fragments of Greek 1 Enoch 103:3–4, 7–8, refuting J. O'Callaghan's 1 Timothy hypothesis.

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

Preserved in over 40 known manuscripts cataloged from the 15th through 19th centuries, classified into two genealogical families:

1. Family $G^1$ (Eth I): The older, unrevised textual recension (15th–16th cent.), exhibiting closest affinity to the Greek Vorlage:

  • Tānāsee 9 (TS): Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9 (15th cent.; complete 1–108).
  • London, BL MS Or. 485 (Lo4 / g): 16th century (base text for Knibb).
  • Berlin, Staatsbibliothek Petermann II, Nachtrag 29 (Be / q): 16th century.
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.
  • EMML 2080 (Co2): Project of Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (15th/16th cent.).
  • Cambridge, University Library Add. 1570 (Ca): Dated 1588–1589.

2. Family $G^2$ (Eth II): The vulgate / learned secondary recension (17th–18th cent.), smoothed and harmonized by Ethiopian scribes:

  • Oxford, Bodleian Bruce 74 (Ox2 / b) and Bodleian Or. 531 (Ox1 / a): 18th century.
  • London, BL MS Or. 8822 (Lo1 / d, olim Curzon 55) and BL Add. 24185 (Lo3 / f).
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

D. Latin, Syriac, and Coptic Fragments

1. Latin:

  • London, BL MS Royal 5 E XIII, fols. 79v–80r (8th cent. CE): Contains 1 Enoch 106:1–18 (the miraculous birth of Noah, discovered and edited by M. R. James, 1893).
  • Pseudo-Cyprian, Ad Novatianum 16.5 (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9).
  • Tertullian (De idololatria 4.2–3, 15.6; De cultu feminarum 1.3, 2.10).

2. Syriac:

  • Chronicle of Michael the Syrian I.4 (ed. Chabot 1899; Brock 1968), preserving an excerpt of 1 Enoch 6:1–7.

3. Coptic:

  • Papyrus fragment from Antinoë (discovered 1937, ed. Donadoni 1960), preserving 1 Enoch 93:3–8 in Sahidic.
  • Related Coptic Enochic fragments (ed. Pearson 1976).

title: Qumran. Dicta Michael (4Q529, 6Q23) (aramaice)
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

1. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36): Early Hellenistic period (3rd cent. BCE). Relates the rebellion of the Watchers (the angels led by Shemihazah and Asael, Gen 6:1–4), Enoch's intercession, and his cosmic journeys through the earth and heavens.

2. The Book of Parables / Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71): Late 1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE. Contains three parables centering on the eschatological figures of the Righteous One, Chosen One, and "Son of Man" (identified with Enoch in ch. 71). Absent from the Qumran Aramaic corpus.

3. The Astronomical Book / Book of the Heavenly Luminaries (1 Enoch 72–82): The oldest Enochic composition (late 3rd cent. BCE or earlier). Details the 364-day solar calendar, lunar phases, and cosmic gates revealed by the angel Uriel.

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).

A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q201 (4QEn$^a$ ar): 4Q Enoch$^a$ (early 2nd cent. BCE; Watchers).
  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

  • Oxford, Bodleian Bruce 74 (Ox2 / b) and Bodleian Or. 531 (Ox1 / a): 18th century.

  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

title: Henoch slauicus
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
2 Enoch (The Book of the Holy Secrets of Enoch, or Slavonic Enoch) is an ancient pseudepigraphic apocalypse preserved exclusively in Old Church Slavonic manuscripts. Composed originally in Greek (likely based on Semitic traditions or a Semitic Vorlage) in the late 1st century CE in Hellenistic Jewish circles (often situated in Alexandria, Egypt), the work is divided into four main sections:

1. Enoch’s Heavenly Ascent (chs. 1–21): Enoch is awakened by two radiant angels and taken on a journey through the seven heavens (extended to ten heavens in the longer recension), observing celestial meteorology, astronomical bodies, fallen angels and Watchers (Grigori) imprisoned in the second and fifth heavens, paradise in the third heaven, and the angelic hierarchies praising the divine throne.

2. The Revelation of Cosmic and Primordial Secrets (chs. 22–38): Enoch stands before God, is anointed with fragrant celestial oil by Michael, transformed into a glorious angelic being, and instructed by God and the recording angel Vereveil (Pravuil) in 360 books of cosmological, astronomical, and historical mysteries, including an esoteric cosmogony featuring the primeval beings Adoil (light) and Arkhas (darkness/matter), and the creation of Adam as a microcosm (ch. 30).

3. Enoch’s Admonition of His Children on Earth (chs. 39–67): Enoch returns to earth for thirty days to deliver moral instructions, ethical testaments, and warnings against sin, idolatry, and animal cruelty to his sons (Methuselah, Regim) and his household, before his final assumption to heaven.

4. The Sacerdotal Epilogue and the Miraculous Birth of Melchizedek (chs. 68–73): The priesthood of Methuselah and his nephew Nir; the miraculous conception of Nir’s elderly, barren wife Sopanim without sexual union; her sudden death and the post-mortem birth of a fully developed infant marked with the priestly seal (hieratikon sphragida) on his chest, named Melchizedek; and his assumption by Michael to the paradise of Eden to escape the impending Deluge.
details.manuscripts:
The text has been transmitted in over thirty known South Slavic (Bulgarian, Serbian) and East Slavic (Russian) manuscripts dating between the 14th and 18th centuries, categorized into two main recensions:

A. The Long Recension ($A$)

Characterized by expanded theological descriptions, astronomical tables, and the ten-heaven schema:

  • MS J (Sankt-Peterburg, Library of the Russian Academy of Sciences [BAN] 13.3.25; late 15th / early 16th cent. Russian manuscript; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • MS R (Belgrade, National Library of Serbia [NLB] 321; 16th cent. Serbian manuscript; destroyed during the bombing of Belgrade in April 1941; ed. Popov 1880, Sokolov 1899/1910).
  • MS P (Moscow, State Historical Museum [GIM], Khlyudov coll. 43; 17th cent. South Russian manuscript; ed. Popov 1880, Franko 1896).

B. The Short Recension ($B$)

Characterized by a more concise narrative, the seven-heaven schema, and often considered by modern critics to reflect a less interpolated form of the translation:

  • MS U (Moscow, GIM, Uvarov coll. 3/18; 16th cent.; base text of André Vaillant’s critical edition 1952).
  • MS A (Sankt-Peterburg, BAN 45.13.4; 16th cent.; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • MS B (Moscow, GIM, Barsov coll. 1515; 14th cent. Russian manuscript, the oldest extant manuscript; ed. Sokolov 1899/1910).
  • MS B$^2$ (Moscow, GIM, Barsov coll. 1516; 16th cent.).
  • MS N (Belgrade, NLB 151/443; 14th cent. Serbian manuscript; ed. Novaković 1884).
  • MS V (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. Slav. 125; 16th cent.).

C. Anthological and Chronographic Witnesses

  • MPr (Merilo Pravednoe / "The Just Balance", Moscow, Russian State Library [RGB], Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra [TSS] 15; 14th cent. legal-ethical florilegium; ed. Tikhomirov 1961, Schneider 1986).
  • Chr / Chr$^2$ (Russian chronographs; Nezhin, Historical-Philological Institute MS 39; Moscow, RGB Rumyantsev coll. 590; ed. Popov 1869).
  • Tr (Moscow, RGB, Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra MS 793; ed. Tikhonravov 1863).
  • TSS 253, 498, 682 (Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra manuscripts; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • G (Gennadius Bible extracts, Novgorod/Moscow, 1499).
  • Ms. No. 42 (Croatian Glagolitic apocryphal fragment on Melchizedek’s birth; ed. S. Ivšić 1930–1931).

title: Henoch hebraicus
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
3 Enoch (The Hebrew Apocalypse of Enoch, commonly titled in Jewish mystical manuscripts ספר היכלות [Sefer Hekhalot, "The Book of Palaces"]) is a major late antique Jewish visionary composition belonging to the Hekhalot and Merkabah mystical corpus. Compiled in Byzantine/early Islamic Palestine or Babylonia between the 5th and 7th centuries CE (incorporating earlier Tannaitic traditions from the 2nd–3rd centuries), the text bridges Second Temple apocalypticism and classical Rabbinic esotericism:

1. The Visionary Ascent of Rabbi Ishmael (chs. 1–2): Rabbi Ishmael ben Elisha ascends to the highest heavenly realm through contemplation of the Chariot (Merkabah), arrives at the entrance of the Seventh Heavenly Palace (Hekhal), and is delivered from hostile angels by the supreme archangel Metatron, the "Prince of the Divine Presence" (Sar ha-Panim).

2. The Metamorphosis of Enoch into Metatron (chs. 3–16): Metatron reveals his human origin as Enoch son of Jared, who was snatched from the corrupt generation of the Deluge (Gen 5:24) to serve as a perpetual witness. He describes his bodily transformation into fiery angelic matter, his reception of a celestial robe, a cosmic crown inscribed with the creative divine letters, seventy cosmic names corresponding to the names of God, and his installation on a throne alongside God as the "Lesser YHWH" (יהוה הקטן, YHWH ha-Qatan).

3. The Incident of Aher and the Demotion of Metatron (ch. 16): When the sage Elisha ben Abuyah ("Aher") enters paradise and sees Metatron seated upon a throne receiving celestial homage, he utters the heresy: "There are indeed two powers in heaven!" (Shtei reshuyot ba-shamayim). God orders the angel Anafiel to strike Metatron with sixty lashes of fire (pulsei de-nura) and force him to stand, proving his creaturely subordination (parallel to b. Hagigah 15a).

4. The Celestial Hierarchy, Angelology, and Cosmic Order (chs. 17–40): Detailed taxonomy of the angelic classes (Ophannim, Seraphim, Cherubim, Hayyot ha-Kodesh), their planetary governors, the angelic liturgy (Qedushah), and the river of fire (Nehar di-Nur) issuing from beneath the Throne.

5. Cosmic Eschatology, the Souls of the Righteous, and the Cosmic Curtain (chs. 41–48): Enoch-Metatron shows Rabbi Ishmael the storehouse of souls, the spirits of the unborn, the punishments of Gehenna, and the Pargod (the cosmic curtain hung before the Divine Throne), upon which are woven all generations of world history from creation to the Messianic redemption.
details.manuscripts:
The textual transmission of 3 Enoch is fluid and complex, preserved as part of larger Hekhalot miscellanies in medieval Ashkenazi, Sephardic, and Italian manuscripts:

A. Primary Hebrew Manuscripts

  • MS B (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Opp. Add. 4to 45; Neubauer 1656): 16th-century manuscript; selected by Philip S. Alexander as the base text for his critical English translation in OTP 1.
  • MS A (Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Cod. ebr. 228): 14th century; the oldest dated continuous manuscript witness of the work; transcribed synoptically in Peter Schäfer’s Synopse zur Hekhalot-Literatur (§§1–80).
  • MS E (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod. hebr. 40): 15th-century Ashkenazi manuscript; transcribed by Adolph Jellinek in Bet ha-Midrasch and by Schäfer in the Synopse.
  • MS C (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Mich. 175; Neubauer 1657): 16th century; preserves long recensional variants in chs. 15B and 22B–C.
  • MS D (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Opp. 241; Neubauer 1653): 16th century.
  • MS F (London, British Library, MS Add. 27199; Margoliouth 751): 16th century.
  • MS G (London, British Library, MS Add. 15299; Margoliouth 752): 15th/16th century.
  • MS K (Cambridge, University Library, Add. 175): 16th century.
  • MS L (Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 44.13): 15th century.
  • MSS Wert (Jerusalem, collection of Shelomo Aharon Wertheimer): Printed in Batei Midrashot, preserving chs. 23–24 and the distinct Alphabet of Metatron (ch. 48B–D).

title: Historia Henoch et Eliae (latine)
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 15 (1 Enoch / History of Enoch and Elijah)

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

1. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36): Early Hellenistic period (3rd cent. BCE). Relates the rebellion of the Watchers (the angels led by Shemihazah and Asael, Gen 6:1–4), Enoch's intercession, and his cosmic journeys through the earth and heavens.

2. The Book of Parables / Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71): Late 1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE. Contains three parables centering on the eschatological figures of the Righteous One, Chosen One, and "Son of Man" (identified with Enoch in ch. 71). Absent from the Qumran Aramaic corpus.

3. The Astronomical Book / Book of the Heavenly Luminaries (1 Enoch 72–82): The oldest Enochic composition (late 3rd cent. BCE or earlier). Details the 364-day solar calendar, lunar phases, and cosmic gates revealed by the angel Uriel.

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).
details.manuscripts:
A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q201 (4QEn$^a$ ar): 4Q Enoch$^a$ (early 2nd cent. BCE; Watchers).
  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr$^c$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • Crucial Finding: No manuscript traces of the Parables of Enoch (chs. 37–71) have been found at Qumran; instead, the Cave 4 library preserved multiple copies of the Book of Giants (see §7 below).

B. Greek Tradition

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

  • 6th-century CE codex discovered in a Christian monk's tomb at Akhmim in 1886–1887.
  • Contains two distinct copies: GrP$^1$ (1 Enoch 1:1–32:6) and GrP$^2$ (1 Enoch 19:3–21:9).

2. Chester Beatty Papyrus 185 (Chester Beatty XII + Michigan Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE papyrus codex leaves.
  • Preserves 1 Enoch 97:6–104:13 and 106:1–107:3 (lacking ch. 105 and 108), followed directly by Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha.

3. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus XVII 2069:

  • Late 4th-century CE papyrus fragments containing 1 Enoch 77:7–78:1, 78:8, 85:10–86:2, 87:1–3.

4. Vatican Greek 1809:

  • 11th-century CE tachygraphic parchment manuscript containing 1 Enoch 89:42–49.

5. Georgius Syncellus, Chronographia (ed. Mosshammer 1984):

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

6. Qumran Cave 7 Greek Fragments (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12):

  • Proposed by E. A. Muro Jr. (1997) and É. Puech (1997) as fragments of Greek 1 Enoch 103:3–4, 7–8, refuting J. O'Callaghan's 1 Timothy hypothesis.

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

Preserved in over 40 known manuscripts cataloged from the 15th through 19th centuries, classified into two genealogical families:

1. Family $G^1$ (Eth I): The older, unrevised textual recension (15th–16th cent.), exhibiting closest affinity to the Greek Vorlage:

  • Tānāsee 9 (TS): Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9 (15th cent.; complete 1–108).
  • London, BL MS Or. 485 (Lo4 / g): 16th century (base text for Knibb).
  • Berlin, Staatsbibliothek Petermann II, Nachtrag 29 (Be / q): 16th century.
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.
  • EMML 2080 (Co2): Project of Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (15th/16th cent.).
  • Cambridge, University Library Add. 1570 (Ca): Dated 1588–1589.

2. Family $G^2$ (Eth II): The vulgate / learned secondary recension (17th–18th cent.), smoothed and harmonized by Ethiopian scribes:

  • Oxford, Bodleian Bruce 74 (Ox2 / b) and Bodleian Or. 531 (Ox1 / a): 18th century.
  • London, BL MS Or. 8822 (Lo1 / d, olim Curzon 55) and BL Add. 24185 (Lo3 / f).
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

D. Latin, Syriac, and Coptic Fragments

1. Latin:

  • London, BL MS Royal 5 E XIII, fols. 79v–80r (8th cent. CE): Contains 1 Enoch 106:1–18 (the miraculous birth of Noah, discovered and edited by M. R. James, 1893).
  • Pseudo-Cyprian, Ad Novatianum 16.5 (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9).
  • Tertullian (De idololatria 4.2–3, 15.6; De cultu feminarum 1.3, 2.10).

2. Syriac:

  • Chronicle of Michael the Syrian I.4 (ed. Chabot 1899; Brock 1968), preserving an excerpt of 1 Enoch 6:1–7.

3. Coptic:

  • Papyrus fragment from Antinoë (discovered 1937, ed. Donadoni 1960), preserving 1 Enoch 93:3–8 in Sahidic.
  • Related Coptic Enochic fragments (ed. Pearson 1976).

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).

A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr$^c$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

2. Chester Beatty Papyrus 185 (Chester Beatty XII + Michigan Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE papyrus codex leaves.
  • Preserves 1 Enoch 97:6–104:13 and 106:1–107:3 (lacking ch. 105 and 108), followed directly by Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha.

3. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus XVII 2069:

  • Late 4th-century CE papyrus fragments containing 1 Enoch 77:7–78:1, 78:8, 85:10–86:2, 87:1–3.

4. Vatican Greek 1809:

  • 11th-century CE tachygraphic parchment manuscript containing 1 Enoch 89:42–49.

5. Georgius Syncellus, Chronographia (ed. Mosshammer 1984):

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.

  • London, BL MS Or. 8822 (Lo1 / d, olim Curzon 55) and BL Add. 24185 (Lo3 / f).
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

  • Pseudo-Cyprian, Ad Novatianum 16.5 (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9).
  • Tertullian (De idololatria 4.2–3, 15.6; De cultu feminarum 1.3, 2.10).

2. Syriac:

  • Chronicle of Michael the Syrian I.4 (ed. Chabot 1899; Brock 1968), preserving an excerpt of 1 Enoch 6:1–7.

3. Coptic:

  • Papyrus fragment from Antinoë (discovered 1937, ed. Donadoni 1960), preserving 1 Enoch 93:3–8 in Sahidic.
  • Related Coptic Enochic fragments (ed. Pearson 1976).

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

6. Qumran Cave 7 Greek Fragments (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12):

  • Proposed by E. A. Muro Jr. (1997) and É. Puech (1997) as fragments of Greek 1 Enoch 103:3–4, 7–8, refuting J. O'Callaghan's 1 Timothy hypothesis.

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

Preserved in over 40 known manuscripts cataloged from the 15th through 19th centuries, classified into two genealogical families:

1. Family $G^1$ (Eth I): The older, unrevised textual recension (15th–16th cent.), exhibiting closest affinity to the Greek Vorlage:

  • Tānāsee 9 (TS): Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9 (15th cent.; complete 1–108).
  • London, BL MS Or. 485 (Lo4 / g): 16th century (base text for Knibb).
  • Berlin, Staatsbibliothek Petermann II, Nachtrag 29 (Be / q): 16th century.
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.
  • EMML 2080 (Co2): Project of Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (15th/16th cent.).
  • Cambridge, University Library Add. 1570 (Ca): Dated 1588–1589.

2. Family $G^2$ (Eth II): The vulgate / learned secondary recension (17th–18th cent.), smoothed and harmonized by Ethiopian scribes:

  • Oxford, Bodleian Bruce 74 (Ox2 / b) and Bodleian Or. 531 (Ox1 / a): 18th century.
  • London, BL MS Or. 8822 (Lo1 / d, olim Curzon 55) and BL Add. 24185 (Lo3 / f).
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 35 (Pa3 / t) and BnF éth. 50 (Pa7 / z).

D. Latin, Syriac, and Coptic Fragments

1. Latin:

  • London, BL MS Royal 5 E XIII, fols. 79v–80r (8th cent. CE): Contains 1 Enoch 106:1–18 (the miraculous birth of Noah, discovered and edited by M. R. James, 1893).
  • Pseudo-Cyprian, Ad Novatianum 16.5 (quoting 1 Enoch 1:9).
  • Tertullian (De idololatria 4.2–3, 15.6; De cultu feminarum 1.3, 2.10).

2. Syriac:

  • Chronicle of Michael the Syrian I.4 (ed. Chabot 1899; Brock 1968), preserving an excerpt of 1 Enoch 6:1–7.

3. Coptic:

  • Papyrus fragment from Antinoë (discovered 1937, ed. Donadoni 1960), preserving 1 Enoch 93:3–8 in Sahidic.
  • Related Coptic Enochic fragments (ed. Pearson 1976).

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 16 (2 Enoch / Priestly Epilogue (Methuselah, Nir, Melchizedek))

details.intro:
2 Enoch (The Book of the Holy Secrets of Enoch, or Slavonic Enoch) is an ancient pseudepigraphic apocalypse preserved exclusively in Old Church Slavonic manuscripts. Composed originally in Greek (likely based on Semitic traditions or a Semitic Vorlage) in the late 1st century CE in Hellenistic Jewish circles (often situated in Alexandria, Egypt), the work is divided into four main sections:

1. Enoch’s Heavenly Ascent (chs. 1–21): Enoch is awakened by two radiant angels and taken on a journey through the seven heavens (extended to ten heavens in the longer recension), observing celestial meteorology, astronomical bodies, fallen angels and Watchers (Grigori) imprisoned in the second and fifth heavens, paradise in the third heaven, and the angelic hierarchies praising the divine throne.

2. The Revelation of Cosmic and Primordial Secrets (chs. 22–38): Enoch stands before God, is anointed with fragrant celestial oil by Michael, transformed into a glorious angelic being, and instructed by God and the recording angel Vereveil (Pravuil) in 360 books of cosmological, astronomical, and historical mysteries, including an esoteric cosmogony featuring the primeval beings Adoil (light) and Arkhas (darkness/matter), and the creation of Adam as a microcosm (ch. 30).

3. Enoch’s Admonition of His Children on Earth (chs. 39–67): Enoch returns to earth for thirty days to deliver moral instructions, ethical testaments, and warnings against sin, idolatry, and animal cruelty to his sons (Methuselah, Regim) and his household, before his final assumption to heaven.

4. The Sacerdotal Epilogue and the Miraculous Birth of Melchizedek (chs. 68–73): The priesthood of Methuselah and his nephew Nir; the miraculous conception of Nir’s elderly, barren wife Sopanim without sexual union; her sudden death and the post-mortem birth of a fully developed infant marked with the priestly seal (hieratikon sphragida) on his chest, named Melchizedek; and his assumption by Michael to the paradise of Eden to escape the impending Deluge.
details.manuscripts:
The text has been transmitted in over thirty known South Slavic (Bulgarian, Serbian) and East Slavic (Russian) manuscripts dating between the 14th and 18th centuries, categorized into two main recensions:

A. The Long Recension ($A$)

Characterized by expanded theological descriptions, astronomical tables, and the ten-heaven schema:

  • MS J (Sankt-Peterburg, Library of the Russian Academy of Sciences [BAN] 13.3.25; late 15th / early 16th cent. Russian manuscript; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • MS R (Belgrade, National Library of Serbia [NLB] 321; 16th cent. Serbian manuscript; destroyed during the bombing of Belgrade in April 1941; ed. Popov 1880, Sokolov 1899/1910).
  • MS P (Moscow, State Historical Museum [GIM], Khlyudov coll. 43; 17th cent. South Russian manuscript; ed. Popov 1880, Franko 1896).

B. The Short Recension ($B$)

Characterized by a more concise narrative, the seven-heaven schema, and often considered by modern critics to reflect a less interpolated form of the translation:

  • MS U (Moscow, GIM, Uvarov coll. 3/18; 16th cent.; base text of André Vaillant’s critical edition 1952).
  • MS A (Sankt-Peterburg, BAN 45.13.4; 16th cent.; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • MS B (Moscow, GIM, Barsov coll. 1515; 14th cent. Russian manuscript, the oldest extant manuscript; ed. Sokolov 1899/1910).
  • MS B$^2$ (Moscow, GIM, Barsov coll. 1516; 16th cent.).
  • MS N (Belgrade, NLB 151/443; 14th cent. Serbian manuscript; ed. Novaković 1884).
  • MS V (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. Slav. 125; 16th cent.).

C. Anthological and Chronographic Witnesses

  • MPr (Merilo Pravednoe / "The Just Balance", Moscow, Russian State Library [RGB], Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra [TSS] 15; 14th cent. legal-ethical florilegium; ed. Tikhomirov 1961, Schneider 1986).
  • Chr / Chr$^2$ (Russian chronographs; Nezhin, Historical-Philological Institute MS 39; Moscow, RGB Rumyantsev coll. 590; ed. Popov 1869).
  • Tr (Moscow, RGB, Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra MS 793; ed. Tikhonravov 1863).
  • TSS 253, 498, 682 (Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra manuscripts; ed. Sokolov 1910).
  • G (Gennadius Bible extracts, Novgorod/Moscow, 1499).
  • Ms. No. 42 (Croatian Glagolitic apocryphal fragment on Melchizedek’s birth; ed. S. Ivšić 1930–1931).

title: Qumran. Apocryphon Genesis (1Q20) (aramaice)
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
The Book of Jubilees (Liber Iubilaeorum / The Little Genesis / Leptogenesis / Ge'ez: መጽሐፈ ፡ ኩፋሌ Mashafa Kufale ["Book of Divisions"]) is one of the monumental masterworks of Second Temple Jewish literature. Composed in Hebrew between 160 and 150 BCE in Judea (early Maccabean / Hasmonean era) by a priestly scribe aligned with proto-Essenic / Enochic circles, the work rewitnesses and rewrites Genesis 1 through Exodus 12 within a rigid chronological, halakhic, and theological framework:

1. The Sinai Frame Narrative (ch. 1): During Moses’ forty days and nights on Mount Sinai, God commands the Angel of the Presence (Mal'akh ha-Panim) to dictate the primordial history of the world and the eternal laws inscribed upon the "Heavenly Tablets" (Luhot ha-Shamayim).

2. The Sabbatical Jubilee Chronology: Sacred history from the six days of Creation to Israel's arrival at the Jordan is measured into exactly fifty Jubilees of forty-nine years each ($50 \times 49 = 2,450$ years). Every biblical event (the Fall, the Flood, the births and deaths of the patriarchs, the Exodus) is assigned a precise date by Jubilee, week of years ($7$ years), and year within the week.

3. The 364-Day Solar Calendar (chs. 4, 6): The text mounts an uncompromising polemic against the 354-day lunar calendar used by the Hellenistic Seleucid empire and mainstream temple circles. The true divine year comprises exactly 52 weeks (364 days), divided into four quarters of 91 days ($13 \times 7$), ensuring that holy days, Sabbaths, and festivals never drift or fall on unauthorized days.

4. Retrojection of Mosaic Halakhah to the Patriarchs: The commandments of the Torah are depicted as eternal cosmic ordinances practiced in heaven by the angels and revealed to the pre-Sinaitic righteous:

  • Adam observes the purification laws of childbirth (ch. 3);
  • Noah institutes the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot) to commemorate the cosmic covenant and is instructed in medicinal herbs to ward off demonic diseases (chs. 6, 10);
  • Abraham celebrates the Feast of Booths (Sukkot) and the first fruits, practices circumcision, and shuns exogamy and idolatry (chs. 16, 21);
  • Jacob institutes the tithes and the Day of Atonement (chs. 32, 34).

5. Cosmic Dualism, Angels, and Mastema: The cosmos is divided between the holy angels (the Angels of the Presence and Angels of Sanctification, created on the first day) and the demonic realm. After the fall of the Watchers (chs. 4–5) and their imprisonment in the depths of the earth, Prince Mastema (the chief of evil spirits) petitions God to retain one-tenth of the disembodied spirits of the giants to tempt and punish wicked humanity, while nine-tenths are cast into the pit of condemnation (ch. 10).

6. Sacred Geography (chs. 8–9): Noah divides the earth by lot among his three sons (Shem, Ham, Japheth) under solemn oaths. Mount Zion is identified as the cosmic center and "navel of the earth" (omphalos gēs), paired with the Garden of Eden and Mount Sinai as the three holy sanctuaries of God.
details.manuscripts:
A. Hebrew Dead Sea Scrolls (Original Hebrew Text)

The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls confirmed that Hebrew was the original language of Jubilees. Over fifteen fragmentary Hebrew manuscripts were recovered from five caves at Qumran:

  • Cave 1: 1Q17 (1QJub$^a$), 1Q18 (1QJub$^b$) (ed. J. T. Milik, DJD 1, 1955).
  • Cave 2: 2Q19 (2QJub$^a$), 2Q20 (2QJub$^b$) (ed. M. Baillet, DJD 3, 1962).
  • Cave 3: 3Q5 (3QJub) (ed. M. Baillet, DJD 3, 1962).
  • Cave 4: The largest collection, dating from ca. 125 BCE to 50 CE:
  • 4Q216 (4QJub$^a$): Late 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls; chs. 1–2).
  • 4Q217 (4QpapJub$^b$?): Papyrus manuscript.
  • 4Q218 (4QJub$^c$); 4Q219 (4QJub$^d$); 4Q220 (4QJub$^e$); 4Q221 (4QJub$^f$); 4Q222 (4QJub$^g$); 4Q223–224 (4QpapJub$^h$).
  • Cave 11: 11Q12 (11QJub) (ed. F. García Martínez et al., DJD 23, 1998).
  • Canonical Status at Qumran: Cited as an authoritative, inspired text in the Damascus Document (CD 16:2–4: "the Book of the Divisions of the Times into their Jubilees and Weeks").

B. Ethiopic (Ge'ez: Mashafa Kufale)

The only textual witness preserving the entire work complete from beginning to end. Preserved in 19 known manuscripts, classified into two major families:

  • Group 1 (Older, Superior Recension; 15th–16th cent.):
  • MS A (Paris, BnF, MS éth. 51, fols. 1r–55v): 15th century.
  • MS B (Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9): 15th century.
  • Tübingen MSS (collated by Ewald).
  • Group 2 (Later, Secondary Recension; 17th–18th cent.):
  • MS C (London, British Library, MS Add. 16188).
  • MS D (London, British Library, MS Or. 485).
  • Critical Editions: August Dillmann (1859); R. H. Charles (1895); James C. VanderKam (CSCO 510–511, 1989).

C. Latin Tradition (Parva Genesis)

  • Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS C. 73 inf. (5th/6th cent. CE uncial palimpsest):
  • Preserves approximately one-third of the text in an ancient Old Latin translation made directly from the Greek Vorlage.
  • Discovered and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani, Monumenta Sacra et Profana 1 (Milan, 1861), pp. 15–54; reedited with exhaustive commentary by Hermann Rönsch (1874).

D. Greek Fragments and External Citations

  • Preserved in extensive excerpts in the Byzantine chronicles of Georgius Syncellus, Georgius Cedrenus, the Chronicon Paschale, and patristic catenae on Genesis; cited also by Epiphanius (Panarion 39.6).
  • Editions: R. H. Charles (1902); Albert-Marie Denis, PVTG 3 (1970).

E. Syriac Fragments

  • Excerpts preserved in London, BL MS Add. 12154 (8th cent. CE), the anonymous Chronicle of 846, and the chronicle of Michael the Syrian (ed. Ceriani, Baumstark).

title: Qumran. Apocalypsis Noe (1Q19, 1Q19bis, 4Q534, 4Q535, 4Q536) (hebraice et aramaice)
section: POSTERI ADAE ET EVAE: ENOSH, HENOCH, LAMECH, NOE, SEM, CHAM

details.intro:
1 Enoch is a vast composite apocalypse formed of five originally distinct tractates (the "Enochic Pentateuch"), preserved complete only in the classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic) canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, but rooted in ancient Aramaic and Greek precursors dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE:

1. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36): Early Hellenistic period (3rd cent. BCE). Relates the rebellion of the Watchers (the angels led by Shemihazah and Asael, Gen 6:1–4), Enoch's intercession, and his cosmic journeys through the earth and heavens.

2. The Book of Parables / Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71): Late 1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE. Contains three parables centering on the eschatological figures of the Righteous One, Chosen One, and "Son of Man" (identified with Enoch in ch. 71). Absent from the Qumran Aramaic corpus.

3. The Astronomical Book / Book of the Heavenly Luminaries (1 Enoch 72–82): The oldest Enochic composition (late 3rd cent. BCE or earlier). Details the 364-day solar calendar, lunar phases, and cosmic gates revealed by the angel Uriel.

4. The Book of Dream-Visions / Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 83–90): Early Maccabean era (ca. 165–160 BCE). Features the vision of the Deluge (chs. 83–84) and the allegorical Animal Apocalypse (chs. 85–90), depicting sacred history from Adam to Judas Maccabeus (the horned ram) and the New Jerusalem.

5. The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108): 2nd cent. BCE. Contains ethical exhortations and eschatological woes against sinners, incorporating the archaic Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17), the birth and wondrous signs of Noah (chs. 106–107), and an appended concluding vision (ch. 108).
details.manuscripts:
A. Aramaic Tradition (Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran Cave 4)

The primary Vorlage of 1 Enoch survived in eleven fragmentary Aramaic manuscripts discovered in Cave 4 at Qumran, copied between the early 2nd century BCE and the late 1st century BCE:

  • 4Q201 (4QEn$^a$ ar): 4Q Enoch$^a$ (early 2nd cent. BCE; Watchers).
  • 4Q202 (4QEn$^b$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Watchers.
  • 4Q204 (4QEn$^c$ ar): Late 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle, and Noah fragments.
  • 4Q205 (4QEn$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, Epistle.
  • 4Q206 (4QEn$^e$ ar): Early 1st cent. BCE; Watchers, Dream-Visions, and Book of Giants.
  • 4Q207 (4QEn$^f$ ar): Mid-2nd cent. BCE; Dream-Visions.
  • 4Q212 (4QEn$^g$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE; Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks.
  • Astronomical Manuscripts:
  • 4Q208 (4QEnastr$^a$ ar): Late 3rd or early 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls at Qumran).
  • 4Q209 (4QEnastr$^b$ ar): Early 1st cent. CE.
  • 4Q210 (4QEnastr$^c$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • 4Q211 (4QEnastr$^d$ ar): Mid-1st cent. BCE.
  • Crucial Finding: No manuscript traces of the Parables of Enoch (chs. 37–71) have been found at Qumran; instead, the Cave 4 library preserved multiple copies of the Book of Giants (see §7 below).

B. Greek Tradition

1. Codex Panopolitanus (Akhmim / Gizeh Papyrus; Cairo, Egyptian Museum JE 10759 / P. Cair. 10759):

  • 6th-century CE codex discovered in a Christian monk's tomb at Akhmim in 1886–1887.
  • Contains two distinct copies: GrP$^1$ (1 Enoch 1:1–32:6) and GrP$^2$ (1 Enoch 19:3–21:9).

2. Chester Beatty Papyrus 185 (Chester Beatty XII + Michigan Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE papyrus codex leaves.
  • Preserves 1 Enoch 97:6–104:13 and 106:1–107:3 (lacking ch. 105 and 108), followed directly by Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha.

3. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus XVII 2069:

  • Late 4th-century CE papyrus fragments containing 1 Enoch 77:7–78:1, 78:8, 85:10–86:2, 87:1–3.

4. Vatican Greek 1809:

  • 11th-century CE tachygraphic parchment manuscript containing 1 Enoch 89:42–49.

5. Georgius Syncellus, Chronographia (ed. Mosshammer 1984):

  • 9th-century Byzantine chronicle citing two extensive extracts: GrS$^1$ (1 Enoch 6:1–9:4) and GrS$^2$ (1 Enoch 8:4–10:14).

6. Qumran Cave 7 Greek Fragments (7Q4, 7Q8, 7Q12):

  • Proposed by E. A. Muro Jr. (1997) and É. Puech (1997) as fragments of Greek 1 Enoch 103:3–4, 7–8, refuting J. O'Callaghan's 1 Timothy hypothesis.

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

Preserved in over 40 known manuscripts cataloged from the 15th through 19th centuries, classified into two genealogical families:

1. Family $G^1$ (Eth I): The older, unrevised textual recension (15th–16th cent.), exhibiting closest affinity to the Greek Vorlage:

  • Tānāsee 9 (TS): Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9 (15th cent.; complete 1–108).
  • London, BL MS Or. 485 (Lo4 / g): 16th century (base text for Knibb).
  • Berlin, Staatsbibliothek Petermann II, Nachtrag 29 (Be / q): 16th century.
  • Paris, BnF d'Abbadie 55 (Pa4 / u): 15th/16th century.
  • EMML 2080 (Co2): Project of Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library (15th/16th cent.).
  • Cambridge, University Library Add. 1570 (Ca): Dated 1588–1589.

2. Family $G^2$ (Eth II): The vulgate / learned secondary recension (17th–18th cent.), smoothed and harmonized by Ethiopian scribes:

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 3 (Testament of Abraham (Greek Recensions A and B))

details.intro: In the Testament of Abraham, Abraham refuses to surrender his soul to the archangel Michael. He is taken on a chariot tour of the inhabited world and sees the judgment of souls. In the end Death comes for him in disguise and takes him by deceit.
details.provenance: The work survives in Greek in a longer (A) and a shorter (B) recension, and in Coptic, Arabic, Ethiopic, Slavonic and Romanian versions. It is usually considered Jewish, from Egypt, around the 1st–2nd c. CE.

  • ** Does not include a critical Greek text, but does include separate French translations of the Testaments of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as preserved in Coptic (Bohairic), Ethiopic, and Arabic which are useful for those without a knowledge of those languages.
  • Denis, Concordance, 825-32.
  • F. Schmidt, Le Testament grec d'Abraham: Introduction, édition critique des deux recensions grecques, traduction (TSAJ 11: Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1986).
  • ** Currently the best text. Based on 23 mss of the long recension (A) and 9 mss of the short recension (B). Schmidt reports the existence of five more mss which he was unable to obtain in preparing his text, at least three of which seem to be mss of recension A (see p. 3). Given the extremely wide variation among the surviving manuscripts, even within each recension, Schmidt declined to reconstruct an eclectic text. Instead, for each textual family he prints in running form the text of one manuscript, providing an apparatus which lists all variants in the other mss of the family (only purely orthographic variants are excluded). Schmidt also sub-divides recension B into two ms families, providing separate texts for each family (mss EACDHI and mss BFG respectively). Schmidt's two texts of the short recension employ mss E and B respectively for their running texts and both differ substantially from James' text of the short recension. In his text of the long recension Schmidt employs ms A as his running text. Since this is the same ms which was employed by James as the basis of his eclectic text, Schmidt's running text of the long recension is much closer to that of James than is the case in the short recension. Schmidt retains the chapter divisions of James. In recension B he employs the verse divisions of P. Riessler, while the verse division in recension A are Schmidt's own work.

details.intro:
The Testament of Abraham is preserved primarily in Greek in two distinct recensions:

  • Recension A (Longer): A fuller, more elaborate narrative focusing on Abraham’s heavenly journey, the judgment of souls, and his refusal to yield his soul to Death.
  • Recension B (Shorter): A concise, more colloquial redaction with distinct apocalyptic and folkloric features.

Primary Greek Manuscripts

  • Recension A:
  • A: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS gr. 770 (dated 1304 CE).
  • B: Jerusalem, Greek Patriarchal Library, Saba 259 (11th c.).
  • C: Paris, BnF, MS gr. 1556 (15th c.).
  • D: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Canonici Greek 19 (15th c.).
  • Additional witnesses: Paris gr. 1313 (15th c.), Paris gr. 1613 (15th c.), Paris Suppl. gr. 162; Vienna theol. gr. 237.
  • Recension B:
  • E: Paris, BnF, MS gr. 1613 (15th c.).
  • F: Paris, BnF, MS gr. 1313 (15th c.).
  • M: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS gr. 405 (C 210 inf.; 13th c.) — collated by F. Schmidt.
  • Rome, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, MS Vat. gr. 1801 (15th c.).

Oriental and Slavonic Versions

  • Coptic:
  • Bohairic version: Rome, Vat. copt. 61, fols. 164v–189v (dated 961/2 CE), ed. I. Guidi (1900).
  • Sahidic fragments: Papyrus Köln Inv. Nr. 3221, noted by C. Römer, H. J. Thissen, and M. Weber.
  • Ethiopic (Ge’ez):
  • Falasha (Beta Israel) and Christian recensions: A. Z. Aešcoly (1951); M. Gaguine (1965).
  • Arabic:
  • Extant in multiple Karshuni and Christian Arabic collections (e.g. Dayr Anba Maqar; ed. W. E. Barnes 1892; catalogue by G. Graf 1944).
  • Church Slavonic and Romanian:
  • Romanian translation: Closely reflects Recension A (ed. M. Gaster 1893/1928).
  • South Slavic and East Slavic miscellanies (Sbornik of Tikveš, ed. V. Antik 1978; D. S. Cooper & H. B. Weber 1976; I. Franko 1896–1910; A. Ja. Jatsimirskij 1921).
  • Ukrainian redaction (Slovo o sviatom Avraame).

The Ladder of Jacob (Scala Jacobi / Old Church Slavonic: Лествица Иакова / Лествица Иаковля) is an early Jewish visionary pseudepigraphon expanding upon Jacob's dream at Bethel (Gen 28:10–22). Composed originally in Greek or a Semitic language (Hebrew/Aramaic) in late 1st-century CE Roman Palestine following the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE, the work is preserved primarily in Old Church Slavonic within the interpretive biblical miscellanies known as the Tolkovaya Paleya (Explanatory Palaia / Palaea Historica) and related florilegia:

1. The Vision of the Ladder and Heavenly Busts (ch. 1): Jacob sets a stone beneath his head at Bethel and dreams of a cosmic ladder of twelve steps extending into the heavens. On each step, he sees a human bust with two faces, while at the summit stands a fiery, transcendent bust resembling God (YHWH). Angels ascend and descend upon the rungs.

2. The Celestial Prayer of Jacob (ch. 2): Awakening in terror, Jacob pours oil upon the stone and recites an extraordinary liturgical hymn of praise to the Almighty God of fire, addressing Him with ancient Semitic mystical names (Sariel, Yahoel, El-El), celebrating God's throne of Cherubim and Seraphim, and begging for the interpretation of the dream.

3. The Descent and Revelation of Archangel Sariel (chs. 3–6): God commissions the archangel Sariel (the heavenly ruler who presides over visionary dreams) to descend to earth. Sariel changes Jacob’s name to Israel and discloses the mystical mystery: Jacob possesses a heavenly counterpart / angelic archetype whose celestial face is eternally engraved upon the Throne of Glory (Kisse ha-Kavod). Sariel then interprets the twelve steps of the ladder as twelve successive world epochs and foreign imperial dynasties. The four most ferocious steps represent the four kingdoms of Danielic prophecy (Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome), culminating in the desecration and destruction of the Temple by Rome and the subsequent eschatological judgment of the nations, the downfall of the fourth beast, and the gathering of Israel.

4. The Christian Christological Epilogue (ch. 7): A late antique or Byzantine Christian appendix (interpolated prior to or during the Slavonic transmission, drawing on the "Tale of Aphroditianus" / Religionsgespräch am Hof der Sasaniden) prophesying the miraculous virgin birth of Christ, the appearance of the star of Bethlehem to the Persian Magi, the conversion of the Gentiles, and the overthrow of pagan idols.

1. Recension A: The fuller, more expansive text:

  • MS S (Sankt-Peterburg, BAN, Solovki coll. 653/712): 15th-century manuscript; chosen by Horace G. Lunt as the base text for the standard English translation.

  • MS U (Moscow, State Historical Museum, Uvarov coll. 288): 16th century.

2. Recension B: A condensed recension preserving independent archaic readings:

  • MS K (Moscow, Kolomna MS 1406 / Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra): Dated 1406 CE (edited by I. Ia. Porfir'ev 1892).
  • MS M (Sankt-Peterburg, BAN, Solovki coll. 646/921): 15th century (edited by I. Ia. Porfir'ev 1877).
  • MS P (Sankt-Peterburg, Russian National Library, Pogodin coll. 1438): 16th century.
  • MSS V$^1$ and V$^2$ (Vilnius, Public Library MSS 115 and 116): 16th century.

3. Recension C: A very brief, epitomized excerpt contained in the Explanatory Palaia of 1414.

details.intro:
The Prayer of Jacob (Greek: Προσευχὴ Ἰακώβ / Latin: Precatio Iacobi) is a short, esoteric Jewish prayer preserved on a single Greek papyrus from late Roman Egypt (dating to the late 3rd or 4th century CE). Distinct from the Hebrew/Slavonic prayer preserved in chapter 2 of the Ladder of Jacob (CAVT No. 102), this text belongs to the syncretistic boundary between Hellenistic Jewish liturgical mysticism and magical papyrology:

1. Invocation of the Sovereign Creator (lines 1–7): The petitioner addresses the God who laid the foundations of the earth and established the stars, the Lord who sat upon Mount Sinai, the rider upon the Cherubim of glory, invoking Him by secret mystical permutations of the divine name (Iaō, Sabaōth, Adōnai, Eloē, Sahar, Ael, Abraō, Zeō, Ieō).

2. Self-Identification as the Angelic Israel (lines 8–15): The speaker identifies himself directly with the patriarch Jacob and claims a transcendent, pre-existent angelic status:

> "I, Jacob, who speak to you, am an earthly angel, an immortal dwelling upon the earth, created by you; [I am] Israel, an archangel of the power of the Lord, an arch-ruler of the hosts of God, a principal spirit!"

3. The Petition for Divine Wisdom and Secret Names (lines 16–22): The supplicant asks for divine illumination, purity of heart, and the revelation of the secret names of the heavenly powers, that the angelic rulers might obey his voice.

Theological Significance: The text provides crucial Hellenistic Egyptian evidence for angelomorphic human transformation and the angelic identity of the patriarch Jacob/Israel. It stands in direct conceptual continuity with the lost Second Temple Prayer of Joseph (Oratio Josephi, quoted by Origen, Commentarius in Johannem 2.31.188–190, where Jacob declares that he is the archangel Israel, the firstborn of all living creatures).
