details.intro: Joseph and Aseneth (CAVT 105) is a Greek narrative expanding Gen 41:45, where Pharaoh gives Joseph Aseneth, daughter of Potiphera priest of On, as his wife. Chapters 1–21 tell of Aseneth's rejection of her idols, her repentance, and her transformation through the visit of a heavenly man, followed by her marriage to Joseph. Chapters 22–29 narrate a plot by Pharaoh's son, aided by Dan and Gad, to abduct Aseneth, which is foiled by Benjamin, Levi and Simeon.
details.provenance: Most scholars place the work in Egyptian Judaism between the 1st c. BCE and the early 2nd c. CE, though a later date and Christian authorship have also been argued (R.S. Kraemer, When Aseneth Met Joseph, 1998). It survives in Greek in two main textual forms, a longer and a shorter, and in Syriac, Armenian, Latin, Serbian Slavonic, Modern Greek and Romanian versions.
details.manuscripts:
The work was translated into six ancient languages and enjoyed enormous popularity throughout the Byzantine, Syriac, and medieval Latin worlds:

A. Greek Tradition

Preserved in sixteen manuscripts classified into four distinct recensional families ($a, b, c, d$):

  • Family $a$ (Longer Recension): Best preserves the original semitizing Greek narrative style:
  • MS A (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. gr. 364, fols. 223r–243v): 11th/12th century; base text of Batiffol's editio princeps.
  • MS C (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Barocci 148, fols. 75v–92v): 15th-century manuscript containing five famous full-page color miniatures illustrating the narrative.
  • MS O (Sinai, Saint Catherine’s Monastery, MS gr. 504): 10th century; the oldest extant Greek witness.
  • MS P (Mount Athos, Konstamonitou Monastery 14): 15th century.
  • MS Q (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. Palatinus gr. 364): 15th century.
  • MS R (Sinai, Saint Catherine’s Monastery, MS gr. 530): 15th/16th century.
  • Family $b$ (Shorter Recension): Smoothed, classicizing text chosen by Marc Philonenko:
  • MS E (Mount Athos, Vatopedi Monastery 600): 15th century.
  • MS F (Bucharest, Romanian Academy MS gr. 966): 17th century.
  • MS G (Greeley Collection, MS McKell): ca. 1580 CE; illustrated.
  • MS W (Sinai, Saint Catherine’s Monastery, MS gr. 1976): 17th century.
  • Family $c$: Late text represented in Jerusalem Patriarchate MSS (Panhagios Taphos 73, Saba 1802).
  • Family $d$: Mixed branch: MS B (Vat. Pal. gr. 17; 11th cent.) and MS D (Bodleian Barocci 147; 15th cent.).

B. Syriac Tradition

  • Preserved in the 6th-century historical chronicle of Pseudo-Zacharias Rhetor (Historia Ecclesiastica 1.6; London, BL MS Add. 17202, copied ca. 569 CE).
  • Translated from Greek into Syriac in 559 CE by Moses of Ingila; provides the earliest fixed historical anchor for the Greek text (ed. J. P. N. Land 1870; E. W. Brooks 1919).

C. Latin Tradition

  • Recension L$^1$: Translated from a Greek Family $a$ manuscript in the late 12th century; preserved in nine manuscripts (e.g., Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 288). Incorporated and epitomized by Vincent of Beauvais in his monumental encyclopedia Speculum Historiale (ca. 1250 CE, Book 1, chs. 118–124).
  • Recension L$^2$: Independent 15th-century Renaissance humanist translation.

D. Armenian Tradition

  • Preserved in 45 manuscripts classified into six groups, translated from an early Greek recension between the 5th and 7th centuries CE (ed. Yovsēp'ianc' 1896; Christoph Burchard).

E. Slavonic, Ethiopic, Romanian, and Middle English Versions

  • Preserved in medieval Old Church Slavonic manuscripts (ed. I. Franko; S. Novaković); Ethiopic Ge'ez florilegia; and an early Middle English poetic paraphrase.

details.intro:
The Prayer of Joseph (Oratio Josephi / Προσευχὴ Ἰωσήφ) is an enigmatic Jewish-Hellenistic visionary work composed in Greek between the late 1st century BCE and the early 2nd century CE (ca. 70–130 CE), almost certainly in Roman Egypt or Syria. According to the Byzantine canon lists (Stichometry of Nicephorus, Synopsis of Pseudo-Athanasius, List of Sixty Books), the complete work originally comprised 1,100 stichoi (lines). Although the continuous text has perished, three extensive fragments survive as quotations in the theological treatises of Origen of Alexandria:

The Surviving Fragments

1. Fragment A (apud Origen, Commentarius in Johannem 2.31.188–190):

  • The patriarch Jacob speaks in the first person, revealing his primordial celestial identity:

> "I, Jacob, whom men call Jacob, but whose name is Israel, am an angel of God and a principal power (archikē dynamis), and Abraham and Isaac were created before every work. But I, Jacob, whom men call Jacob, my name is Israel, whom God called Israel, 'a man seeing God' (anēr horōn theon), because I am the firstborn of every creature (prōtogonos pantos zōou) animated by God!"

  • Jacob describes his descent from the heavenly realm to earthly embodiment and his confrontation with the archangel Uriel at the river Jabbok (Gen 32:24–30):

> "And when I was coming from Syrian Mesopotamia, Uriel the angel of God came forth and said: 'I have descended to earth and tabernacled among men, and I am called by the name of Jacob.' He was envious of me and wrestled with me. And I told him his name and what rank he holds among the sons of God: 'Are you not Uriel, the eighth after me? And am I not Israel, an archangel of the power of the Lord and a chief captain among the sons of God? Am I not Israel, the first minister before the face of God?' And I invoked my inextinguishable Name!"

2. Fragment B (apud Origen, Philocalia 23.15; preserved also in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica 6.11.64; Latin translation in Procopius of Gaza, Commentarius in Genesin 29):

  • Jacob reads the heavenly tablets / cosmic books of heaven, unrolling the future events, trials, and destinies of humankind.

3. Fragment C (apud Origen, Philocalia 23.19):

  • Origen summarizes and paraphrases Fragment A, confirming the angelic status of Jacob and citing Fragment B on the heavenly tablets.

Theological Significance: The Prayer of Joseph is of foundational importance for the history of ancient religions, witnessing to an extraordinary Jewish angelomorphic theology wherein a human patriarch is revealed as the primordial, pre-existent chief archangel of God (prōtogonos / "firstborn of all creation"). This concept provides an indispensable historical bridge between early Jewish wisdom/angelology and the Christological hymns of the New Testament (Col 1:15–18; Phil 2:6–11; John 1:1–18; Heb 1:5–6).

details.intro:
Introduction

The Prayer of Joseph (Oratio Josephi; CAVT 107; CANT 351) is a Jewish pseudepigraphon preserved only in patristic citations, most notably by Origen (Commentarium in Evangelium Johannis II.31 [188-190] and Philocalia XXIII.15, 19). It portrays the patriarch Jacob as the archangel Israel, an archangelic leader and first-begotten of all creation.

details.intro:
The History of Joseph (Historia Josephi / Ἱστορία Ἰωσήφ) is a fragmentary Jewish-Hellenistic narrative composed in Greek during the late Hellenistic or early Roman imperial period (ca. 1st cent. BCE to 2nd cent. CE) in Egypt. Expanding upon the biblical Joseph cycle (Gen 37–50), the work relates an uncanonical, embellished account of Joseph's dreams, his sale into Egypt, his endurance in Potiphar's house, his exaltation as vizier, and his filial piety toward Jacob:

  • The Greek Papyrus Fragments:
  • The primary Greek text survives on two sets of 4th/5th-century CE papyrus fragments from the Fayum (now in London and Oxford).
  • The fragments narrate the dialogue of Jacob mourning Joseph, Joseph's prayer while being carried off by the Ishmaelites, and Joseph's refusal to succumb to the enticements of Potiphar's wife, framing Joseph as an exemplar of chastity, divine wisdom, and prophetic foresight.
  • Related Oriental Traditions:
  • The Greek narrative is closely affiliated with extensive late antique and medieval oriental traditions, including the Coptic Narratio Ioseph and the Ethiopic and Arabic Historia Joseph filii Jacob, which preserve elaborated cycles of Joseph's life, death, and assumption.

details.intro:
The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs is an extensive pseudepigraphon consisting of twelve farewell discourses delivered on their deathbeds by the twelve sons of Jacob (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, and Benjamin) to their assembled children.

Structure of the Individual Testaments

Each testament follows a consistent, threefold tripartite literary pattern:

1. Autobiographical / Haggadic Narrative: The patriarch recounts key episodes from his life (expanding upon Genesis), candidly confessing his primary sin (e.g., Reuben's lust, Simeon's envy, Judah's drunkenness and greed, Gad's hatred) or extolling his characteristic virtue (e.g., Issachar's simplicity, Zebulun's compassion, Joseph's self-control/chastity).

2. Moral Exhortation (Paraenesis): The patriarch warns his descendants against the spiritual perils of vice (especially porneia, anger, jealousy, and double-heartedness) and exhorts them to practice righteousness, single-minded devotion (haplotēs), and fraternal love.

3. Eschatological Prophecy and Farewell: The patriarch predicts the future apostasy, exile, and restoration of his tribe—frequently structured around the Sin-Exile-Return pattern—culminating in an apocalyptic vision of the coming Messiah(s) from the tribes of Levi and Judah, a final resurrection, and instructions for burial in the ancestral tomb at Hebron (Cave of Machpelah).
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Textual Tradition

The complete Greek text survives in 14 principal manuscripts. R. H. Charles initially classified the tradition into two recensions, $\alpha$ (MSS c, h, i) and $\beta$ (MSS a, b, d, e, f, g, j). The modern editio maior (M. de Jonge, H. J. de Jonge, H. W. Hollander, T. Korteweg) replaced this with a division into Family I (MSS b and k) and Family II (all other Greek MSS, alongside the Armenian and Slavonic versions):

  • b: Cambridge University Library, MS Ff. 1.24, fols. 203a–262b (late 10th c.; brought from Athens to England by Robert Grosseteste in the 13th c.; the base text of Sinker and de Jonge's early editions).
  • k: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Gr. Z. 494 (coll. 331), fols. 263r–264v (mid-13th c.; preserves large extracts).
  • a: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Barocci 133, fols. 278r–309r (ca. 1270 CE).
  • c: Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, cod. Vat. gr. 731, fols. 97r–167r (13th c.).
  • d: Vatican, cod. Vat. gr. 1238, fols. 350r–380v (late 12th c.; includes significant marginal variants and scholia).
  • e: Mount Athos, Monastery of Koutloumousiou, cod. 39, fols. 180r–227r (11th c.; celebrated for containing inserted Greek translations of large sections of the Aramaic Levi Document).
  • f: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, cod. gr. 2658, fols. 41r–100v (11th c.).
  • g: Patmos, Monastery of St. John the Theologian, cod. 412, fols. 96r–148v (15th c.).
  • h: Sinai, Saint Catherine's Monastery, cod. gr. 547, fols. 195r–265v (17th c.).
  • i: Sinai, cod. gr. 548 (17th c.).
  • j: Sinai, cod. gr. 2170 (18th c.).
  • l: Mount Athos, Great Lavra, MS I 48, fols. 204r–276r (16th–17th c.; discovered and published by C. Burchard, 1966).
  • m: Ankara, Türk Tarih Kurumu, MS gr. 60, pp. 339–483 (16th c.).
  • n: Mount Athos, Monastery of Vatopedi, cod. 659 (14th c.).

B. Semitic Forebears and Witnesses (Genizah and Qumran)

1. The Aramaic Levi Document (ALD):

  • Cairo Genizah: Cambridge University Library MS T-S 16.94 (10th/11th c., cols. a–f); Oxford Bodleian MS heb. c 27, fol. 56 (10th/11th c., cols. a–d).
  • Qumran Cave 1: 1Q21 (1QTLevi; 60 fragments).
  • Qumran Cave 4: 4Q213 (4QLeviᵃ ar), 4Q213a (4QLeviᵇ ar), 4Q213b (4QLeviᶜ ar), 4Q214 (4QLeviᵈ ar), 4Q214a (4QLeviᵉ ar), 4Q214b (4QLeviᶠ ar), dated to the 2nd–1st c. BCE.
  • Greek Athos Additions: Mount Athos Koutloumousiou MS 39 preserves Greek interpolations representing a direct translation of the missing sections of ALD (prayer of Levi, priestly investiture, ritual halakhah on wood and sacrificial offerings).
  • Syriac Fragment: London, British Library Add. MS 14668, fol. 1 (6th/7th c.).

2. Hebrew Testament of Naphtali:

  • Qumran Cave 4: 4Q215 (4QTNaphtali; 1st c. BCE), preserving a genealogy of Bilhah, Jacob's prayer, and an eschatological column.
  • Medieval Hebrew Recension: Preserved in Oxford Bodleian MS Heb. d. 11 and incorporated into Moses Gaster's edition of the Chronicles of Jerahmeel (ch. 33).

3. Proto-Judah and Proto-Joseph Scrolls:

  • 3Q7 (3QTJud?); 4Q538 (4QTJud ar); 4Q539 (4QTJos ar).

C. Ancient Versions

  • Armenian Version: Survives in at least 48 manuscripts (oldest dated 1220 CE, Venice Mechitarist MSS 345, 1005, 1006; Jerusalem Armenian Patriarchate MSS 1925, 1927). Represents a distinct early translation (Family II), frequently preserving shorter, non-interpolated readings (studied by F. C. Conybeare, C. Burchard, and A. Hultgård).
  • Slavonic Versions: Widespread Old Church Slavonic and Serbian redactions preserved in the Tolkovaja Paleja and chronographic miscellanies (studied by A. Iatsimirskii, I. Franko, H. E. Gaylord, and T. Korteweg).
  • Latin Version: Translated from Greek MS b (Cambridge Ff. 1.24) by Bishop Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln ca. 1242 CE; survived in over 80 medieval manuscripts and exercised immense influence across Western Christendom.
  • Syriac and Coptic: Fragmentary liturgical citations and allusions.

• Charles, R. H. The Greek Versions of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Edited from Nine Mss together with the Variants of the Armenian and Slavonic Versions and Some Hebrew Fragments. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1908; reprinted Hildesheim: Georg Olms, 1966. [Masterwork of text-critical collection, printing Greek, Armenian, Slavonic, Genizah Aramaic, and Hebrew Naphtali synoptically].
  • de Jonge, Marinus. Testamenta XII Patriarcharum: Edited according to Cambridge University Library Ms Ff 1.24, fol. 203a–262b, with Short Notes. Pseudepigrapha Veteris Testamenti Graece 1. Leiden: Brill, 1964; 2nd ed., 1970.
  • de Jonge, Marinus, in coöperation with H. W. Hollander, H. J. de Jonge, and T. Korteweg. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text. Pseudepigrapha Veteris Testamenti Graece 1.2. Leiden: Brill, 1978. [The definitive modern editio maior, fully documenting all 14 Greek manuscripts and ancient versions].
  • Sinker, Robert. Testamenta XII Patriarcharum, ad fidem Codicis Cantabrigiensis edita: accedunt lectiones Cod. Oxoniensis. Cambridge: Deighton, Bell and Co., 1869; Appendix containing a collation of the Roman and Patmos MSS. Cambridge, 1879.
  • Stone, Michael E., and Jonas C. Greenfield. "The Aramaic and Greek Levi Texts." In The Aramaic Levi Document: Edition, Translation, Commentary. Edited by J. C. Greenfield, M. E. Stone, and E. Eshel. SVTP 19. Leiden: Brill, 2004.
  • Stone, Michael E. "Testament of Naphtali." In Qumran Cave 4.XVII: Parabiblical Texts, Part 3. DJD XXII. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1996, 73–82.

details.intro:
The Testament of Moses (historically conflated with or titled the Assumption of Moses, Latin Assumptio Mosis / Testamentum Moysis; Greek Διαθήκη Μωυσέως / Ἀνάληψις Μωυσέως) is an apocalyptic farewell address delivered by Moses to his successor Joshua on Mount Nebo prior to his death. Preserved uniquely in a single 6th-century Latin palimpsest discovered by Antonio Maria Ceriani in 1861, the work is a translation of a lost Greek version, which itself derives from a Semitic (Hebrew or Aramaic) Vorlage composed in Judea.

Modern critical consensus (following R. H. Charles, G. W. E. Nickelsburg, J. J. Collins, and J. Tromp) distinguishes between two originally separate works attested in ancient stichometries (Stichometry of Nicephorus, List of the Sixty Books, Synopsis of Pseudo-Athanasius):

1. The Testament of Moses (approx. 1100 lines): Preserved in the Milan palimpsest, comprising Moses’ historical-prophetic farewell revelation to Joshua.

2. The Assumption of Moses (approx. 1400 lines): The lost conclusion recounting Moses' ascent, physical death, and the cosmic struggle between the Archangel Michael and the Devil over the body of Moses (alluded to in Jude 9 and cited by Origen and Gelasius of Cyzicus).

Chapter-by-Chapter Architectural Breakdown

1. Moses' Commissioning of Joshua and the Secret Books (ch. 1):

  • In his 120th year, in the 2,500th year from the creation of the world, Moses appoints Joshua son of Nun as his successor to lead Israel into the Promised Land.
  • Moses reveals his cosmic pre-existence in the divine purpose: "He created me before the foundation of the world to be the mediator (arbitrem) of His covenant" (1:14).
  • Moses commits to Joshua the secret prophetic writings, instructing him to anoint them with cedar oil (oleum cedri) and store them in earthenware vessels (in vasis fictilibus) so they remain preserved until the Consummation of the End (in diem poenitentiae).

2. The Period of the Tribes and the First Temple (chs. 2–3):

  • Joshua leads the tribes across the Jordan; division of the land; era of the Judges; establishment of the monarchy and the building of Solomon's Temple.
  • Division into the Northern Kingdom (ten tribes) and the Southern Kingdom (two tribes). Both succumb to idolatry and forsake the covenant.

3. The Babylonian Exile and the Return (ch. 4):

  • Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem, burns the Temple, and deports the people to Babylon.
  • In exile, an unnamed intercessor (Daniel) prays to God, confessing the sins of the nation.
  • God stirs up the heart of a foreign king (Cyrus), permitting the return of the two tribes to rebuild Jerusalem, while the ten tribes remain in the eastern Diaspora.

4. Second Temple Apostasy and Hasmonean Rule (chs. 5–6):

  • Priesthood Corruption (ch. 5): The Second Temple is characterized by defective sacrifices, venal priests, and Hellenizing apostasy.
  • The Hasmonean Dynasty and Herod the Great (ch. 6): Tyrannical priest-kings arise, followed by an "insolent king, who will not be of the race of priests, an audacious and ruthless man" (= Herod the Great). He reigns for 34 years, slaughtering the elders, nobles, and common people with sword and fire.
  • His sons succeed him for shorter durations, followed by a powerful Western king who invades Judea (= P. Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, 4 BCE), crucifying rebels, burning parts of the Temple, and enslaving the inhabitants.

5. Sectarian Hypocrites and Religious Pretenders (ch. 7):

  • Bitter polemic against corrupt rulers and religious leaders: deceitful men, feast-lovers, gluttons, devoured by greed, who nevertheless pose as paragons of righteousness and say to the poor: "Do not touch me, lest you pollute me where I stand" (noli me tangere, ne inquines me).

6. The Great Persecution and Forced Epispasm (ch. 8):

  • A brutal foreign monarch (historically Antiochus IV Epiphanes, or a future eschatological tyrant) unleashes systematic persecution: torturing Torah-keepers, crucifying those who circumcise their sons, forcing boys to undergo epispasm (surgical reversal of circumcision), and compelling Jews to blaspheme and desecrate their holy things.

7. The Episode of Taxo and His Seven Sons (ch. 9):

  • In the midst of the crisis, a holy man named Taxo (Taxo de tribu Levi) arises.
  • Addressing his seven sons, Taxo recounts the unyielding sins of the nation and urges total, non-violent surrender to divine vengeance: "Let us fast for three days, and on the fourth day let us enter a cave in the wilderness, and let us die rather than transgress the commandments of the Lord of Lords, the God of our fathers. For if we do this, our blood will be avenged before the Lord" (9:6–7).

8. The Cosmic Eschatological Theophany (ch. 10):

  • A magnificent poetic apocalypse: "Then His kingdom will appear throughout all His creation, and then the Devil will have an end, and sorrow will be banished with him" (10:1).
  • The celestial angel (angelus qui in summo est) is appointed to avenge Israel against all enemies.
  • Cosmic upheaval: The Heavenly King rises from His royal throne; the earth trembles; high mountains are leveled and melt like wax; the sun darkens, the horns of the moon shatter and turn to blood, and the stars fall from their orbits.
  • Exaltation of Israel: God raises Israel upon the wings of eagles into the starry heavens, looking down upon their enemies in Gehenna and rejoicing in eternal triumph.

9. Joshua’s Lament and Moses’ Consolation (chs. 11–12):

  • Joshua tears his garments, throws himself at Moses’ feet, and utters an agonizing lament: Who can replace Moses as intercessor? Who will pray for Israel when famine, sword, or plagues strike? What land or grave is worthy to hold his body?
  • Moses reassures Joshua: God created the cosmos on behalf of His chosen people, foreknew all history from the beginning, and will faithfully uphold His eternal covenant.
  • The palimpsest breaks off abruptly in 12:13 during Moses' final words.
details.manuscripts:
A. The Latin Palimpsest: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS C. 73 inf.

  • Physical Manuscript:
  • The sole surviving continuous witness for chapters 1:1–12:13.
  • Date: 6th century CE, written in uncial script on parchment.
  • History: Acquired from the ancient monastery of St. Columbanus at Bobbio. It is a double palimpsest: the original script contains fragments of the Latin Pentateuch (Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers) and the Testament of Moses; overwritten in the 8th century with liturgical texts.
  • Condition: The text is severely corrupted by scribal blunders, phonetic spellings, and illegible faded passages. The final folios containing the end of chapter 12 and the death/assumption of Moses are entirely lost.
  • Editio Princeps:
  • Discovered and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani, "Fragmenta Assumptionis Mosis," in Monumenta sacra et profana 1.1 (Milan: Bibliotheca Ambrosiana, 1861), pp. 55–64.

B. The Patristic Citations and the "Lost Ending" (The Assumption)

While the Latin manuscript breaks off before Moses' death, numerous ancient Jewish, Christian, and gnostic sources preserve fragments and explicit citations from the lost concluding section of the Assumption of Moses:

1. The Epistle of Jude (v. 9):

  • "Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee."
  • Origen (De Principiis 3.2.1) explicitly identifies this verse as a direct citation from the Assumption of Moses (Ascensio Mosis).

2. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 6.15; Adumbrationes in Epistolam Iudae):

  • Notes that Joshua and Caleb witnessed a twofold Moses at his departure: one Moses ascending alive to heaven in the company of angels, and another Moses buried in the earth.

3. Gelasius of Cyzicus (Historia Ecclesiastica 2.17.17; 2.21.7):

  • Quotes a dramatic debate from the Assumption between the Archangel Michael and the Devil. The Devil claims possession of Moses’ body because Moses murdered the Egyptian taskmaster (Exod 2:12), while Michael accuses the Devil of inspiring the Serpent in Eden.

4. Didymus the Blind (In Epistolam Iudae enarratio):

  • Confirms that Jude 9 is derived from the Assumption of Moses.

5. Greek, Syriac, and Armenian Catenae:

  • Byzantine catenae on Jude and the Catholic Epistles (ed. J. A. Cramer, 1840) and Armenian catenae (ed. C. Renoux, 1994) preserve patristic scholia summarizing the angelic confrontation at Moses' tomb.

  • In exile, an unnamed intercessor (Daniel) prays to God, confessing the sins of the nation.
  • God stirs up the heart of a foreign king (Cyrus), permitting the return of the two tribes to rebuild Jerusalem, while the ten tribes remain in the eastern Diaspora.

4. Second Temple Apostasy and Hasmonean Rule (chs. 5–6):

  • Priesthood Corruption (ch. 5): The Second Temple is characterized by defective sacrifices, venal priests, and Hellenizing apostasy.
  • The Hasmonean Dynasty and Herod the Great (ch. 6): Tyrannical priest-kings arise, followed by an "insolent king, who will not be of the race of priests, an audacious and ruthless man" (= Herod the Great). He reigns for 34 years, slaughtering the elders, nobles, and common people with sword and fire.
  • His sons succeed him for shorter durations, followed by a powerful Western king who invades Judea (= P. Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, 4 BCE), crucifying rebels, burning parts of the Temple, and enslaving the inhabitants.

5. Sectarian Hypocrites and Religious Pretenders (ch. 7):

  • Bitter polemic against corrupt rulers and religious leaders: deceitful men, feast-lovers, gluttons, devoured by greed, who nevertheless pose as paragons of righteousness and say to the poor: "Do not touch me, lest you pollute me where I stand" (noli me tangere, ne inquines me).

6. The Great Persecution and Forced Epispasm (ch. 8):

  • A brutal foreign monarch (historically Antiochus IV Epiphanes, or a future eschatological tyrant) unleashes systematic persecution: torturing Torah-keepers, crucifying those who circumcise their sons, forcing boys to undergo epispasm (surgical reversal of circumcision), and compelling Jews to blaspheme and desecrate their holy things.

7. The Episode of Taxo and His Seven Sons (ch. 9):

  • In the midst of the crisis, a holy man named Taxo (Taxo de tribu Levi) arises.
  • Addressing his seven sons, Taxo recounts the unyielding sins of the nation and urges total, non-violent surrender to divine vengeance: "Let us fast for three days, and on the fourth day let us enter a cave in the wilderness, and let us die rather than transgress the commandments of the Lord of Lords, the God of our fathers. For if we do this, our blood will be avenged before the Lord" (9:6–7).

8. The Cosmic Eschatological Theophany (ch. 10):

  • A magnificent poetic apocalypse: "Then His kingdom will appear throughout all His creation, and then the Devil will have an end, and sorrow will be banished with him" (10:1).
  • The celestial angel (angelus qui in summo est) is appointed to avenge Israel against all enemies.
  • Cosmic upheaval: The Heavenly King rises from His royal throne; the earth trembles; high mountains are leveled and melt like wax; the sun darkens, the horns of the moon shatter and turn to blood, and the stars fall from their orbits.
  • Exaltation of Israel: God raises Israel upon the wings of eagles into the starry heavens, looking down upon their enemies in Gehenna and rejoicing in eternal triumph.

9. Joshua’s Lament and Moses’ Consolation (chs. 11–12):

  • Joshua tears his garments, throws himself at Moses’ feet, and utters an agonizing lament: Who can replace Moses as intercessor? Who will pray for Israel when famine, sword, or plagues strike? What land or grave is worthy to hold his body?
  • Moses reassures Joshua: God created the cosmos on behalf of His chosen people, foreknew all history from the beginning, and will faithfully uphold His eternal covenant.
  • The palimpsest breaks off abruptly in 12:13 during Moses' final words.

A. The Latin Palimpsest: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS C. 73 inf.

  • Physical Manuscript:
  • The sole surviving continuous witness for chapters 1:1–12:13.
  • Date: 6th century CE, written in uncial script on parchment.
  • History: Acquired from the ancient monastery of St. Columbanus at Bobbio. It is a double palimpsest: the original script contains fragments of the Latin Pentateuch (Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers) and the Testament of Moses; overwritten in the 8th century with liturgical texts.
  • Condition: The text is severely corrupted by scribal blunders, phonetic spellings, and illegible faded passages. The final folios containing the end of chapter 12 and the death/assumption of Moses are entirely lost.
  • Editio Princeps:
  • Discovered and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani, "Fragmenta Assumptionis Mosis," in Monumenta sacra et profana 1.1 (Milan: Bibliotheca Ambrosiana, 1861), pp. 55–64.

B. The Patristic Citations and the "Lost Ending" (The Assumption)

While the Latin manuscript breaks off before Moses' death, numerous ancient Jewish, Christian, and gnostic sources preserve fragments and explicit citations from the lost concluding section of the Assumption of Moses:

1. The Epistle of Jude (v. 9):

  • "Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee."
  • Origen (De Principiis 3.2.1) explicitly identifies this verse as a direct citation from the Assumption of Moses (Ascensio Mosis).

2. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 6.15; Adumbrationes in Epistolam Iudae):

  • Notes that Joshua and Caleb witnessed a twofold Moses at his departure: one Moses ascending alive to heaven in the company of angels, and another Moses buried in the earth.

3. Gelasius of Cyzicus (Historia Ecclesiastica 2.17.17; 2.21.7):

  • Quotes a dramatic debate from the Assumption between the Archangel Michael and the Devil. The Devil claims possession of Moses’ body because Moses murdered the Egyptian taskmaster (Exod 2:12), while Michael accuses the Devil of inspiring the Serpent in Eden.

4. Didymus the Blind (In Epistolam Iudae enarratio):

  • Confirms that Jude 9 is derived from the Assumption of Moses.

5. Greek, Syriac, and Armenian Catenae:

  • Byzantine catenae on Jude and the Catholic Epistles (ed. J. A. Cramer, 1840) and Armenian catenae (ed. C. Renoux, 1994) preserve patristic scholia summarizing the angelic confrontation at Moses' tomb.

The Testament of Moses (historically conflated with or titled the Assumption of Moses, Latin Assumptio Mosis / Testamentum Moysis; Greek Διαθήκη Μωυσέως / Ἀνάληψις Μωυσέως) is an apocalyptic farewell address delivered by Moses to his successor Joshua on Mount Nebo prior to his death. 1. The Testament of Moses (approx. 1100 lines): Preserved in the Milan palimpsest, comprising Moses’ historical-prophetic farewell revelation to Joshua.

details.intro:
The Apocryphon of Jannes and Jambres (Liber de Ianis et Mambres / Ἰάννης καὶ Ἰαμβρῆς / Poenitentia Iamnis et Mambres) is an ancient Jewish narrative pseudepigraphon composed in Greek in Roman Egypt during the 1st or early 2nd century CE. Expanding upon Exodus 7:11 and the legend of Pharaoh’s court sorcerers who contended with Moses and Aaron, the work tells the dramatic story of the brothers Jannes and Jambres (Mambres), their rivalry with Moses, their fatal humiliation by divine power, and their repentance and post-mortem vision of hell:

1. The Magicians’ Challenge and the Egyptian Plagues: Jannes and Jambres, famed magicians dwelling in Memphis with their aged mother, are summoned to the royal court to counter Moses’ wonders. Although initially able to duplicate the lesser signs through demonic magic, they are stricken by the plagues (boils, darkness), acknowledging the "finger of God."

2. The Fatal Sickness and Death of Jannes: Stricken by a mysterious, incurable wasting disease, Jannes takes to his bed. He opens his secret grimoires and realizes that the divine decree against Egypt is irreversible. Confessing the futility of human sorcery against the God of the Hebrews, Jannes dies in spiritual agony and descends to Hades.

3. The Necromancy of Jambres: Surviving in grief and isolation, Jambres resolves to consult his dead brother. Performing a necromantic ritual with his magical books beside Jannes’ tomb, Jambres summons the shade (eidōlon) of Jannes from the abyss.

4. The Ghost’s Testimony from the Underworld: The shade of Jannes emerges from the underworld and delivers an agonizing monologue. He confirms the absolute justice of God's judgment, describes the terrifying topography of Hades, the relentless torments suffered by the damned, and the inescapable retribution awaiting magicians and idolaters. He implores Jambres to repent and burn their magical books, lamenting that they have forfeited eternal life for fleeting earthly renown.
details.manuscripts:
Long known only through external patristic citations, New Testament allusions, and a medieval Latin fragment, the actual Greek text was dramatically recovered in the 20th century through major papyrological discoveries:

A. The Greek Papyri

1. Chester Beatty Papyrus XVI (P. Chester Beatty XVI; Dublin, Chester Beatty Library):

  • 4th-century CE Greek papyrus codex, acquired by Sir Alfred Chester Beatty in Egypt ca. 1930.
  • Identified and assembled by Albert Pietersma in the 1970s and 1980s. Preserves approximately 98 fragmentary leaves containing extensive continuous sections of the narrative (Jannes' illness, family laments, death, burial, and Jambres' necromancy).

2. Papyrus Vindobonensis Graecus 29456 + 29828 verso (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek):

  • 3rd-century CE Greek papyrus roll from Hermopolis; preserves continuous columns from the earlier portion of the apocryphon on the verso of an astronomical text (edited by Pierre Maraval, 1977; reedited by Pietersma, 1994).

B. The Latin–Old English Bilingual Witness

  • London, British Library, MS Cotton Tiberius B. V, Part 1, fol. 87 (olim 97):
  • 11th-century Anglo-Saxon illustrated miscellany preserving a Latin text with an accompanying interlinear Old English gloss (Poenitentia Iamnis et Mambres).
  • Features a famous colored pen drawing depicting Mambres sitting beside a hell-mouth, opening his magic book to summon the fiery, dragon-headed shade of Jannes from the abyss.
  • Editions: Cockayne (1861); James (1901); Förster (1902); Biggs & Hall (1996).

C. Ancient External Attestations

  • New Testament: 2 Timothy 3:8 ("As Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth...").
  • Dead Sea Scrolls: Damascus Document (CD 5:17–19: "Yohana and his brother in their cunning stood up against Moses and Aaron").
  • Pagan Sources: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia 30.11); Apuleius of Madaura (Apologia 90); Numenius of Apamea (apud Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica 9.8.1–2).
  • Patristic Testimonies: Origen (Commentarius in Matthaeum 27.9; Contra Celsum 4.51); Ambrosiaster (In 2 Tim 3:8); Decretum Gelasianum (listing the Liber qui appellatur Paenitentia Iamne et Mambre among forbidden apocrypha).
  • Rabbinic & Targumic Literature: b. Menahot 85a (Yohani and Mamre); Exodus Rabbah 9.7; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exod 1:15; 7:11; Num 22:22.

details.intro:
The Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum (commonly abbreviated LAB, also known as Pseudo-Philo or Biblical Antiquities) is one of the most substantial and significant works of Second Temple Jewish literature. Spanning sixty-five chapters, the work is a monumental "Rewritten Bible" narrative recounting sacred history from Adam to the tragic death of King Saul. Pseudepigraphically ascribed to the 1st-century Jewish-Alexandrian philosopher Philo Judaeus—having survived in medieval Latin manuscripts alongside Latin translations of genuine Philonic treatises—the work was decisively reclaimed for Jewish scholarship by Leopold Cohn in 1898.

Scholarly consensus demonstrates that the extant Latin text was translated from a lost Greek intermediary, which itself was translated from an authentic Palestinian Hebrew original composed in the late 1st century CE (ca. 70–135 CE, or shortly before the fall of Jerusalem).

Architectural Breakdown (65 Chapters)

1. Primeval History: From Adam to the Tower of Babel (chs. 1–7):

  • Extensive genealogies enumerating descendants unmentioned in Genesis (sons and daughters of Adam, Seth, and Cain).
  • The Flood and the repopulation of the earth under Noah’s sons.
  • The Rebellion of Babel and Nimrod (chs. 5–7): Nimrod and the leaders of the earth build the Tower of Babel. Abraham, along with eleven righteous men, refuses to contribute bricks; Abraham is cast into a blazing furnace, but God sends the angel of fire (Zeruel) to rescue him unharmed, while the flames consume 84,000 onlookers.

2. The Patriarchs, Egypt, and the Exodus (chs. 8–10):

  • Covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
  • Amram's Resistance and Miriam’s Prophecy (ch. 9): Facing Pharaoh’s decree to drown male infants, Amram leads the elders of Israel in refusing celibacy, trusting in divine covenant fidelity; Miriam receives an angelic night vision foretelling that her brother Moses will save Israel.
  • Moses’ birth, preservation by Pharaoh’s daughter Thermuthis, the Plagues, and the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea.

3. The Theophany at Sinai and the Law (chs. 11–14):

  • Cosmic Sinai theophany: heaven bows down, the deeps tremble, and celestial angels tremble at the voice of God.
  • Promulgation of the Decalogue and statutory laws; the Golden Calf apostasy; Moses intercedes, smashes the tablets, and reconstructs the Tabernacle.

4. The Wilderness Wandering and the Death of Moses (chs. 15–19):

  • The twelve spies; the rebellion and subterranean destruction of Korah; the miraculous budding of Aaron’s rod.
  • Moses' Farewell and Heavenly Vision (ch. 19): Before dying, Moses is shown the celestial sanctuary, the measurements of the cosmos, the path of the stars, and the storehouses of souls; God Himself buries Moses on the high mountain in heavenly light, weeping over His servant while angels lament.

5. Joshua and the Conquest of the Land (chs. 20–24):

  • Joshua succeeds Moses; Rahab’s faith; crossing the Jordan; destruction of Jericho and Ai; renewal of the covenant at Shechem; Joshua's testament and death.

6. The Great Kenaz Epic: Judge and Deliverer (chs. 25–28):

  • The centerpiece of LAB's narrative innovation, transforming the minor biblical figure Kenaz (Judg 3:9–11) into an epic national hero:
  • Kenaz uncovers hidden idolatrous cults within the twelve tribes, casting lots and extracting confessions.
  • He receives twelve luminous celestial stones from Mount Hermon that shine in darkness and liquefy idols like water.
  • The Nocturnal Battle: Armed with divine courage and accompanied by angels (Ingethel and Zeruel) who strike the Philistines with blindness and numbness, Kenaz rides alone into the enemy camp and slaughters 100,000 Philistines in a single night.
  • Kenaz experiences an apocalyptic vision of the creation of the heavens, the firmament, and the final judgment before dying peacefully.

7. Zebul, Deborah, and the Victory over Sisera (chs. 29–33):

  • Zebul rules as righteous judge.
  • Deborah arises as prophetess, judge, and mother in Israel; her victory song over Sisera; Jael slays Sisera.
  • The Death of Deborah: A poignant testamentary farewell where the people weep and Deborah instructs them to set their hearts upon the Law, for after death no intercession is possible (ch. 33).

8. Gideon, Abimelech, and the Tragedy of Seila (chs. 34–41):

  • Gideon’s defeat of Midian; Abimelech’s murderous reign; Jair’s idolatrous shrine.
  • Jephthah and Seila (chs. 39–40): Jephthah vows to sacrifice whatever meets him first; his daughter Seila (Seila filia Iephte) voluntarily accepts her sacrificial death, asking for two months to wander the mountains.
  • The Lament of Seila: A sublime poetic dirge lamenting her unwed bridal chamber, weeping among the hills, and embracing her death as an offering to God.

9. Samson and the End of the Judges (chs. 42–47):

  • Manoah and his barren wife Eluma; the angelic annunciation; Samson's supernatural exploits and self-sacrifice against the Philistines.
  • The idol of Micah; the atrocity of the concubine of Gibeah and the war against Benjamin; Phinehas the high priest intercedes and is assumed to heaven to reappear as Elijah (ch. 48).

10. Eli, Samuel, and the Tragedy of King Saul (chs. 48–65):

  • Hannah’s prophetic song; birth and divine calling of Samuel; defeat of the Philistines and recovery of the Ark.
  • Israel requests an earthly king; Samuel anoints Saul.
  • Saul’s disobedience regarding Agag and Amalek; David anointed by Samuel; David sings mystical exorcism hymns to soothe Saul’s tormenting evil spirit (ch. 60).
  • Saul consults the Witch of Endor; Samuel rises from Sheol and pronounces irrevocable doom upon Saul.
  • Mount Gilboa: Saul commits suicide, requesting an Amalekite to dispatch him; David laments Saul and Jonathan, and is acclaimed king over Israel (ch. 65).
details.manuscripts:
The Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum has been preserved through a remarkably cohesive Latin manuscript tradition originating in medieval German and Austrian Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries.

A. The Latin Manuscript Tradition

Extant in eighteen complete and fragmentary codices (11th–15th centuries), categorized into two primary stemmatic branches ($\Pi$ and $\Delta$) by Guido Kisch, Daniel J. Harrington, and Howard Jacobson:

1. Primary Witnesses:

  • MS A (Admont, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. 359): 11th century; the oldest, purest, and most authoritative extant manuscript of LAB.
  • MS C (Fulda / Kassel, Murhardsche Bibliothek, Cod. 4° Theol. 6): 11th century; closely allied with MS A.
  • MS D (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 17133): 12th century; from the monastery of Schäftlarn.
  • MS B (Basel, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. F. III. 15b): 15th century.
  • MS E (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. 4460): 15th century.
  • MS F (Melk, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. 1477): 15th century.
  • MS G (Graz, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. 749): 14th century.
  • Fragment 63 (Freiburg im Breisgau, Universitätsbibliothek): 12th-century fragment preserving portions of chapters 26–28; identified and edited by F. Petit and V. Sack (1983).

B. The Editio Princeps (1527)

  • Johannes Sichardus (Sichardt) published the editio princeps in Basel (Philonis Iudaei Alexandrini libri antiquitatum, apud Henricum Petrum, August 1527).
  • Sichardus utilized an ancient manuscript (now lost) belonging to the abbey of Lorsch or Fulda, which represented an independent textual witness often preserving superior readings over surviving codices.

C. Medieval Hebrew Retroversions: The Chronicles of Jerahmeel

  • Preserved in Oxford Bodleian MS Heb. d. 11 (fols. 34r–58r), a 14th-century compilation assembled by Eleazar ben Asher ha-Levi incorporating texts from Jerahmeel ben Solomon (12th c., northern Italy/southern France).
  • The Hebrew Portions: Chapters 1–8 (Babel, Abraham in the furnace) and 25–28 (the Kenaz cycle) survive in Hebrew in the Chronicles of Jerahmeel.
  • Critical Status: Moses Gaster (1896, 1899) initially claimed that Jerahmeel preserved the lost Semitic original of LAB. However, Adolf Neubauer (1887), Leopold Cohn (1915), Daniel J. Harrington (1974), and Howard Jacobson (1983, 1997) proved decisively that Jerahmeel's Hebrew text is a medieval Hebrew translation made directly from a Latin manuscript of LAB.

details.intro:
Portions of Jubilees survive in the Hebrew original as well as in Greek, Syriac, Latin, and Ethiopic translations.

The Qumran Hebrew evidence is preserved across 15 fragmentary scrolls: 4Q216–224, 4Q176a, 1Q17–18, 2Q19–20, 3Q5, and 11Q12. The text presented here is based on the transcriptions of Martin G. Abegg, Jr. (with J. E. Bowley and E. M. Cook, via ETCBC/dss), aligned to the standard chapter-and-verse framework established by J. C. VanderKam and J. T. Milik in DJD XIII (1994). Used by permission of M. G. Abegg.

The surviving Greek fragments of Jubilees are presented here as they appear in A.-M. Denis, Fragmenta, 70–102.

About one quarter of Jubilees has survived in Latin translation in a 5th–6th century manuscript published by A. M. Ceriani in 1861 (see below). Ceriani’s edition is presented here without critical apparatus as it is reprinted in Denis, Concordance latine, 552–65.

The complete Ethiopic text and the Syriac fragments wait to be encoded.
details.manuscripts:
A. Hebrew Dead Sea Scrolls (Original Hebrew Text)

The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls confirmed that Hebrew was the original language of Jubilees. Over fifteen fragmentary Hebrew manuscripts were recovered from five caves at Qumran:

  • Cave 1: 1Q17 (1QJub$^a$), 1Q18 (1QJub$^b$) (ed. J. T. Milik, DJD 1, 1955).
  • Cave 2: 2Q19 (2QJub$^a$), 2Q20 (2QJub$^b$) (ed. M. Baillet, DJD 3, 1962).
  • Cave 3: 3Q5 (3QJub) (ed. M. Baillet, DJD 3, 1962).
  • Cave 4: The largest collection, dating from ca. 125 BCE to 50 CE:
  • 4Q216 (4QJub$^a$): Late 2nd cent. BCE (one of the oldest scrolls; chs. 1–2).
  • 4Q217 (4QpapJub$^b$?): Papyrus manuscript.
  • 4Q218 (4QJub$^c$); 4Q219 (4QJub$^d$); 4Q220 (4QJub$^e$); 4Q221 (4QJub$^f$); 4Q222 (4QJub$^g$); 4Q223–224 (4QpapJub$^h$).
  • Cave 11: 11Q12 (11QJub) (ed. F. García Martínez et al., DJD 23, 1998).
  • Canonical Status at Qumran: Cited as an authoritative, inspired text in the Damascus Document (CD 16:2–4: "the Book of the Divisions of the Times into their Jubilees and Weeks").

B. Ethiopic (Ge'ez: Mashafa Kufale)

The only textual witness preserving the entire work complete from beginning to end. Preserved in 19 known manuscripts, classified into two major families:

  • Group 1 (Older, Superior Recension; 15th–16th cent.):
  • MS A (Paris, BnF, MS éth. 51, fols. 1r–55v): 15th century.
  • MS B (Lake Tana, Kebran Gabriel Monastery MS 9): 15th century.
  • Tübingen MSS (collated by Ewald).
  • Group 2 (Later, Secondary Recension; 17th–18th cent.):
  • MS C (London, British Library, MS Add. 16188).
  • MS D (London, British Library, MS Or. 485).
  • Critical Editions: August Dillmann (1859); R. H. Charles (1895); James C. VanderKam (CSCO 510–511, 1989).

C. Latin Tradition (Parva Genesis)

  • Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS C. 73 inf. (5th/6th cent. CE uncial palimpsest):
  • Preserves approximately one-third of the text in an ancient Old Latin translation made directly from the Greek Vorlage.
  • Discovered and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani, Monumenta Sacra et Profana 1 (Milan, 1861), pp. 15–54; reedited with exhaustive commentary by Hermann Rönsch (1874).

D. Greek Fragments and External Citations

  • Preserved in extensive excerpts in the Byzantine chronicles of Georgius Syncellus, Georgius Cedrenus, the Chronicon Paschale, and patristic catenae on Genesis; cited also by Epiphanius (Panarion 39.6).
  • Editions: R. H. Charles (1902); Albert-Marie Denis, PVTG 3 (1970).

E. Syriac Fragments

  • Excerpts preserved in London, BL MS Add. 12154 (8th cent. CE), the anonymous Chronicle of 846, and the chronicle of Michael the Syrian (ed. Ceriani, Baumstark).

title: Eldad et Modad (fragmentum graecum in citatione)

details.intro:
The sole surviving verbatim citation from the Greek work is preserved in the 2nd-century Christian writing The Shepherd of Hermas (Vis. 2.3.4):

  • Greek Text:

> Ἐγγὺς κύριος τοῖς ἐπιστρεφομένοις, ὡς γέγραπται ἐν τῷ Ἐλδὰδ καὶ Μωδὰδ, τοῖς προφητεύσασιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ τῷ λαῷ.

> (“The Lord is near to those who turn to him, as it is written in Eldad and Modad, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness.”)

details.intro:
The Testament of Moses (historically conflated with or titled the Assumption of Moses, Latin Assumptio Mosis / Testamentum Moysis; Greek Διαθήκη Μωυσέως / Ἀνάληψις Μωυσέως) is an apocalyptic farewell address delivered by Moses to his successor Joshua on Mount Nebo prior to his death. Preserved uniquely in a single 6th-century Latin palimpsest discovered by Antonio Maria Ceriani in 1861, the work is a translation of a lost Greek version, which itself derives from a Semitic (Hebrew or Aramaic) Vorlage composed in Judea.

Modern critical consensus (following R. H. Charles, G. W. E. Nickelsburg, J. J. Collins, and J. Tromp) distinguishes between two originally separate works attested in ancient stichometries (Stichometry of Nicephorus, List of the Sixty Books, Synopsis of Pseudo-Athanasius):

1. The Testament of Moses (approx. 1100 lines): Preserved in the Milan palimpsest, comprising Moses’ historical-prophetic farewell revelation to Joshua.

2. The Assumption of Moses (approx. 1400 lines): The lost conclusion recounting Moses' ascent, physical death, and the cosmic struggle between the Archangel Michael and the Devil over the body of Moses (alluded to in Jude 9 and cited by Origen and Gelasius of Cyzicus).

Chapter-by-Chapter Architectural Breakdown

1. Moses' Commissioning of Joshua and the Secret Books (ch. 1):

  • In his 120th year, in the 2,500th year from the creation of the world, Moses appoints Joshua son of Nun as his successor to lead Israel into the Promised Land.
  • Moses reveals his cosmic pre-existence in the divine purpose: "He created me before the foundation of the world to be the mediator (arbitrem) of His covenant" (1:14).
  • Moses commits to Joshua the secret prophetic writings, instructing him to anoint them with cedar oil (oleum cedri) and store them in earthenware vessels (in vasis fictilibus) so they remain preserved until the Consummation of the End (in diem poenitentiae).

2. The Period of the Tribes and the First Temple (chs. 2–3):

  • Joshua leads the tribes across the Jordan; division of the land; era of the Judges; establishment of the monarchy and the building of Solomon's Temple.
  • Division into the Northern Kingdom (ten tribes) and the Southern Kingdom (two tribes). Both succumb to idolatry and forsake the covenant.

3. The Babylonian Exile and the Return (ch. 4):

  • Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem, burns the Temple, and deports the people to Babylon.
  • In exile, an unnamed intercessor (Daniel) prays to God, confessing the sins of the nation.
  • God stirs up the heart of a foreign king (Cyrus), permitting the return of the two tribes to rebuild Jerusalem, while the ten tribes remain in the eastern Diaspora.

4. Second Temple Apostasy and Hasmonean Rule (chs. 5–6):

  • Priesthood Corruption (ch. 5): The Second Temple is characterized by defective sacrifices, venal priests, and Hellenizing apostasy.
  • The Hasmonean Dynasty and Herod the Great (ch. 6): Tyrannical priest-kings arise, followed by an "insolent king, who will not be of the race of priests, an audacious and ruthless man" (= Herod the Great). He reigns for 34 years, slaughtering the elders, nobles, and common people with sword and fire.
  • His sons succeed him for shorter durations, followed by a powerful Western king who invades Judea (= P. Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, 4 BCE), crucifying rebels, burning parts of the Temple, and enslaving the inhabitants.

5. Sectarian Hypocrites and Religious Pretenders (ch. 7):

  • Bitter polemic against corrupt rulers and religious leaders: deceitful men, feast-lovers, gluttons, devoured by greed, who nevertheless pose as paragons of righteousness and say to the poor: "Do not touch me, lest you pollute me where I stand" (noli me tangere, ne inquines me).

6. The Great Persecution and Forced Epispasm (ch. 8):

  • A brutal foreign monarch (historically Antiochus IV Epiphanes, or a future eschatological tyrant) unleashes systematic persecution: torturing Torah-keepers, crucifying those who circumcise their sons, forcing boys to undergo epispasm (surgical reversal of circumcision), and compelling Jews to blaspheme and desecrate their holy things.

7. The Episode of Taxo and His Seven Sons (ch. 9):

  • In the midst of the crisis, a holy man named Taxo (Taxo de tribu Levi) arises.
  • Addressing his seven sons, Taxo recounts the unyielding sins of the nation and urges total, non-violent surrender to divine vengeance: "Let us fast for three days, and on the fourth day let us enter a cave in the wilderness, and let us die rather than transgress the commandments of the Lord of Lords, the God of our fathers. For if we do this, our blood will be avenged before the Lord" (9:6–7).

8. The Cosmic Eschatological Theophany (ch. 10):

  • A magnificent poetic apocalypse: "Then His kingdom will appear throughout all His creation, and then the Devil will have an end, and sorrow will be banished with him" (10:1).
  • The celestial angel (angelus qui in summo est) is appointed to avenge Israel against all enemies.
  • Cosmic upheaval: The Heavenly King rises from His royal throne; the earth trembles; high mountains are leveled and melt like wax; the sun darkens, the horns of the moon shatter and turn to blood, and the stars fall from their orbits.
  • Exaltation of Israel: God raises Israel upon the wings of eagles into the starry heavens, looking down upon their enemies in Gehenna and rejoicing in eternal triumph.

9. Joshua’s Lament and Moses’ Consolation (chs. 11–12):

  • Joshua tears his garments, throws himself at Moses’ feet, and utters an agonizing lament: Who can replace Moses as intercessor? Who will pray for Israel when famine, sword, or plagues strike? What land or grave is worthy to hold his body?
  • Moses reassures Joshua: God created the cosmos on behalf of His chosen people, foreknew all history from the beginning, and will faithfully uphold His eternal covenant.
  • The palimpsest breaks off abruptly in 12:13 during Moses' final words.
details.manuscripts:
A. The Latin Palimpsest: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS C. 73 inf.

  • Physical Manuscript:
  • The sole surviving continuous witness for chapters 1:1–12:13.
  • Date: 6th century CE, written in uncial script on parchment.
  • History: Acquired from the ancient monastery of St. Columbanus at Bobbio. It is a double palimpsest: the original script contains fragments of the Latin Pentateuch (Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers) and the Testament of Moses; overwritten in the 8th century with liturgical texts.
  • Condition: The text is severely corrupted by scribal blunders, phonetic spellings, and illegible faded passages. The final folios containing the end of chapter 12 and the death/assumption of Moses are entirely lost.
  • Editio Princeps:
  • Discovered and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani, "Fragmenta Assumptionis Mosis," in Monumenta sacra et profana 1.1 (Milan: Bibliotheca Ambrosiana, 1861), pp. 55–64.

B. The Patristic Citations and the "Lost Ending" (The Assumption)

While the Latin manuscript breaks off before Moses' death, numerous ancient Jewish, Christian, and gnostic sources preserve fragments and explicit citations from the lost concluding section of the Assumption of Moses:

1. The Epistle of Jude (v. 9):

  • "Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee."
  • Origen (De Principiis 3.2.1) explicitly identifies this verse as a direct citation from the Assumption of Moses (Ascensio Mosis).

2. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 6.15; Adumbrationes in Epistolam Iudae):

  • Notes that Joshua and Caleb witnessed a twofold Moses at his departure: one Moses ascending alive to heaven in the company of angels, and another Moses buried in the earth.

3. Gelasius of Cyzicus (Historia Ecclesiastica 2.17.17; 2.21.7):

  • Quotes a dramatic debate from the Assumption between the Archangel Michael and the Devil. The Devil claims possession of Moses’ body because Moses murdered the Egyptian taskmaster (Exod 2:12), while Michael accuses the Devil of inspiring the Serpent in Eden.

4. Didymus the Blind (In Epistolam Iudae enarratio):

  • Confirms that Jude 9 is derived from the Assumption of Moses.

5. Greek, Syriac, and Armenian Catenae:

  • Byzantine catenae on Jude and the Catholic Epistles (ed. J. A. Cramer, 1840) and Armenian catenae (ed. C. Renoux, 1994) preserve patristic scholia summarizing the angelic confrontation at Moses' tomb.

details.intro:
The Primary Adam Literature encompasses a multifaceted cycle of closely related Jewish and Christian narratives recounting the creation, fall, penance, death, and burial of the protoplasts Adam and Eve. The literature is extant in six principal ancient and medieval versions:

A. Greek Apocalypse of Moses (Apocalypsis Mosis / Greek Life of Adam and Eve [GLAE])

  • Primary Witnesses:
  • A₁: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Marcianus gr. VII 22 (11th c.).
  • B: Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. theol. gr. 237 (13th/14th c.).
  • C: Vienna, ÖNB, cod. theol. gr. 247 (14th c.).
  • D: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, cod. C 210 inf. (13th c.) — ed. A. M. Ceriani (1868).
  • Additional witnesses: Paris gr. 1313, Paris Suppl. gr. 162.

B. Latin Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae)

  • Classification: Divided by Wilhelm Meyer (1878) into four manuscript classes spanning the 9th to 15th centuries across Continental Europe (especially Munich Bayerische Staatsbibliothek: Clm 4807, Clm 5601, Clm 8470, Clm 13002) and England (12 Insular MSS classified by J. H. Mozley 1928–1929; analyzed by J.-P. Pettorelli 1999).
  • Notable for interpolations such as the Fall of Satan (chs. 12–16) and the quest of Seth for the Oil of Mercy.

C. Armenian Version (The Penitence of Adam / Book of Adam)

  • Discovered in the Library of the Mechitharist Congregation of San Lazzaro (Venice) and the Matenadaran (Yerevan), edited critically by Michael E. Stone (CSCO 429–430, 1981). Closer than the Greek or Latin to the lost archetype in its preservation of the penance in the rivers.

D. Georgian Book of Adam (K‘art‘uli versia)

  • Preserved in 16th/17th-century manuscripts (Tbilisi S-354 and H-1691), critically studied and translated by J.-P. Mahé (1981) and C. Kurtsikidze (1964). Parallels the Armenian text very closely.

E. Slavonic Life of Adam and Eve (Slovo o Adame i Eve)

  • Transmitted in Serbian, Russian, and Bulgarian redactions embedded in Palea collections, edited by V. Jagić (1893), N. S. Tikhonravov (1863), and I. Franko (1896–1910). Includes the related Bohemian (Old Czech) vernacular fragment.

F. Coptic Fragments

  • Sahidic and Fayyumic papyri preserving portions of the Vita and Apocalypse of Moses (Manchester John Rylands Coptic MS 84, ed. W. E. Crum 1909; Berlin Papyrus 181, ed. J. Leipoldt 1904).

Introduction

The Oratio Moysi in die obitus sui (CAVT 138; CANT 314) is a Latin apocryphal fragment discovered and edited by M. R. James from the 11th-century Cheltenham manuscript (Codex Phillippicus 391, fol. 87b). It narrates the final prayer of Moses on the day of his death, inquiring about the remaining duration of world history, followed by his glorious burial by God Himself.

details.intro:
Introduction

The Visio Kenaz (or Visio Zenez patris Gothoniel; CAVT 147) is a Latin apocalyptic fragment recounting the ecstatic deathbed vision of the judge Kenaz (father of Othniel). He envisions the pre-cosmic void, unburning flames, the dormant primordial springs, and the weaving of the upper and lower firmaments for the seven-thousand-year habitation of Adam's race.
details.provenance:
Provenance

Preserved in Codex Phillippicus 391 (fol. 87b-88a) and closely related to the Latin text of Pseudo-Philo's Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum (LAB chapter 28).
details.manuscripts:
The Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum has been preserved through a remarkably cohesive Latin manuscript tradition originating in medieval German and Austrian Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries.

A. The Latin Manuscript Tradition

Extant in eighteen complete and fragmentary codices (11th–15th centuries), categorized into two primary stemmatic branches ($\Pi$ and $\Delta$) by Guido Kisch, Daniel J. Harrington, and Howard Jacobson:

1. Primary Witnesses:

  • MS A (Admont, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. 359): 11th century; the oldest, purest, and most authoritative extant manuscript of LAB.
  • MS C (Fulda / Kassel, Murhardsche Bibliothek, Cod. 4° Theol. 6): 11th century; closely allied with MS A.
  • MS D (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 17133): 12th century; from the monastery of Schäftlarn.
  • MS B (Basel, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. F. III. 15b): 15th century.
  • MS E (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. 4460): 15th century.
  • MS F (Melk, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. 1477): 15th century.
  • MS G (Graz, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. 749): 14th century.
  • Fragment 63 (Freiburg im Breisgau, Universitätsbibliothek): 12th-century fragment preserving portions of chapters 26–28; identified and edited by F. Petit and V. Sack (1983).

B. The Editio Princeps (1527)

  • Johannes Sichardus (Sichardt) published the editio princeps in Basel (Philonis Iudaei Alexandrini libri antiquitatum, apud Henricum Petrum, August 1527).
  • Sichardus utilized an ancient manuscript (now lost) belonging to the abbey of Lorsch or Fulda, which represented an independent textual witness often preserving superior readings over surviving codices.

C. Medieval Hebrew Retroversions: The Chronicles of Jerahmeel

  • Preserved in Oxford Bodleian MS Heb. d. 11 (fols. 34r–58r), a 14th-century compilation assembled by Eleazar ben Asher ha-Levi incorporating texts from Jerahmeel ben Solomon (12th c., northern Italy/southern France).
  • The Hebrew Portions: Chapters 1–8 (Babel, Abraham in the furnace) and 25–28 (the Kenaz cycle) survive in Hebrew in the Chronicles of Jerahmeel.
  • Critical Status: Moses Gaster (1896, 1899) initially claimed that Jerahmeel preserved the lost Semitic original of LAB. However, Adolf Neubauer (1887), Leopold Cohn (1915), Daniel J. Harrington (1974), and Howard Jacobson (1983, 1997) proved decisively that Jerahmeel's Hebrew text is a medieval Hebrew translation made directly from a Latin manuscript of LAB.

details.intro:
The Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum (commonly abbreviated LAB, also known as Pseudo-Philo or Biblical Antiquities) is one of the most substantial and significant works of Second Temple Jewish literature. Spanning sixty-five chapters, the work is a monumental "Rewritten Bible" narrative recounting sacred history from Adam to the tragic death of King Saul. Pseudepigraphically ascribed to the 1st-century Jewish-Alexandrian philosopher Philo Judaeus—having survived in medieval Latin manuscripts alongside Latin translations of genuine Philonic treatises—the work was decisively reclaimed for Jewish scholarship by Leopold Cohn in 1898.

Scholarly consensus demonstrates that the extant Latin text was translated from a lost Greek intermediary, which itself was translated from an authentic Palestinian Hebrew original composed in the late 1st century CE (ca. 70–135 CE, or shortly before the fall of Jerusalem).

Architectural Breakdown (65 Chapters)

1. Primeval History: From Adam to the Tower of Babel (chs. 1–7):

  • Extensive genealogies enumerating descendants unmentioned in Genesis (sons and daughters of Adam, Seth, and Cain).
  • The Flood and the repopulation of the earth under Noah’s sons.
  • The Rebellion of Babel and Nimrod (chs. 5–7): Nimrod and the leaders of the earth build the Tower of Babel. Abraham, along with eleven righteous men, refuses to contribute bricks; Abraham is cast into a blazing furnace, but God sends the angel of fire (Zeruel) to rescue him unharmed, while the flames consume 84,000 onlookers.

2. The Patriarchs, Egypt, and the Exodus (chs. 8–10):

  • Covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
  • Amram's Resistance and Miriam’s Prophecy (ch. 9): Facing Pharaoh’s decree to drown male infants, Amram leads the elders of Israel in refusing celibacy, trusting in divine covenant fidelity; Miriam receives an angelic night vision foretelling that her brother Moses will save Israel.
  • Moses’ birth, preservation by Pharaoh’s daughter Thermuthis, the Plagues, and the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea.

3. The Theophany at Sinai and the Law (chs. 11–14):

  • Cosmic Sinai theophany: heaven bows down, the deeps tremble, and celestial angels tremble at the voice of God.
  • Promulgation of the Decalogue and statutory laws; the Golden Calf apostasy; Moses intercedes, smashes the tablets, and reconstructs the Tabernacle.

4. The Wilderness Wandering and the Death of Moses (chs. 15–19):

  • The twelve spies; the rebellion and subterranean destruction of Korah; the miraculous budding of Aaron’s rod.
  • Moses' Farewell and Heavenly Vision (ch. 19): Before dying, Moses is shown the celestial sanctuary, the measurements of the cosmos, the path of the stars, and the storehouses of souls; God Himself buries Moses on the high mountain in heavenly light, weeping over His servant while angels lament.

5. Joshua and the Conquest of the Land (chs. 20–24):

  • Joshua succeeds Moses; Rahab’s faith; crossing the Jordan; destruction of Jericho and Ai; renewal of the covenant at Shechem; Joshua's testament and death.

6. The Great Kenaz Epic: Judge and Deliverer (chs. 25–28):

  • The centerpiece of LAB's narrative innovation, transforming the minor biblical figure Kenaz (Judg 3:9–11) into an epic national hero:
  • Kenaz uncovers hidden idolatrous cults within the twelve tribes, casting lots and extracting confessions.
  • He receives twelve luminous celestial stones from Mount Hermon that shine in darkness and liquefy idols like water.
  • The Nocturnal Battle: Armed with divine courage and accompanied by angels (Ingethel and Zeruel) who strike the Philistines with blindness and numbness, Kenaz rides alone into the enemy camp and slaughters 100,000 Philistines in a single night.
  • Kenaz experiences an apocalyptic vision of the creation of the heavens, the firmament, and the final judgment before dying peacefully.

7. Zebul, Deborah, and the Victory over Sisera (chs. 29–33):

  • Zebul rules as righteous judge.
  • Deborah arises as prophetess, judge, and mother in Israel; her victory song over Sisera; Jael slays Sisera.
  • The Death of Deborah: A poignant testamentary farewell where the people weep and Deborah instructs them to set their hearts upon the Law, for after death no intercession is possible (ch. 33).

8. Gideon, Abimelech, and the Tragedy of Seila (chs. 34–41):

  • Gideon’s defeat of Midian; Abimelech’s murderous reign; Jair’s idolatrous shrine.
  • Jephthah and Seila (chs. 39–40): Jephthah vows to sacrifice whatever meets him first; his daughter Seila (Seila filia Iephte) voluntarily accepts her sacrificial death, asking for two months to wander the mountains.
  • The Lament of Seila: A sublime poetic dirge lamenting her unwed bridal chamber, weeping among the hills, and embracing her death as an offering to God.

9. Samson and the End of the Judges (chs. 42–47):

  • Manoah and his barren wife Eluma; the angelic annunciation; Samson's supernatural exploits and self-sacrifice against the Philistines.
  • The idol of Micah; the atrocity of the concubine of Gibeah and the war against Benjamin; Phinehas the high priest intercedes and is assumed to heaven to reappear as Elijah (ch. 48).

10. Eli, Samuel, and the Tragedy of King Saul (chs. 48–65):

  • Hannah’s prophetic song; birth and divine calling of Samuel; defeat of the Philistines and recovery of the Ark.
  • Israel requests an earthly king; Samuel anoints Saul.
  • Saul’s disobedience regarding Agag and Amalek; David anointed by Samuel; David sings mystical exorcism hymns to soothe Saul’s tormenting evil spirit (ch. 60).
  • Saul consults the Witch of Endor; Samuel rises from Sheol and pronounces irrevocable doom upon Saul.
  • Mount Gilboa: Saul commits suicide, requesting an Amalekite to dispatch him; David laments Saul and Jonathan, and is acclaimed king over Israel (ch. 65).

details.intro:
The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs is an extensive pseudepigraphon consisting of twelve farewell discourses delivered on their deathbeds by the twelve sons of Jacob (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, and Benjamin) to their assembled children.

Structure of the Individual Testaments

Each testament follows a consistent, threefold tripartite literary pattern:

1. Autobiographical / Haggadic Narrative: The patriarch recounts key episodes from his life (expanding upon Genesis), candidly confessing his primary sin (e.g., Reuben's lust, Simeon's envy, Judah's drunkenness and greed, Gad's hatred) or extolling his characteristic virtue (e.g., Issachar's simplicity, Zebulun's compassion, Joseph's self-control/chastity).

2. Moral Exhortation (Paraenesis): The patriarch warns his descendants against the spiritual perils of vice (especially porneia, anger, jealousy, and double-heartedness) and exhorts them to practice righteousness, single-minded devotion (haplotēs), and fraternal love.

3. Eschatological Prophecy and Farewell: The patriarch predicts the future apostasy, exile, and restoration of his tribe—frequently structured around the Sin-Exile-Return pattern—culminating in an apocalyptic vision of the coming Messiah(s) from the tribes of Levi and Judah, a final resurrection, and instructions for burial in the ancestral tomb at Hebron (Cave of Machpelah).
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Textual Tradition

The complete Greek text survives in 14 principal manuscripts. R. H. Charles initially classified the tradition into two recensions, $\alpha$ (MSS c, h, i) and $\beta$ (MSS a, b, d, e, f, g, j). The modern editio maior (M. de Jonge, H. J. de Jonge, H. W. Hollander, T. Korteweg) replaced this with a division into Family I (MSS b and k) and Family II (all other Greek MSS, alongside the Armenian and Slavonic versions):

  • b: Cambridge University Library, MS Ff. 1.24, fols. 203a–262b (late 10th c.; brought from Athens to England by Robert Grosseteste in the 13th c.; the base text of Sinker and de Jonge's early editions).
  • k: Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Gr. Z. 494 (coll. 331), fols. 263r–264v (mid-13th c.; preserves large extracts).
  • a: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Barocci 133, fols. 278r–309r (ca. 1270 CE).
  • c: Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, cod. Vat. gr. 731, fols. 97r–167r (13th c.).
  • d: Vatican, cod. Vat. gr. 1238, fols. 350r–380v (late 12th c.; includes significant marginal variants and scholia).
  • e: Mount Athos, Monastery of Koutloumousiou, cod. 39, fols. 180r–227r (11th c.; celebrated for containing inserted Greek translations of large sections of the Aramaic Levi Document).
  • f: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, cod. gr. 2658, fols. 41r–100v (11th c.).
  • g: Patmos, Monastery of St. John the Theologian, cod. 412, fols. 96r–148v (15th c.).
  • h: Sinai, Saint Catherine's Monastery, cod. gr. 547, fols. 195r–265v (17th c.).
  • i: Sinai, cod. gr. 548 (17th c.).
  • j: Sinai, cod. gr. 2170 (18th c.).
  • l: Mount Athos, Great Lavra, MS I 48, fols. 204r–276r (16th–17th c.; discovered and published by C. Burchard, 1966).
  • m: Ankara, Türk Tarih Kurumu, MS gr. 60, pp. 339–483 (16th c.).
  • n: Mount Athos, Monastery of Vatopedi, cod. 659 (14th c.).

B. Semitic Forebears and Witnesses (Genizah and Qumran)

1. The Aramaic Levi Document (ALD):

  • Cairo Genizah: Cambridge University Library MS T-S 16.94 (10th/11th c., cols. a–f); Oxford Bodleian MS heb. c 27, fol. 56 (10th/11th c., cols. a–d).
  • Qumran Cave 1: 1Q21 (1QTLevi; 60 fragments).

  • Greek Athos Additions: Mount Athos Koutloumousiou MS 39 preserves Greek interpolations representing a direct translation of the missing sections of ALD (prayer of Levi, priestly investiture, ritual halakhah on wood and sacrificial offerings).
  • Syriac Fragment: London, British Library Add. MS 14668, fol. 1 (6th/7th c.).

2. Hebrew Testament of Naphtali:

  • Qumran Cave 4: 4Q215 (4QTNaphtali; 1st c. BCE), preserving a genealogy of Bilhah, Jacob's prayer, and an eschatological column.
  • Medieval Hebrew Recension: Preserved in Oxford Bodleian MS Heb. d. 11 and incorporated into Moses Gaster's edition of the Chronicles of Jerahmeel (ch. 33).

3. Proto-Judah and Proto-Joseph Scrolls:

  • 3Q7 (3QTJud?); 4Q538 (4QTJud ar); 4Q539 (4QTJos ar).

  • Armenian Version: Survives in at least 48 manuscripts (oldest dated 1220 CE, Venice Mechitarist MSS 345, 1005, 1006; Jerusalem Armenian Patriarchate MSS 1925, 1927). Represents a distinct early translation (Family II), frequently preserving shorter, non-interpolated readings (studied by F. C. Conybeare, C. Burchard, and A. Hultgård).
  • Slavonic Versions: Widespread Old Church Slavonic and Serbian redactions preserved in the Tolkovaja Paleja and chronographic miscellanies (studied by A. Iatsimirskii, I. Franko, H. E. Gaylord, and T. Korteweg).
  • Latin Version: Translated from Greek MS b (Cambridge Ff. 1.24) by Bishop Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln ca. 1242 CE; survived in over 80 medieval manuscripts and exercised immense influence across Western Christendom.
  • Syriac and Coptic: Fragmentary liturgical citations and allusions.

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 53 (Eupolemus / Letters of Solomon to Hiram and Vaphris)

details.intro:
Eupolemus is one of the most prominent Jewish statesmen and historians of the Hasmonaean era. A member of a priestly aristocratic family in Jerusalem, he was chosen by Judas Maccabaeus in 161 BCE to lead the diplomatic embassy to the Roman Senate to ratify the first official Roman-Jewish treaty of mutual defense (1 Macc 8:17).

In Fragment 5, Eupolemus explicitly synchronizes his historical chronology to the fifth year of Demetrius I Soter (158/157 BCE), establishing that he composed his historical work—titled Περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ βασιλέων (On the Kings in Judaea)—in Jerusalem during the immediate aftermath of the Maccabean uprising (ca. 158 BCE).

Eupolemus's work represents a nationalistic, apologetic rewriting of 1–2 Kings and 1–2 Chronicles. Writing in Hellenistic Greek with noticeable Semitic idioms, Eupolemus sought to demonstrate that Israel's monarchic history, particularly under David and Solomon, rivaled or surpassed the wealth, imperial reach, and architectural grandeur of the great Hellenistic empires (the Seleucids and Ptolemies).

The Five Surviving Fragments

1. Fragment 1 (Moses the First Sage and the Alphabet):

  • Moses was the "first sage" (prōtos sophos). He invented the alphabet and writing, teaching it to the Jews; the Phoenicians received the alphabet from the Jews, and the Greeks in turn received it from the Phoenicians. (A direct refutation of the Greek claim that Cadmus the Phoenician invented writing).

2. Fragment 2 (David, Solomon, and the Temple):

  • The centerpiece of Eupolemus's historiography:
  • David's Empire: Extends David's conquests across Syria, Phoenicia, the Euphrates, and Arabia. God restrains David from building the temple because he is a "man of blood," commanding him to leave the task to his son Solomon, who ascends the throne at age twelve.
  • The Diplomatic Correspondence: Eupolemus fabricates formal Hellenistic royal letters exchanged between King Solomon, King Vaphris of Egypt (who dispatches 80,000 Egyptian laborers), and King Souron (Hiram) of Tyre (who sends 120,000 Tyrian craftsmen).
  • The Colossal Temple: Exaggerates the physical scale, gold plating, and bronze cast work of the Jerusalem sanctuary, turning it into the architectural wonder of the ancient world.

3. Fragment 3 (The Golden Shield):

  • Solomon dedicates a monumental golden shield in the sanctuary of the temple.

4. Fragment 4 (The Babylonian Exile):

  • King Jonachim (Jehoiakim) commits apostasy; the prophet Jeremiah warns of imminent doom. Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem, carrying away the temple vessels, while Jeremiah preserves the Ark of the Covenant.

5. Fragment 5 (Chronological Eras):

  • Calculates that from Adam to the fifth year of Demetrius (158 BCE) was exactly 5,149 years; and from the Exodus from Egypt to Demetrius was 2,580 years.
