details.intro:
The Testament of Solomon (Greek: Διαθήκη Σολομῶντος / Diatheke Solomōntos; Latin: Testamentum Salomonis) is an ancient Greek magical, demonological, and testamentary narrative that recounts how King Solomon built the Temple of Jerusalem by enslaving and commanding demons with a celestial signet ring granted to him by God through the Archangel Michael. Combining Jewish haggadic legend with Hellenistic Egyptian astrology, demonology, and folk medicine, the work functions simultaneously as an entertaining narrative of Solomon’s glory and tragic fall, and as a comprehensive handbook of demonological diagnosis and apotropaic therapy.

Modern scholarship (following C. C. McCown, D. C. Duling, and P. S. Alexander) identifies two foundational structural components:

1. The Haggadic Narrative Frame: A legendary folktale chronicling how Solomon subdued the demonic world to extract forced labor for the construction of the Temple, entertained the Queen of the South, and ultimately lost his wisdom, divine favor, and royal power through idolatrous infatuation with a foreign Jebusite/Shunammite woman.

2. The Demonological and Astrological Catalog (Onomasticon): A systematic series of interrogations wherein individual demons are brought before Solomon, forced to reveal their true names, astral affiliations, physiological ailments they cause in humans, and the specific angels or divine names capable of neutralizing their power.

Narrative Architecture (26 Chapters in McCown’s Critical Edition)

1. The Oppression of the Workman and the Heavenly Ring (ch. 1):

  • During the building of the Temple in Jerusalem, a favored young master workman is attacked nightly by an invisible vampire-demon named Ornias, who steals half his wages and sucks out his vitality through his right thumb.
  • Solomon prays in the Temple for divine aid; the Archangel Michael descends, bringing a magical signet ring (sphragis theou) engraved with a five-pointed pentalpha / Seal of Solomon.
  • Armed with the ring, the young workman hurls it at Ornias's chest, binding him and dragging him to Solomon.

2. The Interrogation and Enslavement of the Demons (chs. 2–17):

  • Solomon uses Ornias to capture and compel Beelzeboul (Beelzebub), the supreme prince of demons (prōtos tōn daimonōn).
  • Beelzeboul is forced to summon the demonic hierarchy one by one before Solomon's judgment seat:
  • Onoskelis (ch. 4): A female demon with the legs of an ass, dwelling in caves and cliffs, seducing men and driving them to ruin; thwarted by the holy name of God.
  • Asmodeus (Asmodaios, ch. 5): The destructive demon of Tobit, born of a human mother and a fallen angel. He confesses that he destroys the beauty of virgins, alienates married couples, and causes insanity; his thwarting angel is Raphael, and he is driven away by the burning liver and gall of a Glanos river-fish. Solomon forces Asmodeus to saw marble slabs for the Temple walls.
  • Tephras (ch. 7): The demon of the ash-wind, bringing darkness and eye disease.
  • The Seven World-Rulers of Darkness / Pleiades (ch. 8): Seven intertwined female spirits of Deception, Strife, Battle, Jealousy, Error, Power, and the Worst (to kakiston); bound and compelled to dig the foundations of the Temple.
  • Abezethibou (ch. 25): A ferocious, one-winged demon who was the spiritual power behind Jannes and Jambres in Egypt, hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and remained trapped in the Red Sea until summoned by Solomon.

3. The Thirty-Six Decans of the Zodiac (Stoicheia) (ch. 18):

  • Solomon summons the thirty-six astral decans (stoicheia tou kosmou), cosmic rulers who govern the human body:
  • Each decan steps forward, revealing its demonic identity, the exact illness it inflicts (e.g., headache, blindness, deafness, sciatica, spasms, fevers, delirium), and the precise angelic counter-name that forces it to flee.

4. The Queen of Sheba and the Demonic Capstone (chs. 19–24):

  • The Queen of the South visits Solomon; her servant-boy is saved from a demon of premature death.
  • A gigantic cornerstone / capstone (akrogōniaios) is too heavy for human workers; Solomon commands an aerial demon and the bound demon from the Red Sea to fly through the air and hoist the colossal stone directly to the pinnacle of the Temple (22:7–23:4).

5. Solomon's Idolatrous Fall and Final Testament (chs. 25–26):

  • In his old age, Solomon falls madly in love with a beautiful Jebusite woman.
  • Her pagan priests refuse to grant her to Solomon unless he worships Moloch and Raphan. When Solomon hesitates, the woman presents him with five grasshoppers and demands that he crush them in Moloch's name.
  • Overcome by lust, Solomon crushes the insects; instantly, the Holy Spirit and divine glory depart from him.
  • His signet ring loses its power; demons rise up in mockery; enemies revolt across his kingdom.
  • Broken and disgraced, Solomon writes this Testament as a solemn admonition to all humanity, warning against the snares of women, pride, and idolatry.
details.manuscripts:
The Testament of Solomon survives in over a dozen Greek manuscripts dating from the 12th to the 17th centuries, categorized into four distinct recensions (A, B, C, D) by Chester Charlton McCown.

A. The Greek Manuscript Recensions

1. Recension A (The Long, Primitive Text):

  • MS P (Paris, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, MS gr. 500, fols. 71r–93v): 15th century; the base text for the editions of F. F. Fleck, J.-P. Migne, and F. C. Conybeare.
  • MS H (Jerusalem, Patriarchal Library, Holy Saba MS 422): 12th/14th century; an important Eastern monastic witness.

2. Recension B (The Expanded/Glossed Text):

  • MS I (Paris, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, MS gr. 38, fols. 138r–164r): 16th century.
  • MS Q (Mount Athos, Dionysiou Monastery MS 204): 16th century.

3. Recension C (The Re-ordered/Apotropaic Text):

  • MS L (London, British Library, MS Harleian 5596, fols. 8v–18r): 15th century; incorporates numerous magical recipes and incantations.

4. Recension D (The Abridged/Epitomized Text):

  • MS N (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. Theol. Gr. 334): 15th century.
  • MS V (Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Cod. Vat. Gr. 2008): 15th century.

5. The Papyrus Fragment:

  • Papyrus Vindobonensis Graecus 39707 (Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek): 5th century CE; preserves portions of chapter 18 (the Decans), proving that the text circulated in Byzantine Egypt by the 5th century.

B. Ancient Versions and Cognate Magico-Medical Texts

  • Arabic Version: Preserved in Christian Arabic manuscripts cataloged by Georg Graf (Geschichte der christlichen arabischen Literatur, 1:210, 245).
  • The Hebrew and Aramaic Solomonic Magical Tradition: While TSol survives in Greek, its traditions parallel Aramaic incantation bowls, the Cairo Genizah magical texts, and the Sefer ha-Razim (Book of Mysteries).
  • The Hygromanteia and the Key of Solomon: In late Byzantium and the Latin West, TSol spawned a vast family of Solomonic grimoires, including the Hygromanteia (The Magical Treatise of Solomon, ed. P. Torijano, 2002) and the Clavicula Salomonis (The Key of Solomon).

details.intro: The Testament of Solomon tells how Solomon, given a ring by the archangel Michael, controls the demons, questions each one about its name, activity and the angel who thwarts it, and makes them build the Temple. It ends with Solomon's fall into idolatry.
details.provenance: The work is Christian in its present form, though it draws on Jewish magical and demonological traditions. Its present form is usually dated to the early 3rd c. CE, drawing on traditions that may go back to the 1st c. Its Greek manuscripts differ so much that they represent several recensions.

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 46 (History of the Rechabites (Story of Zosimus))

details.intro:
The History of the Rechabites (also preserved under the titles The Story, Apocalypse, or Testament of Zosimus) is a composite ancient narrative recounting the supernatural voyage of the desert anchorite Zosimus to the pristine, earthly paradise of the Blessed Ones—identified as the descendants of Jonadab, son of Rechab (the Rechabites of Jeremiah 35).

Literary Stratigraphy: Frame and Jewish Core

Textual and source-critical investigations (notably by M. R. James, J. H. Charlesworth, E. G. Martin, and C. H. Knights) demonstrate that the work consists of two primary literary strata:

1. The Core "History of the Rechabites" (Chapters 8–10):

  • A distinct Second Temple Jewish haggadic narrative composed in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Jewish-Greek (1st c. BCE–1st c. CE).
  • Expanding on Jeremiah 35, the narrative explains how during the reign of King Zedekiah, the Rechabites were pressured to abandon the ascetic ordinances of their ancestor Jonadab (to drink no wine, sow no seed, and inhabit no stone houses).
  • When they refused, Zedekiah threw them into prison. God miraculously delivered them, and angels transported them across an impenetrable Ocean of Clouds and Darkness to an Edenic paradise isolated from the corrupt outside world.

2. The Christian Monastic Frame: "The Story of Zosimus" (Chapters 1–7, 11–18):

  • Composed in Byzantine monastic circles (4th–6th c. CE) to adapt the ancient Jewish utopian tale into a model of Christian ascetic contemplation (hesychia).
  • Zosimus spends 40 years praying in the desert to be granted a vision of the Blessed Ones. He is guided by an angel and animals to the banks of an impassable river of darkness/cloud (Eikos), conveyed across on the branches of two sentient trees, spends seven days interviewing the Rechabites, receives their written tablets, and is returned to his monastery to commit his testament to writing before dying.
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Witnesses

  • A: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, cod. gr. 1217, fols. 145a–153b (12th c.; base text for M. R. James's editio princeps).
  • B: Oxford, Bodleian Library, cod. Canon. gr. 19, fols. 289a–294a (15th/16th c.; preserves chs. 1.1–9.10).
  • C: Moscow, State Historical Museum, Synod. gr. 290 (Vladimir 14), fols. 112b–118b (16th c.).
  • D: Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, cod. Vat. gr. 1631, fols. 222b–227a (11th c.; missing fol. containing 16.8b–21.5a).
  • E: Moscow, Synod. gr. 3 (13th c.).
  • F: Moscow, Synod. gr. 351 (15th c.).
  • Lost Witnesses: Berlin, Deutsche Staatsbibliothek gr. qu. 22.7 (destroyed in WWII); Dresden, Bibliotheca Regia gr. A.187–18 (destroyed in WWII).

B. Syriac Witnesses

The Syriac textual tradition represents the most intact, coherent, and expansive recension of the History of the Rechabites:

  • Paris, BnF syr. 236, fols. 156b–167b (12th c.; published by F. Nau, 1898–1899).
  • Birmingham, Selly Oak Colleges, Mingana Syr. 21, fols. 17b–26b (ca. 1600 CE); and Mingana Syr. 40, fols. 26a–34a (ca. 1750 CE).
  • Cambridge, MA, Harvard College Library, Syr. 33 (formerly Union Theological Seminary 33).
  • Tehran, Private Chaldean Manuscript (dated 16th c., described by A. Desreumaux, 1994).
  • Krasnoyarsk / St. Petersburg MS (Syriac restored MS studied by J.-M. Sauget).

C. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Witnesses

Known as The History of the Blessed Ones Who Lived in the Days of Jeremiah the Prophet (often included in the Ethiopic Acts of the Martyrs and the Synaxarium):

  • London, British Library, Orient. 660 and 661; Orient. 683, fols. 87a–98b (edited and translated by E. A. Wallis Budge, 1896/1928).
  • Paris, BnF, d'Abbadie MSS 145 and 179.

D. Slavonic, Arabic, and Armenian Versions

  • Old Church Slavonic: Widespread in early Russian and South Slavic miscellanies under the title The Journey of Zosimus to the Brahmans/Blessed (edited by I. Franko, A. I. Iatsimirskii, and N. S. Tikhonravov). The transliteration Raxmanom demonstrates direct lexical cross-pollination with the Alexander Romance traditions of the Indian Brahmans.
  • Arabic and Karshuni: Preserved in dozens of Christian-Arabic manuscripts throughout the Levant and Egypt (catalogued by Georg Graf and E. G. Martin).
  • Armenian: Preserved in synaxarion collections and monastic anthologies.

concordance.ditommaso: Ch. 21 (Ascension of Isaiah / Testament of Hezekiah)

details.intro:
The Ascension of Isaiah (Ascensio Isaiae / Ἀναβατικὸν Ἡσαΐου) is a composite apocalypse combining ancient Jewish haggadic traditions with early Jewish-Christian visionary literature. Redacted in its final form in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE (likely in Roman Syria or Asia Minor), the work consists of three historically and thematically distinct components:

1. The Martyrdom of Isaiah (Asc. Isa. 1:1–3:12; 5:1–16):

  • An ancient Jewish narrative composed in Semitic (Hebrew or Aramaic) during the 1st century BCE or 1st century CE. King Hezekiah instructs his wicked son Manasseh. Upon Manasseh’s accession, the demonic ruler Beliar (Sammael) inspires apostasy and idolatry in Jerusalem. Isaiah flees with his prophetic disciples (including Habakkuk and Joel) to a mountain near Bethlehem. The Samaritan false prophet Belkira (Malkira) denounces Isaiah to Manasseh. Isaiah is arrested and horribly executed by being sawn in two with a wooden saw (serratus sectus est). Throughout the ordeal, Isaiah converses with the Holy Spirit, shedding neither tears nor uttering cries.
  • Ancient External Attestations: Alluded to in the New Testament (Heb 11:37: "they were sawn in two"); Justin Martyr (Dialogus cum Tryphone 120.5); Tertullian (De patientia 14; Scorpiace 8); Origen (Comm. in Mt. 13.57; Epistula ad Africanum 9); and the Babylonian Talmud (b. Yevamot 49b; b. Sanhedrin 103b).

2. The Testament of Hezekiah (Asc. Isa. 3:13–4:22):

  • An independent Christian apocalyptic interpolation dating from the late 1st century CE (ca. 80–100 CE). Isaiah delivers a prospective vision of the descent of the Beloved (Christ), His ministry with the Twelve, His crucifixion, and His resurrection. He foretells the corruption, lawlessness, and greed of the post-apostolic elders and bishops, followed by the descent of the cosmic prince Beliar in the likeness of the matricidal Roman emperor Nero ("a lawless king, the murderer of his mother"). Beliar-Nero works deceptive signs, establishes worldwide imperial worship, and persecutes the faithful for 3 years, 7 months, and 27 days (1335 days), after which the Lord arrives from the seventh heaven with his angelic host to cast Beliar and his armies into Gehenna.

3. The Vision / Ascension of Isaiah (Asc. Isa. 6:1–11:43):

  • An early 2nd-century CE (ca. 110–130 CE) visionary apocalypse originally circulating independently. In the 20th year of Hezekiah, Isaiah falls into an ecstatic trance before the king and prophets. A radiant angel guides him in an ascent through the seven heavens: in the second through fifth heavens, he witnesses the angelic orders praising the divine throne; in the sixth heaven, all praise is directed upward in unison; in the seventh heaven, Isaiah sees the righteous souls clothed in light, with their garments, thrones, and crowns awaiting them.
  • The Cosmic Descensus and Ascensus: God commissions the Beloved to descend through all seven heavens down to the earthly realm and the underworld (Sheol). In His descent, the Beloved conceals His glory, transforming His appearance in each heaven so that the resident archons do not recognize Him. On earth, He is born miraculously of the virgin Mary without labour or pain (11:2–14), lives unrecognized, is crucified by the rulers of the cosmos under the instigation of Beliar, rises on the third day, and ascends back to the seventh heaven in full, dazzling majesty, receiving the adoration of all cosmic powers.
details.manuscripts:
While fragmentary remains survive in Greek, Latin, Coptic, and Slavonic, the complete text of chapters 1–11 is preserved only in classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic):

A. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

The primary witness for the entire work, preserved in nine manuscripts:

  • MS A (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Aeth. d. 13, fols. 95r–115r): 15th-century codex; the base text for Laurence and Dillmann.
  • MS B (London, British Library, MS Or. 501, fols. 62r–69v): 15th century.
  • MS C (London, British Library, MS Or. 503, fols. 57r–62v): 18th century.
  • MS E (EMML 1768, fols. 83r–88v): 15th century.
  • MS F (EMML 3067, fols. 99r–117v): 15th century.
  • MS G (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. Aeth. 263, fols. 85v–104v): 14th/15th century.
  • MS H (Paris, BnF, d'Abbadie 195, fols. 74r–87r): 17th/18th century.
  • MS I (Paris, BnF, d'Abbadie 156, fols. 46r–52v): 18th century.
  • MS L (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod. Aeth. 63): 18th/19th century.

B. Greek Tradition

1. Amherst Papyrus 1 (P. Amherst I.1; London, Pierpont Morgan Library / British Library):

  • 5th-century CE papyrus preserving Greek Asc. Isa. 2:4b–4:4a (the flight of Isaiah and the beginning of the Testament of Hezekiah).
  • Editio princeps: Grenfell, B. P., and A. S. Hunt. The Amherst Papyri. London, 1900, 1:1–22.

2. Patristic Citations:

  • Origen (Comm. in Mt. 13.57; Ep. ad Afr. 9).
  • Didymus the Blind (Comm. in Eccl., P. Tura; ed. D. Lührmann, ZAW 104 [1992]: 231–249 at 233–239).
  • Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 40.2.2–4; 67.3.3).

3. Medieval Greek "Legend of Isaiah":

  • A Byzantine hagiographical adaptation of the Ascension preserved in Paris BnF gr. 1534 (12th cent.) and Vat. Palat. gr. 27 (10th/11th cent.); edited by C. Tischendorf (1866) and B. Flusin in CCSA 8 (1995).

C. Latin Tradition

Two independent partial Latin witnesses:

  • Lat$^1$ (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. Lat. 5750, fols. 278–284): 5th/6th-century palimpsest uncial preserving Asc. Isa. 2:14–3:13 and 7:1–19 (ed. Angelo Mai 1828; C. Leonardi in CCSA 7, 1995).

details.intro: The Prayer of Manasseh (CAVT 178 / CANT 203) is a short penitential prayer attributed to King Manasseh of Judah during his Babylonian captivity (2 Chron 33:11-13). Extant in Greek in the Septuagint Odes (Ode 12) and the Didascalia Apostolorum, and in Latin as an appendix to the Vulgate. This edition provides the Greek text from H. B. Swete, The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint, Vol. 3 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1896), pp. 802-804, in parallel with the Clementine Vulgate Latin text.
details.manuscripts: Greek witnesses include Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Turicensis (T), Codex Veronensis (R), and the Didascalia Apostolorum. Latin witnesses include the Clementine Vulgate Appendix and medieval Parisian Bibles.

details.intro:
4 Ezra was originally composed as a pseudepigraphal Jewish apocalypse, most likely in Hebrew, at some point after 70 CE (see discussion below).

The original Hebrew version, which is now lost, was translated into Greek. The Greek version, which survives only in fragmentary quotations and paraphrases by later Christian authors, was translated into Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian and Coptic. Additional translations from the Latin and Syriac versions also exist (Stone, 4 Ezra, 2). The apocalypse takes the name, 4 Ezra, from the Latin version, which was labeled 4 Esdras to distinguish it from 1 Esdras (=Ezra), 2 Esdras (=Nehemiah), and 3 Esdras (the apocryphal book now normally designated 1 Esdras). To make matters more complicated, 4 Ezra is often called 2 Esdras by modern English translations, such as the KJV, RSV and NRSV, that adopt the traditional Hebrew names for Ezra and Nehemiah and include the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras. The Latin version included as an appendix to the Vulgate was transformed into a Christian text by the addition of an introduction (chapters 1-2) and conclusion (chapters 15-16), commonly designated 5th and 6th Ezra by modern scholars. Most modern English translations follow the Vulgate in printing the Christian 5th and 6th Ezra along with the Jewish apocalypse of 4 Ezra. As a result, the chapter and verse numbering of the apocalypse begin at chapter 3 verse 1.
details.provenance:
Date

Terminus ante quem

The earliest definite quotation from 4 Ezra occurs in Clement of Alexandria’s Stromateis. Since Stromateis is dated to the end of the 2nd century CE, 4 Ezra must have been written and translated into Greek no later than the end of the 2nd century. If the possible reference in Barnabas 12:1 is accepted as a quotation, 4 Ezra will have been composed by the end of the first century.

4 Ezra is also closely related to 2 Baruch, which is normally dated to the end of the first or the beginning of the second century, but the precise date of 2 Baruch is uncertain, and the nature of the relationship between the two documents remains disputed. (See the introduction to 2 Baruch for more discussion.)

Terminus post quem

4 Ezra’s preoccupation with the destruction of Jerusalem indicates that the book was composed after 70 CE, but near enough to the event still to raise deep theological questions. If the “three heads” in Ezra’s eagle vision (12:22-28), that appear immediately before a description of the “end” (12:29-36), are coded references to Vespasian and his two sons Titus and Domitian, the book will have been composed during the reign of Domitian (81-96 CE). This corresponds to the reference to “the thirtieth year after the destruction of the city” in 3:1, although this date may simply recall Ezek 1:1 (cf. Stone, 4 Ezra, 9-10; Schürer III.1, 299-300).

Original Language

Although L. Gry argued that 4 Ezra was originally composed in Aramaic, most recent scholars agree with Wellhausen, Gunkel and, more recently, Klijn, that the original language was Hebrew (Schürer III.1, 300; Stone, 4 Ezra, 10-11; Metzger, “4 Ezra,” 519-520).

details.intro:
4 Ezra (chapters 3–14 of the composite book preserved in the Latin Vulgate as 2 Esdras / 4 Esdras) is a Jewish apocalypse composed in Roman Palestine (Judea) around 95–100 CE, thirty years after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple by Titus in 70 CE (historicized under the pseudonym of "Salathiel who is also Ezra" thirty years after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, 3:1). Written originally in Hebrew or Aramaic, translated early into Greek, and transmitted through multiple ancient versions, the apocalypse is structured into seven visionary episodes:

1. First Episode (3:1–5:20): Ezra laments in Babylon over the desolation of Zion and the prosperity of pagan Rome. The archangel Uriel rebukes him, declaring that human understanding cannot fathom divine ways, that the present age is pregnant with evil because of Adam's "evil heart" (cor malignum), and that the end-time harvest must await the predetermined number of the righteous.

2. Second Episode (5:21–6:34): Ezra questions why God delivered His chosen people to the nations. Uriel reveals that creation has grown old like an aging mother, and explains the transition of cosmic epochs: "Esau is the end of this age, and Jacob is the beginning of the age that follows" (6:9).

3. Third Episode (6:35–9:25): The lengthiest theological dialogue, exploring the fate of souls after death, the intermediate rest in celestial chambers/promptuaries, the 400-year temporal kingdom of the Messiah, the final death of all mortals (including the Messiah) followed by seven days of primeval silence, the universal resurrection, and the irreversible judgment where no intercession is possible for the damned (the famous "Lost Fragment," 7:36–105).

4. Fourth Episode (9:26–10:59): Ezra sees a weeping, disheveled woman mourning the sudden death of her only son on his wedding night. As Ezra consoles her, she is transfigured into a vast, shining, founded city. Uriel explains that the woman is Zion, her thirty barren years represent the period before Solomon, her son is the Temple destroyed by the Romans, and the radiant city is the eschatological heavenly Jerusalem.

5. Fifth Episode: The Eagle Vision (11:1–12:51): An imperial eagle with twelve wings, three heads, and eight contrary winglets arises from the sea, exercising oppressive global dominion. A roaring lion emerges from the forest and pronounces the eagle's annihilation. Uriel identifies the eagle as the fourth kingdom of Daniel 7 (Rome, reigning from Julius Caesar and Augustus through the Flavian emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian), and the lion as the Davidic Messiah who will judge and destroy the empire.

6. Sixth Episode: The Man from the Sea (13:1–58): A cosmic man rises from the depths of the sea, flies with the clouds of heaven, carves out a great mountain (Mount Zion) without hands, incinerates a hostile attacking army with a stream of fire and flaming breath from his mouth, and then gathers a peaceful multitude: the lost Ten Tribes of Israel, who had crossed the Euphrates to the distant, unpolluted land of Arzareth.

7. Seventh Episode: The Voice from the Bush and the Restoration of the Scriptures (14:1–48): God calls Ezra from a thornbush as He did Moses. Ezra drinks a cup of glowing water like fire, receiving divine wisdom for forty days. Assisted by five rapid scribes, he dictates 94 books: 24 exoteric books to be made public for the worthy and unworthy alike (the Hebrew biblical canon), and 70 esoteric books reserved exclusively for the wise.
details.manuscripts:
The original Semitic text is lost, but the text is preserved across eight major ancient language traditions, all translated directly or indirectly from a lost Greek translation:

A. Latin Tradition (Versio Latina)

The Latin version is the primary witness for Western biblical transmission. It falls into two groups depending on the presence of the "Missing Fragment" (7:36–105), which was omitted from the Clementine Vulgate because a single leaf had been deliberately cut out of the primary archetype:

  • MS S (Codex Sangermanensis I; Paris, BnF lat. 11504–11505): Copied at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 821/822 CE. Archetype of all European Vulgate manuscripts lacking 7:36–105.
  • The Eight Independent Latin Manuscripts (preserving the missing section):
  • MS A (Codex Ambianensis; Amiens, Bibliothèque Municipale 10): 9th-century manuscript in which Robert L. Bensly discovered the "Lost Fragment" in 1874.
  • MS C (Codex Complutensis 1; Madrid, Universidad Central 31): 9th/10th century.
  • MS E (Codex Epternacensis; Luxembourg, Bibliothèque Nationale 264): Dated 1051–1081 CE.
  • MS L (Codex Legionensis 2; León, Real Colegiata de San Isidoro I,3): Dated 1162 CE.
  • MS M (Codex Mazarinaeus; Paris, Bibliothèque Mazarine 3–4): 11th/12th century.
  • MS N (Codex Bruxellensis; Brussels, Bibliothèque Royale 9107–9110): 12th century.
  • MS V (Codex Abulensis / Avila; Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional Vitr. 15–1): 12th/13th century.

B. Syriac Tradition (Versio Syra)

  • Preserved complete in the famous 6th/7th-century Peshitta codex: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 Inf. (fols. 267v–276v). Provides the most faithful and reliable oriental translation of the lost Greek text.
  • Critical Editions:
  • Ceriani, Antonio Maria. Liber IV Esdrae syriace. Monumenta Sacra et Profana 5. Milan, 1868, pp. 41–111; and photolithographic edition, MSP 6, 1876.
  • Bidawid, R. J. "4 Esdras." In The Old Testament in Syriac according to the Peshitta Version, Part IV, fasc. 3. Leiden: Brill, 1973.

C. Greek Citations and Fragments

  • Patristic Citations: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.22.149.3 and 3.16.100.3; Apostolic Constitutions 2.14.9 and 8.7.6.
  • Papyrus Fragment: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus VII 1010 (4th cent. CE, containing 4 Ezra 15–16 [= 6 Ezra]).
  • Palimpsest Fragment: Rubinkiewicz, Ryszard. "Un fragment grec du IV$^e$ Livre d’Esdras (chapitres XI et XII)." Le Muséon 89 (1976): 75–89 [Preserves Greek text of the Eagle Vision in codex Marcianus Gr. 498].
  • Denis, Albert-Marie. Fragmenta pseudepigraphorum quae supersunt graeca. PVTG 3. Leiden: Brill, 1970, pp. 130–132.

D. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

  • Preserved in over 20 manuscripts (e.g., Tānāsee 51; Paris BnF éth. 50; British Library Add. 16188).
  • Laurence, Richard. Primi Ezrae libri, qui apud Vulgatam appellatur quartus, versio Aethiopica. Oxford: Parker, 1820 [Editio princeps].
  • Dillmann, August. Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici. V. Libri apocryphi. Berlin: Asher, 1894, pp. 152–193 [Critical edition].

E. Arabic Traditions

Two distinct Arabic translations made from different Vorlagen:

  • Arabic 1 (Arab. 1): Oxford, Bodleian MS Huntington 254 (translated from the Syriac; ed. Ewald 1863).
  • Arabic 2 (Arab. 2): Mount Sinai Arabic MS 589 (9th/10th cent. CE; ed. A. Drint, CSCO 563–564, 1997).

F. Georgian Tradition

  • Preserved in the Jerusalem Georgian MS 43 (11th/12th cent.) and Mount Athos Iviron MS (10th cent.).
  • Edition: Blake, Robert P. "The Georgian Version of Fourth Esdras from the Jerusalem Manuscript." Harvard Theological Review 19 (1926): 299–375; and "from the Athos Manuscript," HTR 22 (1929): 57–105.

G. Armenian Tradition

  • Preserved in 28 biblical manuscripts, representing a highly paraphrastic, interpretive (targumic) recension.
  • Editions:
  • Yovsēp'ianc', Sahak. Ankanon girk' Hin Ktakaranac'. Venice: San Lazzaro, 1896, pp. 251–299.

  • Stone, Michael E. A Textual Commentary on the Armenian Version of IV Ezra. SBLSCS 34. Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1990.

H. Coptic Tradition

  • Sahidic papyrus fragment preserving 4 Ezra 13:29–48.
  • Edition: Leipoldt, Johannes, and Bruno Violet. "Ein saidisches Bruchstück des vierten Esrabuches." Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde 41 (1904): 138–140.

details.provenance: The date is uncertain; estimates range from the 2nd to the 9th century CE. The work depends on 4 Ezra and belongs to a family of Ezra apocalypses that includes the Vision of Ezra and the Apocalypse of Sedrach.
details.manuscripts: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS gr. 929 (15th cent.), fols. 512-521.

details.intro:
4 Ezra (chapters 3–14 of the composite book preserved in the Latin Vulgate as 2 Esdras / 4 Esdras) is a Jewish apocalypse composed in Roman Palestine (Judea) around 95–100 CE, thirty years after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple by Titus in 70 CE (historicized under the pseudonym of "Salathiel who is also Ezra" thirty years after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, 3:1). Written originally in Hebrew or Aramaic, translated early into Greek, and transmitted through multiple ancient versions, the apocalypse is structured into seven visionary episodes:

1. First Episode (3:1–5:20): Ezra laments in Babylon over the desolation of Zion and the prosperity of pagan Rome. The archangel Uriel rebukes him, declaring that human understanding cannot fathom divine ways, that the present age is pregnant with evil because of Adam's "evil heart" (cor malignum), and that the end-time harvest must await the predetermined number of the righteous.

2. Second Episode (5:21–6:34): Ezra questions why God delivered His chosen people to the nations. Uriel reveals that creation has grown old like an aging mother, and explains the transition of cosmic epochs: "Esau is the end of this age, and Jacob is the beginning of the age that follows" (6:9).

3. Third Episode (6:35–9:25): The lengthiest theological dialogue, exploring the fate of souls after death, the intermediate rest in celestial chambers/promptuaries, the 400-year temporal kingdom of the Messiah, the final death of all mortals (including the Messiah) followed by seven days of primeval silence, the universal resurrection, and the irreversible judgment where no intercession is possible for the damned (the famous "Lost Fragment," 7:36–105).

4. Fourth Episode (9:26–10:59): Ezra sees a weeping, disheveled woman mourning the sudden death of her only son on his wedding night. As Ezra consoles her, she is transfigured into a vast, shining, founded city. Uriel explains that the woman is Zion, her thirty barren years represent the period before Solomon, her son is the Temple destroyed by the Romans, and the radiant city is the eschatological heavenly Jerusalem.

5. Fifth Episode: The Eagle Vision (11:1–12:51): An imperial eagle with twelve wings, three heads, and eight contrary winglets arises from the sea, exercising oppressive global dominion. A roaring lion emerges from the forest and pronounces the eagle's annihilation. Uriel identifies the eagle as the fourth kingdom of Daniel 7 (Rome, reigning from Julius Caesar and Augustus through the Flavian emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian), and the lion as the Davidic Messiah who will judge and destroy the empire.

6. Sixth Episode: The Man from the Sea (13:1–58): A cosmic man rises from the depths of the sea, flies with the clouds of heaven, carves out a great mountain (Mount Zion) without hands, incinerates a hostile attacking army with a stream of fire and flaming breath from his mouth, and then gathers a peaceful multitude: the lost Ten Tribes of Israel, who had crossed the Euphrates to the distant, unpolluted land of Arzareth.

7. Seventh Episode: The Voice from the Bush and the Restoration of the Scriptures (14:1–48): God calls Ezra from a thornbush as He did Moses. Ezra drinks a cup of glowing water like fire, receiving divine wisdom for forty days. Assisted by five rapid scribes, he dictates 94 books: 24 exoteric books to be made public for the worthy and unworthy alike (the Hebrew biblical canon), and 70 esoteric books reserved exclusively for the wise.
details.manuscripts:
The original Semitic text is lost, but the text is preserved across eight major ancient language traditions, all translated directly or indirectly from a lost Greek translation:

A. Latin Tradition (Versio Latina)

The Latin version is the primary witness for Western biblical transmission. It falls into two groups depending on the presence of the "Missing Fragment" (7:36–105), which was omitted from the Clementine Vulgate because a single leaf had been deliberately cut out of the primary archetype:

  • MS S (Codex Sangermanensis I; Paris, BnF lat. 11504–11505): Copied at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 821/822 CE. Archetype of all European Vulgate manuscripts lacking 7:36–105.
  • The Eight Independent Latin Manuscripts (preserving the missing section):
  • MS A (Codex Ambianensis; Amiens, Bibliothèque Municipale 10): 9th-century manuscript in which Robert L. Bensly discovered the "Lost Fragment" in 1874.
  • MS C (Codex Complutensis 1; Madrid, Universidad Central 31): 9th/10th century.
  • MS E (Codex Epternacensis; Luxembourg, Bibliothèque Nationale 264): Dated 1051–1081 CE.
  • MS L (Codex Legionensis 2; León, Real Colegiata de San Isidoro I,3): Dated 1162 CE.
  • MS M (Codex Mazarinaeus; Paris, Bibliothèque Mazarine 3–4): 11th/12th century.
  • MS N (Codex Bruxellensis; Brussels, Bibliothèque Royale 9107–9110): 12th century.
  • MS V (Codex Abulensis / Avila; Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional Vitr. 15–1): 12th/13th century.

B. Syriac Tradition (Versio Syra)

  • Preserved complete in the famous 6th/7th-century Peshitta codex: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 Inf. (fols. 267v–276v). Provides the most faithful and reliable oriental translation of the lost Greek text.
  • Critical Editions:
  • Ceriani, Antonio Maria. Liber IV Esdrae syriace. Monumenta Sacra et Profana 5. Milan, 1868, pp. 41–111; and photolithographic edition, MSP 6, 1876.
  • Bidawid, R. J. "4 Esdras." In The Old Testament in Syriac according to the Peshitta Version, Part IV, fasc. 3. Leiden: Brill, 1973.

C. Greek Citations and Fragments

  • Patristic Citations: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.22.149.3 and 3.16.100.3; Apostolic Constitutions 2.14.9 and 8.7.6.
  • Papyrus Fragment: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus VII 1010 (4th cent. CE, containing 4 Ezra 15–16 [= 6 Ezra]).
  • Palimpsest Fragment: Rubinkiewicz, Ryszard. "Un fragment grec du IV$^e$ Livre d’Esdras (chapitres XI et XII)." Le Muséon 89 (1976): 75–89 [Preserves Greek text of the Eagle Vision in codex Marcianus Gr. 498].
  • Denis, Albert-Marie. Fragmenta pseudepigraphorum quae supersunt graeca. PVTG 3. Leiden: Brill, 1970, pp. 130–132.

D. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

  • Preserved in over 20 manuscripts (e.g., Tānāsee 51; Paris BnF éth. 50; British Library Add. 16188).
  • Laurence, Richard. Primi Ezrae libri, qui apud Vulgatam appellatur quartus, versio Aethiopica. Oxford: Parker, 1820 [Editio princeps].
  • Dillmann, August. Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici. V. Libri apocryphi. Berlin: Asher, 1894, pp. 152–193 [Critical edition].

E. Arabic Traditions

Two distinct Arabic translations made from different Vorlagen:

  • Arabic 1 (Arab. 1): Oxford, Bodleian MS Huntington 254 (translated from the Syriac; ed. Ewald 1863).
  • Arabic 2 (Arab. 2): Mount Sinai Arabic MS 589 (9th/10th cent. CE; ed. A. Drint, CSCO 563–564, 1997).

F. Georgian Tradition

  • Preserved in the Jerusalem Georgian MS 43 (11th/12th cent.) and Mount Athos Iviron MS (10th cent.).
  • Edition: Blake, Robert P. "The Georgian Version of Fourth Esdras from the Jerusalem Manuscript." Harvard Theological Review 19 (1926): 299–375; and "from the Athos Manuscript," HTR 22 (1929): 57–105.

G. Armenian Tradition

  • Preserved in 28 biblical manuscripts, representing a highly paraphrastic, interpretive (targumic) recension.
  • Editions:
  • Yovsēp'ianc', Sahak. Ankanon girk' Hin Ktakaranac'. Venice: San Lazzaro, 1896, pp. 251–299.
  • Stone, Michael E. The Armenian Version of IV Ezra. University of Pennsylvania Armenian Texts and Studies 1. Missoula: Scholars Press, 1979.
  • Stone, Michael E. A Textual Commentary on the Armenian Version of IV Ezra. SBLSCS 34. Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1990.

H. Coptic Tradition

  • Sahidic papyrus fragment preserving 4 Ezra 13:29–48.
  • Edition: Leipoldt, Johannes, and Bruno Violet. "Ein saidisches Bruchstück des vierten Esrabuches." Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde 41 (1904): 138–140.

details.intro:
4 Ezra (chapters 3–14 of the composite book preserved in the Latin Vulgate as 2 Esdras / 4 Esdras) is a Jewish apocalypse composed in Roman Palestine (Judea) around 95–100 CE, thirty years after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple by Titus in 70 CE (historicized under the pseudonym of "Salathiel who is also Ezra" thirty years after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, 3:1). Written originally in Hebrew or Aramaic, translated early into Greek, and transmitted through multiple ancient versions, the apocalypse is structured into seven visionary episodes:

1. First Episode (3:1–5:20): Ezra laments in Babylon over the desolation of Zion and the prosperity of pagan Rome. The archangel Uriel rebukes him, declaring that human understanding cannot fathom divine ways, that the present age is pregnant with evil because of Adam's "evil heart" (cor malignum), and that the end-time harvest must await the predetermined number of the righteous.

2. Second Episode (5:21–6:34): Ezra questions why God delivered His chosen people to the nations. Uriel reveals that creation has grown old like an aging mother, and explains the transition of cosmic epochs: "Esau is the end of this age, and Jacob is the beginning of the age that follows" (6:9).

3. Third Episode (6:35–9:25): The lengthiest theological dialogue, exploring the fate of souls after death, the intermediate rest in celestial chambers/promptuaries, the 400-year temporal kingdom of the Messiah, the final death of all mortals (including the Messiah) followed by seven days of primeval silence, the universal resurrection, and the irreversible judgment where no intercession is possible for the damned (the famous "Lost Fragment," 7:36–105).

4. Fourth Episode (9:26–10:59): Ezra sees a weeping, disheveled woman mourning the sudden death of her only son on his wedding night. As Ezra consoles her, she is transfigured into a vast, shining, founded city. Uriel explains that the woman is Zion, her thirty barren years represent the period before Solomon, her son is the Temple destroyed by the Romans, and the radiant city is the eschatological heavenly Jerusalem.

5. Fifth Episode: The Eagle Vision (11:1–12:51): An imperial eagle with twelve wings, three heads, and eight contrary winglets arises from the sea, exercising oppressive global dominion. A roaring lion emerges from the forest and pronounces the eagle's annihilation. Uriel identifies the eagle as the fourth kingdom of Daniel 7 (Rome, reigning from Julius Caesar and Augustus through the Flavian emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian), and the lion as the Davidic Messiah who will judge and destroy the empire.

6. Sixth Episode: The Man from the Sea (13:1–58): A cosmic man rises from the depths of the sea, flies with the clouds of heaven, carves out a great mountain (Mount Zion) without hands, incinerates a hostile attacking army with a stream of fire and flaming breath from his mouth, and then gathers a peaceful multitude: the lost Ten Tribes of Israel, who had crossed the Euphrates to the distant, unpolluted land of Arzareth.

7. Seventh Episode: The Voice from the Bush and the Restoration of the Scriptures (14:1–48): God calls Ezra from a thornbush as He did Moses. Ezra drinks a cup of glowing water like fire, receiving divine wisdom for forty days. Assisted by five rapid scribes, he dictates 94 books: 24 exoteric books to be made public for the worthy and unworthy alike (the Hebrew biblical canon), and 70 esoteric books reserved exclusively for the wise.
details.manuscripts:
The original Semitic text is lost, but the text is preserved across eight major ancient language traditions, all translated directly or indirectly from a lost Greek translation:

A. Latin Tradition (Versio Latina)

The Latin version is the primary witness for Western biblical transmission. It falls into two groups depending on the presence of the "Missing Fragment" (7:36–105), which was omitted from the Clementine Vulgate because a single leaf had been deliberately cut out of the primary archetype:

  • MS S (Codex Sangermanensis I; Paris, BnF lat. 11504–11505): Copied at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 821/822 CE. Archetype of all European Vulgate manuscripts lacking 7:36–105.
  • The Eight Independent Latin Manuscripts (preserving the missing section):
  • MS A (Codex Ambianensis; Amiens, Bibliothèque Municipale 10): 9th-century manuscript in which Robert L. Bensly discovered the "Lost Fragment" in 1874.
  • MS C (Codex Complutensis 1; Madrid, Universidad Central 31): 9th/10th century.
  • MS E (Codex Epternacensis; Luxembourg, Bibliothèque Nationale 264): Dated 1051–1081 CE.
  • MS L (Codex Legionensis 2; León, Real Colegiata de San Isidoro I,3): Dated 1162 CE.
  • MS M (Codex Mazarinaeus; Paris, Bibliothèque Mazarine 3–4): 11th/12th century.
  • MS N (Codex Bruxellensis; Brussels, Bibliothèque Royale 9107–9110): 12th century.

details.intro:
The Words of Ahiqar is one of the most ancient and widely dispersed wisdom and narrative cycles of the ancient Near East and Mediterranean world. It comprises two distinct literary components:

1. The Narrative Frame: The biographical account of Ahiqar, wise chancellor (ummânu) and keeper of the signet to Sennacherib and Esarhaddon of Assyria; his betrayal by his adopted nephew/pupil Nadan; his secret preservation by the executioner Nabusumiskun; and his triumphant restoration when he solves the impossible architectural and riddle contests posed by the Pharaoh of Egypt.

2. The Sayings and Fables: An extensive collection of instructional wisdom sayings, proverbs, and beast fables addressed by Ahiqar to Nadan.

The historical reality of Ahiqar's high office was confirmed by the discovery of an 11th-century BCE/Seleucid cuneiform tablet at Uruk-Warka (W 20030,7; ed. J. van Dijk 1962), listing the Assyrian kings and their chief sages: Aba-Enlil-dari, whom the Arameans call Aḫu’qar, serving as sage under King Esarhaddon.

details.intro: 3 Maccabees tells how Ptolemy IV Philopator was prevented from entering the Jerusalem Temple. Back in Egypt, he tries to destroy the Jews by having them trampled by drunken elephants, but they are miraculously delivered.
details.provenance: It was written in Greek by an Egyptian Jew, probably in the 1st c. BCE, and is preserved in some manuscripts of the Septuagint.
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Septuagint Tradition

3 Maccabees was accepted into the Septuagint manuscript tradition of the Eastern Greek Church, though excluded from the Roman Catholic Vulgate canon (relegated in some Latin traditions to an apocryphal appendix).

1. Uncial Codices:

  • Codex Alexandrinus (A / 02): London, British Library, Royal 1 D. V–VIII (5th c.). The primary uncial witness for critical editions.
  • Codex Venetus (V / 23): Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Gr. 1 (8th–9th c.). A critical independent uncial text.
  • (Note: Omitted by Codex Sinaiticus [$\aleph$], which contains 1 and 4 Maccabees, and Codex Vaticanus [B], which omits all books of Maccabees).

2. Minuscule Witnesses:

  • Preserved across dozens of Septuagint minuscules categorized into families by Robert Hanhart (e.g., MSS 46, 55, 58, 62, 71, 74, 98, 120, 130, 243, 311, 771).
  • Sinai Gr. 1342 (fols. 179r–185r): 13th-century minuscule containing 3 Macc 1:1–7:23, identified by W. Baars (1963).

3. Lexicographical and Patristic Citations:

  • Quoted or cataloged in Apostolic Canons 85, the Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (Pseudo-Athanasius), the Stichometry of Nicephorus, and Byzantine florilegia.

B. Syriac Peshitta Tradition

3 Maccabees is preserved in the Syriac Peshitta Old Testament:

  • Codex Ambrosianus (7a1): Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 inf. (6th/7th c.), fols. 636–646. Editio princeps by A. M. Ceriani (1876); critical collation by P. A. de Lagarde (1861).

  • Lexicon: W. Strothmann, Wörterverzeichnis der apokryphen-deuterokanonischen Schriften des Alten Testaments in der Peshitta (1988).

C. Armenian Version

  • Fully integrated into the Armenian biblical tradition.
  • Edited by Y. Zōhrapean, Astowacašownč‘k‘ matean Hin ew Nor Ktakaranac‘ (Venice, 1805, pp. 381–388; reprinted by the Mechitharist Fathers, Venice, 1860, pp. 553–563).

details.intro: 4 Maccabees is a philosophical discourse arguing that devout reason is master of the passions. Its main proof is the martyrdom of the aged Eleazar and of the seven brothers and their mother under Antiochus IV.
details.provenance: It was written in Greek by a Jew trained in Stoic thought, probably in the 1st c. CE, perhaps in Antioch or Alexandria. It is preserved in some manuscripts of the Septuagint.
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Septuagint and Josephus Manuscript Traditions

4 Maccabees circulated in two major branches of Greek transmission: within major uncial Septuagint Bibles, and in Byzantine codices of the complete works of Flavius Josephus (owing to early patristic attribution).

1. Biblical Uncial Codices:

  • Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$ / 01): London, British Library, Add. 43725 (4th c.). Contains 4 Maccabees complete (fols. 129v–138r).
  • Codex Alexandrinus (A / 02): London, British Library, Royal 1 D. V–VIII (5th c.). Base text for Swete's edition.
  • Codex Venetus (V / 23): Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Gr. 1 (8th/9th c.). Preserves an important independent uncial witness.
  • (Note: Codex Vaticanus [B] omits 1–4 Maccabees entirely).

2. The Flavius Josephus Manuscript Tradition:

  • Transmitted as an appendix or authentic work of Josephus (under the title Eis tous Makkabaious logos / Flavii Iosephi de imperio rationis):
  • Codex Laurentianus plut. 69, 22 (11th c., Florence).
  • Codex Vaticanus gr. 148 (11th c., Rome).
  • Codex Palatinus gr. 14 (10th/11th c., Heidelberg).
  • Included in Renaissance Josephus editions: Arlenius (Basel, 1544), Hudson (Oxford, 1720), Havercamp (Amsterdam, 1726), Oberthür (Leipzig, 1782–1785), Dindorf (Paris, 1845), Richter (Leipzig, 1826), and Bekker (Leipzig, 1856, 6:270–303).

3. Minuscule Codices:

  • Collated in the Göttingen Septuaginta database (A. Rahlfs, Verzeichnis, 1914, pp. 387–390; MSS 46, 52, 58, 62, 71, 74, 98, 120, 130, 243, 311, etc.).

B. Old Latin Version (Passio SS. Machabaeorum)

  • A remarkably early Old Latin translation survives under the title Passio Sanctorum Machabaeorum, preserved in several early medieval Latin manuscripts (e.g., Karlsruhe Aug. Perg. 254; Cologne Dombibl. 45; Brussels Bibl. Roy. 8981).
  • Date: While H. Anderson placed the archetype around the 8th century, Emil Schürer and Heinrich Dörrie definitively proved that the Old Latin translation originated in the 4th century CE in North Africa or northern Italy.
  • Used extensively by Saint Ambrose (De Iacob et vita beata II), Saint Augustine, and Desiderius Erasmus for his 1524 Latin paraphrase of 4 Maccabees.
  • Traces of this translation are embedded in the West Visigothic / Mozarabic liturgy (Inlatio of the Feast of the Maccabees, ed. L. Eizenhöfer, 1961).
  • Critical Edition: Heinrich Dörrie, Passio SS. Machabaeorum: die antike lateinische Übersetzung des IV. Makkabäerbuches (Göttingen, 1938).

details.intro:
4 Maccabees (Μακκαβαίων Δʹ / Liber IV Maccabaeorum; titled in patristic antiquity Περὶ αὐτοκράτορος λογισμοῦ, On the Sovereignty of Reason) is a masterpiece of Hellenistic Jewish philosophical rhetoric. Cast in the form of a formal Greek diatribe or epideictic encomium, the work synthesizes Stoic and Platonic philosophical ethics with strict devotion to the Mosaic Torah. The author sets out to demonstrate a singular philosophical thesis: that pious reason (ho eusebēs logismos) exercises absolute mastery over the emotions and passions (autokratōr estin tōn pathōn). To establish this proposition, the author presents the heroic martyrdoms of the aged priest Eleazar, the seven young brothers, and their mother under the Seleucid tyrant Antiochus IV Epiphanes (expanding and dramatically reinterpreting the narrative of 2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42).

The book comprises eighteen chapters, logically structured into two major divisions:

Part I: The Philosophical Thesis and Proofs from Scripture (1:1–3:18)

1. The Philosophical Prooemium and Definitions (1:1–12):

  • The author states the thesis: Pious reason is sovereign over the passions (1:1).
  • Philosophical definitions: Reason (logismos) is the intellect choosing with sound judgment the life of wisdom (sophia); wisdom is defined along classical Stoic lines as "the knowledge of divine and human affairs and their causes" (1:15–16).
  • This wisdom is acquired through the discipline of the Mosaic Law (hē tou nomou paideia).
  • Classification of the four Cardinal Virtues (prudence/phronēsis, temperance/sōphrosynē, justice/dikaiosynē, and courage/andreia), all governed by devout reason (1:18–35).

2. The Anatomy of the Passions and Biblical Illustrations (1:36–3:18):

  • The passions are rooted in pleasure (hēdonē) and pain (ponos), branching into malevolence, anger, fear, and grief.
  • Proof that reason does not eradicate (ekkoptein) the passions, but masters and subdues them (epikratein / kratein).
  • Biblical exempla of mastery over desire: Joseph mastering sexual desire for Potiphar's wife (2:2–3); Moses subduing wrath against Dathan and Abiram (2:16–20); and King David pouring out the water of Bethlehem as an offering to God rather than indulging physical thirst bought at the risk of his soldiers' blood (3:6–18).

Part II: The Historical Demonstration: The Maccabean Martyrs (3:19–18:24)

1. Historical Introduction: Seleucid Oppression (3:19–4:26):

  • The peaceful era under Seleucus Nicator disrupted by Simon's treachery regarding the Jerusalem Temple treasury.
  • Apollonius / Heliodorus attempts to confiscate the sacred funds but is repelled by terrifying celestial horsemen and angels.
  • Accession of Antiochus IV Epiphanes; usurpation of the high priesthood by Jason; introduction of Greek customs, the gymnasium, and the citadel.
  • Antiochus decrees that all Jews must defile the covenant by eating swine’s flesh or suffer horrific torture and death (4:15–26).

2. The Martyrdom of the Priest Eleazar (5:1–7:23):

  • Eleazar, a ninety-year-old priest and legal scholar, is summoned before Antiochus.
  • Antiochus urges him to abandon superstitious Jewish scruples, arguing that nature provided pork as a benign gift.
  • Eleazar's philosophic apologia: The Creator knows human nature best and legislates what is beneficial; even minor transgressions of divine law carry equal gravity because they undermine the divine Lawgiver (5:16–38).
  • Horrific tortures: Eleazar is scourged, kicked, racked on the wheel, and thrown into flames.
  • Eleazar's climactic vicarious prayer: "You know, O God, that though I could have saved myself, I die in burning torment for the sake of the Law. Be merciful to your people, and let our punishment suffice for them. Make my blood their purification, and take my life as a ransom for theirs" (katharsion autōn poiēson to emon haima, kai antipsychon autōn labe tēn emēn psychēn, 6:27–29).
  • Encomium on Eleazar as the sacred helmsman steering the ship of piety through the tempestuous sea of torture into the harbor of divine immortality (7:1–23).

3. The Martyrdom of the Seven Brothers (8:1–14:10):

  • Antiochus confronts the seven noble brothers and their mother, offering wealth, royal patronage, and high office if they yield, and savage execution if they refuse.
  • In unified harmony, the brothers refuse to betray ancestral law, declaring that death for virtue secures eternal communion with God, while the tyrant faces unquenchable subterranean torments (9:1–9).
  • Serial martyrdoms of escalating brutality:
  • First brother: flayed, dismembered on the wheel, and roasted alive in a pan (tēganon, 9:10–25).
  • Second brother: strapped to catapults, sinews severed, flayed with iron claws (9:26–10:11).
  • Third brother: hands and feet disjointed, tongue cut out, stretched on the rack (10:12–21).
  • Fourth brother: tongue excised, broken on the wheel (11:1–13).
  • Fifth brother: crushed in brazen machinery, joints torn apart (11:14–27).
  • Sixth brother: roasted over coals while being prodded with heated spits (12:1–19).
  • Seventh (youngest) brother: leaps voluntarily into the burning brazier after scorning the tyrant's mock clemency (12:1–13:27).

4. The Heroism of the Mother and the Cosmic Arena (14:11–17:24):

  • Encomium on the mother: maternal love (philoteknia) was utterly subordinated to devout reason (eusebēs logismos).
  • Rather than permit any pagan soldier to lay hands upon her modesty, she casts herself into the flames, joining her sons (16:1–17:1).
  • The agōn (athletic contest) of holiness: "Truly divine was the contest (theios ho agōn)... Virtue was the umpire, endurance was the prize-judge, the arena was the universe, humanity was the spectator, and the prize was incorruptibility in everlasting life" (stephanos aphtharsias en zōē aidiō, 17:11–16).
  • Expiatory soteriology: Through the blood of these pious martyrs and their propitiatory death (tou hilastēriou thanatou autōn), divine Providence saved Israel and purged the land of the tyrant (17:21–22).

5. The Household Testament and Exaltation (18:1–24):

  • The mother's recollection of the father's biblical teaching in their home: instructing the boys in Abraham, Isaac, Phinehas, Daniel, Hananiah-Azariah-Mishael, and the messianic promises of Isaiah and Ezekiel.
  • The martyrs are enthroned in heaven among the choir of the stars, enjoying eternal life with the patriarchs (18:20–24).
details.manuscripts:
A. Greek Septuagint and Josephus Manuscript Traditions

4 Maccabees circulated in two major branches of Greek transmission: within major uncial Septuagint Bibles, and in Byzantine codices of the complete works of Flavius Josephus (owing to early patristic attribution).

1. Biblical Uncial Codices:

  • Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$ / 01): London, British Library, Add. 43725 (4th c.). Contains 4 Maccabees complete (fols. 129v–138r).
  • Codex Alexandrinus (A / 02): London, British Library, Royal 1 D. V–VIII (5th c.). Base text for Swete's edition.
  • Codex Venetus (V / 23): Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, Gr. 1 (8th/9th c.). Preserves an important independent uncial witness.
  • (Note: Codex Vaticanus [B] omits 1–4 Maccabees entirely).

2. The Flavius Josephus Manuscript Tradition:

  • Transmitted as an appendix or authentic work of Josephus (under the title Eis tous Makkabaious logos / Flavii Iosephi de imperio rationis):
  • Codex Laurentianus plut. 69, 22 (11th c., Florence).
  • Codex Vaticanus gr. 148 (11th c., Rome).
  • Codex Palatinus gr. 14 (10th/11th c., Heidelberg).
  • Included in Renaissance Josephus editions: Arlenius (Basel, 1544), Hudson (Oxford, 1720), Havercamp (Amsterdam, 1726), Oberthür (Leipzig, 1782–1785), Dindorf (Paris, 1845), Richter (Leipzig, 1826), and Bekker (Leipzig, 1856, 6:270–303).

3. Minuscule Codices:

  • Collated in the Göttingen Septuaginta database (A. Rahlfs, Verzeichnis, 1914, pp. 387–390; MSS 46, 52, 58, 62, 71, 74, 98, 120, 130, 243, 311, etc.).

B. Old Latin Version (Passio SS. Machabaeorum)

  • A remarkably early Old Latin translation survives under the title Passio Sanctorum Machabaeorum, preserved in several early medieval Latin manuscripts (e.g., Karlsruhe Aug. Perg. 254; Cologne Dombibl. 45; Brussels Bibl. Roy. 8981).
  • Date: While H. Anderson placed the archetype around the 8th century, Emil Schürer and Heinrich Dörrie definitively proved that the Old Latin translation originated in the 4th century CE in North Africa or northern Italy.
  • Used extensively by Saint Ambrose (De Iacob et vita beata II), Saint Augustine, and Desiderius Erasmus for his 1524 Latin paraphrase of 4 Maccabees.
  • Traces of this translation are embedded in the West Visigothic / Mozarabic liturgy (Inlatio of the Feast of the Maccabees, ed. L. Eizenhöfer, 1961).
  • Critical Edition: Heinrich Dörrie, Passio SS. Machabaeorum: die antike lateinische Übersetzung des IV. Makkabäerbuches (Göttingen, 1938).

C. Syriac Peshitta Tradition

  • Preserved in the Syriac Peshitta Old Testament:
  • Codex Ambrosianus (7a1): Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 inf. (6th/7th c.), fols. 646–659. Editio princeps by A. M. Ceriani (1876).
  • British Library Syriac MSS: BL Add. 14446 (6th c.) and Add. 12174 (dated 1196 CE); cataloged by William Wright (1870–1872, pp. 1137, 1143).
  • Critical Edition: Robert L. Bensly and William E. Barnes, The Fourth Book of Maccabees and Kindred Documents in Syriac (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1895). Includes Syriac text with English translation and critical comparison against the Greek.

D. Coptic Witness

  • In 1981, Enzo Lucchesi discovered Sahidic Coptic manuscript fragments of 4 Maccabees (BHG 1006) preserved in the Bibliothèque Nationale de France in Paris (MS copte 129¹⁷) and the Austrian National Library in Vienna:
  • Lucchesi, Enzo. "Découverte d’une traduction copte du quatrième livre des Maccabées (BHG 1006)." Analecta Bollandiana 99 (1981): 302.
  • Lucchesi, Enzo. "Encore trois feuillets coptes du Quatrième livre des Maccabées." In Écriture et traductions dans la littérature copte, CahBC 1:21–22. Louvain: Peeters, 1983.

E. Old Church Slavonic Tradition

  • Preserved in early Slavic Menologia and liturgical Cheti-Minei for the feast of August 1st.
  • Cataloged by N. Bonwesch in A. Harnack, Geschichte der altchristlichen Literatur bis Eusebius (Leipzig, 1893; 2nd ed. 1913, 1:886–917 at 917).

title: Psalmus 151
section: PSALMI - ODAE SALOMONIS - PROVERBIA - JOB - SAPIENTIA - SIRACIDES - PSALMI SALOMONIS

details.intro:
Introduction

Psalm 151 (CAVT 202; CANT 151) is a short poetic composition celebrating David's selection and victory over Goliath. Found outside the standard 150-psalm Masoretic Psalter, it is preserved in Greek (Septuagint, where it is designated idiographos), Hebrew (the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11, 11Q5 / 11QPsa col. XXVIII), and Latin (Clementine Vulgate appendiceal tradition).
details.provenance:
Provenance

Composed in Hebrew in Hellenistic Judaea (likely 3rd-2nd century BCE), as confirmed by the discovery of 11Q5 at Qumran.
details.manuscripts:
A. Hebrew Witnesses (Dead Sea Scrolls)

1. 11QPsᵃ (11Q5):

  • Date: Herodian script, ca. 30–50 CE.
  • Provenance: Qumran Cave 11; discovered 1956, editio princeps by J. A. Sanders (DJD IV, 1965).
  • Contents: 41 biblical psalms in non-traditional sequence, interspersed with seven non-Masoretic texts:
  • Col. xviii 1–18: Psalm 154 (vv. 3–19).
  • Col. xix 1–18: Plea for Deliverance (non-canonical penitential apotropaic psalm).
  • Col. xxi 11–17, xxii 1a: Sirach 51:13–30 (acrostic Hymn to Wisdom).
  • Col. xxii 1b–15: Apostrophe to Zion (alphabetic acrostic celebration of the New Jerusalem).
  • Col. xxiv 3–18: Psalm 155 (vv. 1–19).
  • Col. xxvi 9–15: Hymn to the Creator (celebrating cosmic order and the solar calendar).
  • Col. xxvii 2–11: David's Compositions (historical prose notice attributing 4,050 compositions to David: 3,600 tehillim and 450 shir for daily, Sabbath, and festival offerings).
  • Col. xxviii 3–12: Psalm 151A.
  • Col. xxviii 13–14: Psalm 151B.

2. 11QPsᵇ (11Q6):

  • Cave 11 fragments containing parts of Apostrophe to Zion (frr. 1–3) and Plea for Deliverance (frr. 4–5).

3. 4QPsᶠ (4Q88):

  • Cave 4 manuscript containing Apostrophe to Zion (cols. vii–viii), followed by two unique non-Masoretic psalms: Eschatological Hymn (col. ix) and Apostrophe to Judah (col. x).

4. 4Q448 (Prayer for King Jonathan and Psalm 154):

  • Column A preserves fragments corresponding to Hebrew Psalm 154:17–20, embedded before or alongside a liturgical prayer invoking blessing upon "King Jonathan" (Alexander Jannaeus, 103–76 BCE).

B. Syriac Witnesses

1. Baghdad, Library of the Chaldean Patriarchate, MS 1113 (formerly Diyarbakır, Archbishopric MS 12t4):

  • Date: 12th century (1113 CE).
  • Contents: Fols. 118b–120b contain all five Syriac Apocryphal Psalms (I–V), complete with detailed titles and marginal scholia describing the historical occasions in David's life.

2. London, British Library, Add. MS 14568:

  • Date: 6th century (one of the oldest surviving Syriac biblical manuscripts).
  • Contents: Fols. 49b–50a contain Syriac Apocryphal Psalms I, II (Ps 154), and III (Ps 155).

3. Manchester, John Rylands Library, Syr. MS 7:

  • Date: 16th century. Fol. 135a preserves Syriac Psalm 151 only.

4. Berlin, Staatsbibliothek, Sachau 209:

  • Witness for the liturgical reception of the apocryphal psalms.

C. Greek Witnesses (Psalm 151)

  • Preserved in all major uncial Bibles containing the Septuagint Psalter:
  • Codex Vaticanus (B, 03), 4th c.
  • Codex Sinaiticus (א, 01), 4th c.
  • Codex Alexandrinus (A, 02), 5th c. (titled Idiógraphos eis Dabid éxōthen tou arithmoú).
  • Zurich Purple Psalter (Turicensis, T), 7th c.

D. Latin and Ethiopic Witnesses

  • Old Latin (Vetus Latina): Preserved in Psalterium Veronense, Sangallense, Mozarabic psalter, and Roman liturgies (collated by A.-M. Denis and J. Verheyden).
  • Ge'ez (Mashafa Mazmur): Regular inclusion in standard Ethiopic Psalters following Psalm 150.

title: Qumran. Psalmi apocryphi (4Q88, 4Q380, 4Q381, 4Q448, 11Q11) (hebraice)
section: PSALMI - ODAE SALOMONIS - PROVERBIA - JOB - SAPIENTIA - SIRACIDES - PSALMI SALOMONIS

details.intro:
The Syriac Apocryphal Psalms I–V comprise a corpus of five non-Masoretic poetic compositions traditionally appended to the canonical 150 Psalms in Eastern Syriac Psalter manuscripts (most notably Baghdad, Chaldean Patriarchate MS 1113 [formerly Diyarbakır 12t4] and BL Add. MS 14568).

Before the discovery of Cave 11 at Qumran in 1956, modern scholarship (beginning with William Wright in 1887, followed by Mingana, Harris, and Martin Noth in 1928–1930) knew these poems primarily as Christian or Jewish-Syriac curiosities preserved in the Peshitta textual stream. The field was revolutionized by J. A. Sanders's publication of the great Dead Sea Psalms Scroll (11QPsᵃ / 11Q5) in 1962–1965:

1. Psalm 151: Discovered in 11Q5 col. xxviii as two distinct Hebrew poetic compositions:

  • Psalm 151A (xxviii 3–12): A Davidic autobiographical hymn recountings his youth as a shepherd, his crafting of musical instruments (kinnor and nevel) to praise God, and his anointing by Samuel over his taller, more handsome brothers.
  • Psalm 151B (xxviii 13–14): A fragmentary hymn detailing David's combat with the Philistine giant Goliath and his decapitation with Goliath's own sword.
  • In the Greek Septuagint, these two separate Hebrew poems were redacted and condensed into a single Greek psalm (LXX Ps 151), designated idiógraphos eis Dabid éxōthen tou arithmoú ("an autograph of David outside the number"). The Syriac (ApocPs I), Old Latin, and Ge'ez (Ethiopic) versions derive from this Greek recension.

2. Psalm 154 (= Syriac Apocryphal Psalm II): Preserved in Hebrew in 11Q5 col. xviii 1–18 (with verses 1–2 reconstructed from Syriac and 4Q448). It is a sapiential-communal hymn praising God in the assembly of the righteous (qahal, ḥaverim), celebrating table fellowship, Torah study, and the glorification of YHWH over pagan sacrifices.

3. Psalm 155 (= Syriac Apocryphal Psalm III): Preserved in Hebrew in 11Q5 col. xxiv 3–18. A deeply personal penitential psalm and individual plea for deliverance from sin, judgment, and demonic oppression ("let not Satan rule over me, nor an unclean spirit"), structured closely upon the language of biblical psalms (especially Psalm 51).

4. Psalms 152 and 153 (= Syriac Apocryphal Psalms IV and V): These two poems are preserved uniquely in Syriac:

  • Psalm 152 (IV): "Spoken by David when he was contending with the lion and the wolf which took a sheep from his flock" (1 Sam 17:34–37). A prayer of distress invoking God's past salvation.
  • Psalm 153 (V): "Spoken by David when he gave thanks to God, who delivered him from the lion and the wolf and he slew both of them." A hymn of thanksgiving.
  • Linguistic and retroversion studies (Martin Noth, A. S. van der Woude, H. F. van Rooy) demonstrate that both compositions translate an original Hebrew Vorlage composed in late Second Temple Palestine (2nd–1st c. BCE), sharing the vocabulary, meter, and Davidic haggadah of the Qumran poetic scrolls.

  • Cave 11 fragments containing parts of Apostrophe to Zion (frr. 1–3) and Plea for Deliverance (frr. 4–5).

3. 4QPsᶠ (4Q88):

  • Cave 4 manuscript containing Apostrophe to Zion (cols. vii–viii), followed by two unique non-Masoretic psalms: Eschatological Hymn (col. ix) and Apostrophe to Judah (col. x).

4. 4Q448 (Prayer for King Jonathan and Psalm 154):

  • Column A preserves fragments corresponding to Hebrew Psalm 154:17–20, embedded before or alongside a liturgical prayer invoking blessing upon "King Jonathan" (Alexander Jannaeus, 103–76 BCE).

B. Syriac Witnesses

1. Baghdad, Library of the Chaldean Patriarchate, MS 1113 (formerly Diyarbakır, Archbishopric MS 12t4):

  • Date: 12th century (1113 CE).
  • Contents: Fols. 118b–120b contain all five Syriac Apocryphal Psalms (I–V), complete with detailed titles and marginal scholia describing the historical occasions in David's life.

2. London, British Library, Add. MS 14568:

  • Date: 6th century (one of the oldest surviving Syriac biblical manuscripts).
  • Contents: Fols. 49b–50a contain Syriac Apocryphal Psalms I, II (Ps 154), and III (Ps 155).

3. Manchester, John Rylands Library, Syr. MS 7:

  • Date: 16th century. Fol. 135a preserves Syriac Psalm 151 only.

4. Berlin, Staatsbibliothek, Sachau 209:

  • Witness for the liturgical reception of the apocryphal psalms.

C. Greek Witnesses (Psalm 151)

  • Preserved in all major uncial Bibles containing the Septuagint Psalter:
  • Codex Vaticanus (B, 03), 4th c.
  • Codex Sinaiticus (א, 01), 4th c.
  • Codex Alexandrinus (A, 02), 5th c. (titled Idiógraphos eis Dabid éxōthen tou arithmoú).
  • Zurich Purple Psalter (Turicensis, T), 7th c.

D. Latin and Ethiopic Witnesses

  • Old Latin (Vetus Latina): Preserved in Psalterium Veronense, Sangallense, Mozarabic psalter, and Roman liturgies (collated by A.-M. Denis and J. Verheyden).
  • Ge'ez (Mashafa Mazmur): Regular inclusion in standard Ethiopic Psalters following Psalm 150.

title: Odae Salomonis
section: PSALMI - ODAE SALOMONIS - PROVERBIA - JOB - SAPIENTIA - SIRACIDES - PSALMI SALOMONIS

details.intro:
The Odes of Solomon (Syriac: Zmīrāthā d-Shlēmūn; Greek: Ὠιδαὶ Σολομῶντος / Ōidai Solomōntos; Latin: Odae Salomonis) is a collection of forty-two ecstatic lyrical hymns (Odes 1–42; Ode 2 is lost due to a physical lacuna in the manuscript traditions). Composed around the late 1st or early 2nd century CE (ca. 100–125 CE) in Roman Syria (most likely Antioch or Edessa/Osrhoene), the Odes constitute the earliest surviving Christian hymnal. Imbued with profound mystical intimacy, realized eschatology, and poetic passion, the collection reflects a bilingual Semitic-Hellenistic milieu that bridges the theological world of the Dead Sea Scrolls (Hodayot), the Gospel of John, and the letters of Saint Ignatius of Antioch.

Attributed pseudepigraphically to King Solomon—celebrated in 1 Kings 4:32 (LXX 3 Kgs 5:12) as having composed 1,005 songs—the Odes speak in the first-person voice of the redeemed believer, the prophet-singer, and at times Christ Himself (Christus loquens).

Major Thematic and Theological Motifs

1. The Crown / Wreath of Truth (Odes 1, 5, 9, 17):

  • The collection opens with the iconic image: "The Lord is on my head like a crown, and I shall not be without Him. Woven for me is the crown of truth, and it caused your branches to bud in me" (Ode 1:1–2). The crown represents divine life, truth, and imperishability.

2. The Living Water and the River of Life (Odes 6, 11, 30):

  • A river of the Holy Spirit flows from the divine throne, carrying living water across the whole earth: "A stream went forth and became a river great and broad... it carried away everything and broke down the Temple... all the thirsty upon earth drank, and thirst was relieved and quenched" (Ode 6:8–18).

3. The Circumcision of the Heart and the Robe of Light (Ode 11):

  • Preserved in Greek (Papyrus Bodmer XI) and Syriac: The singer's heart is circumcised by the Spirit; the old earthly garment is stripped away, and the soul is clothed in celestial light, translated into Paradise to feast on the fruits of the Tree of Life.

4. Startling Trinitarian and Maternal Imagery (Ode 19):

  • One of the most famous and unique passages in early Christian poetry: "A cup of milk was offered to me, and I drank it in the sweetness of the Lord's delight. The Son is the cup, and the Father is He who was milked; and the Holy Spirit is She who milked Him... The Holy Spirit opened her womb and gave birth to the Son without pain... without requiring a midwife" (19:1–9).

5. The Descent into Sheol / The Harrowing of Hell (Odes 17, 22, 42):

  • The triumphant voice of Christ recounting His descent into the underworld: "Sheol saw me and was shattered, and Death cast me up and many along with me. I was gall and vinegar to it, and I descended with it to the depth of its abyss... and I made a congregation of living men among its dead" (Ode 42:11–17).

6. The Gesture of Prayer as the Cross / Orante (Odes 27, 42):

  • The bodily posture of the orante—arms outstretched in prayer—is identified with the wood of the Cross: "I extended my hands and hallowed my Lord, for the expansion of my hands is His sign, and my outspreading is the upright cross" (Ode 27:1–3; 42:1–2).
details.manuscripts:
The Odes of Solomon are preserved across three ancient linguistic traditions:

A. The Syriac Manuscript Tradition

The principal and most complete text survives in two Syriac manuscripts where the Odes immediately precede the Psalms of Solomon:

1. MS H (Manchester, John Rylands University Library, Syriac MS 9, olim Cod. Harris 1):

  • Date: 16th century CE (paper codex).
  • Provenance: Discovered in 1909 by James Rendel Harris on the shelves of his study in Birmingham, having been brought from the Tigris region.
  • Preserves Odes 3:1b through 42:20 (Odes 1:1–3:1a lost due to missing leaves).

2. MS N (London, British Library, MS Add. 14538, fols. 148v–155v):

  • Date: 10th century CE (vellum codex in Estrangela script).
  • Provenance: St. Mary Deipara in the Nitrian Desert, Egypt (cataloged by W. Wright, 1872, Part 3, No. 936, pp. 1003–1008).
  • Preserves Odes 17:7 through 42:20.

B. The Greek Witness: Papyrus Bodmer XI

  • Papyrus Bodmer XI (G) (Cologny-Geneva, Bibliotheca Bodmeriana):
  • Date: 3rd century CE (early 4th c.).
  • Content: Preserves Ode 11 complete in Greek under the rubric Ὠιδὴ Σολομῶντος (Ōidē Solomōntos), bound within a famous miscellaneous papyrus codex alongside the Protoevangelium of James (Pap. Bodmer V) and 1–2 Peter.
  • Editio Princeps: Michel Testuz, Papyrus Bodmer XI (Cologny-Geneva, 1959).

C. The Coptic Gnostic Witness (Pistis Sophia)

  • London, British Library, MS Add. 5114 (The Askew Codex):
  • Date: 4th century CE (written in Sahidic Coptic).
  • Content: The gnostic treatise Pistis Sophia quotes five complete Odes in Sahidic Coptic, providing theological interpretations by the disciples:
  • Ode 1 (Pistis Sophia ch. 59)
  • Ode 5 (Pistis Sophia ch. 58)
  • Ode 6 (Pistis Sophia ch. 65)
  • Ode 22 (Pistis Sophia ch. 71)
  • Ode 25 (Pistis Sophia ch. 69)
  • Critical Edition: Carl Schmidt and Violet MacDermot, Pistis Sophia (Nag Hammadi Studies 9; Leiden: Brill, 1978).

D. Latin Patristic Witness

  • Lactantius (Divinae Institutiones IV.12.3, ca. 310 CE):
  • "Salomon in ode undevicesima ita dicit: Infirmatus est uterus virginis et accepit foetum et gravata est et facta est in multa miseratione mater virgo..."
  • This explicit citation of Ode 19:6 demonstrates that a Latin translation of the numbered Odes was circulating in North Africa by the early 4th century.

title: Testamentum Job
section: PSALMI - ODAE SALOMONIS - PROVERBIA - JOB - SAPIENTIA - SIRACIDES - PSALMI SALOMONIS

details.intro: The Testament of Job retells the story of Job as a deathbed address to his children. Job destroys an idol's temple, is attacked by Satan in return, and endures with patience until Satan concedes defeat. The kings who visit him, the death of his wife Sitis, and the heavenly sashes he gives his daughters, who then speak in angelic tongues, are distinctive features.
details.provenance:
Original Language

The Testament of Job was most likely composed in Greek (so Spittler, 830, 833). It shows no obvious signs of being translated from a semitic language, and no evidence has been found of versions in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Syriac.

Date of Composition

The Testament of Job was composed some time prior to the 5th century CE, when the earliest surviving fragments were copied. Since that 5th century evidence preserves a Coptic translation, the original Greek composition would probably have been made at least several decades earlier. It may have been composed in the first century BCE or first century CE (so Spittler, 833).

Social Setting

The Testament of Job has generally been viewed as a Jewish composition, free in its present form from any extensive Christian editing (Spittler, 833-34; see Brock, 8). James Davila has recently dissented from this consensus and argued that the document is a Christian composition, or at least that an origin in early Christian circles cannot be ruled out.
details.manuscripts:
P Paris BN gr 2658, fols. 72r-97r (complete, 11th century CE)
For ms information see F. Halkin, Manuscrits grecs de Paris: Inventaire hagiographique (Subsidia hagiographica 44; Bruxelles: Société des bollandistes, 1968), 235. The editions of James and Brock (see below) are essentially corrected transcriptions of this manuscript. Brock holds that P is "in many ways the best witness to the text of this work" (7; cf. 15-16), though he recognizes that the other Greek mss sometimes preserve superior readings (15).
P2 Paris BN gr 938, fols. 172v-192v (copy of P, 16th century CE)
For ms information see F. Halkin, Manuscrits grecs de Paris: Inventaire hagiographique (Subsidia hagiographica 44; Bruxelles: Société des bollandistes, 1968), 92. Since this ms is evidently a copy of P (so James, lxxiii; Brock, 5, 10) it has no independent value as a witness and not been included in the OCP edition.
S Messina San Salvatore 29, fols. 35v-41v (complete, 1307-1308 CE)
This manuscript was held by the Basilian monastery of San Salvatore in Messina, Sicily. When the monastery was closed, its manuscripts are reported to have been transfered to the Université degli Studi di Messina. So far, though, my attempts to locate the manuscript in the university's collections (or elsewhere in Italy) have failed. This ms has never before been published in running form. Brock reports that the orthography of S is extremely unstable and vowels, in particular, are often substituted in apparently arbitrary ways (see Brock, 8-9). Kraft departs from Brock's preference for P and argues that S betrays fewer indications of "self-conscious recensional work" than does P (Kraft, 5-7). Even Brock, however, acknowledges that in places the S form of the text is likely closer to the original (Brock, 15).
V Rome Vat gr 1238, fols. 340r-349v (complete, 13th century CE)
The transcription of V published by Mai in 1833 (see below) was the first publication of the Testament of Job. Mai's edition is reasonably accurate, but not without significant errors. This ms has not been published since in running form, and the partial transcription by F. C. Conybeare in 1901 (see below) is less accurate than that of Mai. Manuscript V is closer to S in the form of its text than to P, so that S and V appear to represent a common textual trajectory distinct from that represented in P (Brock, 14; Kraft, 9-10). Nevertheless, V does not appear to be directly dependent on ms S. V is generally agreed to depart further than P or S from the early form of the Greek text, and it includes many periphrastic expansions (Brock, 9; Kraft, 5).
Coptic Papyrus Cologne 3221 (fragmentary and incomplete, 5th century CE)
This ms has been published just recently in Gesa Shenk, Der Koptische Kölner Papyruskodex 3221: Teil I: Das Testament des Iob (Paderborn: Schöningh, 2009). Prior to this C. Römer and H. J. Thissen published a preliminary report in 1989 (see below) which includes several readings from the ms.
Slavonic This designates the MS published by G. Polívka in Starine 24 (1891): 135-55, together with the variants provided there from two other mss: Belgrade National Library, no. 149 (incomplete) and Moscow Rumjancov Museum, no. 1472. The Slavonic tradition is only marginally useful in the reconstruction of the early text of TJob since the translation is evidently very free and periphrastic (Brock, 7, 10-14). Many of its periphrastic expansions parallel the kind of editorial work evident in ms V. Nevertheless, the Slavonic tradition is not clearly derived from either the P or the S V textual traditions, but seems to translate a Vorlage which included readings characteristic of both streams of textual transmission (Brock, 14-15).
