details.intro:
The Psalms of Solomon (PssSol) is a Jewish pseudepigraphical collection of eighteen poetic psalms composed in Judea during the turbulent midpoint of the first century BCE (ca. 63–37 BCE) and brought into its final composite form prior to the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Pseudepigraphically attributed to King Solomon—celebrated in biblical tradition for his wisdom, proverbs, and thousands of songs (cf. 1 Kgs 4:32; canonical Ps 72)—the collection captures the acute communal trauma, factional conflict, and fervent eschatological longings of Jewish society following the collapse of Hasmonean sovereignty and the Roman conquest of Jerusalem by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE.

Although not preserved in the canonical Hebrew Bible or among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Psalms of Solomon was faithfully transmitted through Christian ecclesiastical channels in the Greek East. Ancient canonical catalogues—most notably the fifth-century table of contents (Pinax) of Codex Alexandrinus (which lists the eighteen psalms among the antilegomena following 1–2 Clement), the sixth-century Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (pseudo-Athanasius), and the ninth-century Stichometry of Nicephorus (which measures the work at 2,100 stichoi)—demonstrate that the collection was read and copied as a significant ecclesiastical appendix to Septuagint and New Testament codices.

Spanning an array of classical biblical poetic genres, the collection includes communal laments (PssSol 1, 2, 8), individual prayers of thanksgiving and penitence (PssSol 3, 5, 6, 9, 13, 15, 16), wisdom and didactic reflections (PssSol 4, 10, 14), and royal messianic hymns (PssSol 17, 18). It stands alongside the Dead Sea Scrolls as one of the most vital textual witnesses to late Second Temple Palestinian Jewish theology, articulating a profound theodicy in the face of foreign subjugation, an acute ethical dualism between the "righteous" and "sinners," an explicit hope in the bodily resurrection of the righteous to eternal life, and the most detailed pre-Christian portrait of a personal, Davidic Messiah (huios Dauid) in ancient Jewish literature.
details.provenance:
Date and Historical Setting

The historical backdrop of the Psalms of Solomon is anchored in the dramatic political convulsions of first-century BCE Judea. Three psalms in particular—2, 8, and 17—contain vivid, transparent historical allusions that allow modern scholars to date their composition with remarkable precision:

  • The Siege and Fall of Jerusalem (63 BCE): Psalm 8 recounts the approach of a foreign conqueror from the ends of the earth who was welcomed by the city's corrupt leadership, assaulted the fortified walls with battering rams (8:15–21; cf. 2:1), and desecrated the Temple sanctuary, trampling the holy altar with pagan feet (2:2). As first recognized by F. K. Movers in the nineteenth century, this corresponds exactly to the Roman siege led by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE, intervening in the civil war between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II as recounted by Flavius Josephus (Ant. 14.3–4; J.W. 1.6–7).
  • The Denunciation of Late Hasmonean Usurpation: The psalms deliver a scathing theological polemic against the native Hasmonean priest-kings (Aristobulus II, Hyrcanus II, and Alexander Jannaeus). The psalmist charges them with unlawfully arrogating royal majesty to themselves without Davidic covenantal legitimacy (17:5–8) and defiling the altar, sanctuary, and sacrificial rites with ritual impurity and incest (8:11–13, 22; 2:3–14). The Roman assault is thus interpreted not as a tragic defeat of God's people, but as a deserved divine punishment upon an apostate aristocracy.
  • The Ignominious Fate of Pompey (48 BCE): Psalm 2:26–27 provides a decisive terminus post quem for the collection, describing the dishonorable end of the Roman conqueror: "I did not have to wait long before God showed me the insolent one lying dead on the mountains of Egypt, despised more than the smallest on land and sea, his body decomposed by the waves with no one to bury him." This matches Pompey's assassination on the beach of Pelusium in Egypt in 48 BCE following his defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus, where his headless body was left exposed on the shore.
  • Herod the Great's Siege and the Atkinson Redating Thesis: While earlier scholars (e.g., Ewald, Bretschneider, Cellier) proposed obsolete dates ranging from Ptolemy I to Titus, Kenneth Atkinson ("Toward a Redating of the Psalms of Solomon," 1998; "Herod the Great, Sosius, and the Siege of Jerusalem," 1996) argues that Psalm 17 reflects the bloody siege of Jerusalem in 37/36 BCE by Herod the Great and the Roman general Gaius Sosius. Atkinson suggests that the collection spans the historical transition from the late Hasmonean period to the early Herodian era (ca. 63–30 BCE), reflecting an ongoing community that weathered both crises.

The complete absence of any allusion to the cataclysmic destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE firmly establishes that the collection attained its final redacted form before 70 CE, with the majority of psalms composed between 63 and 40 BCE (as proposed by R. B. Wright, E. P. Sanders, and M. de Jonge).

Authorship, Provenance, and Sectarian Milieu

The collection was composed in Judea, almost certainly in Jerusalem or its immediate environs. The identity of the community behind the psalms has been one of the most vigorously debated problems in Second Temple scholarship:

  • The Pharisaic Hypothesis: Pioneered by Julius Wellhausen (Die Pharisäer und die Sadducäer, 1874) and popularized by H. E. Ryle and M. R. James in their landmark edition Psalms of the Pharisees, Commonly Called the Psalms of Solomon (1891), this view held that the authors were Pharisees opposing the Sadducean Hasmonean hierarchy. The thesis was supported by the poems' fierce devotion to Torah, belief in divine sovereignty alongside human free will, insistence on bodily resurrection, and strict purity regulations. Mikael Winninge (Sinners and the Righteous, 1995) has defended a modified version of this stance.
  • The Post-Qumran Critique: The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls decisively shattered the exclusivity of the Pharisaic identification. As demonstrated by J. O'Dell (1961) and R. B. Wright (1972), doctrines such as divine retribution, bodily resurrection, messianic deliverance, and hatred for Hasmonean corruption were not distinctive to Pharisees, but were widely shared across the broader apocalyptic and pietistic streams of Palestinian Judaism. The internal evidence proves firmly that the authors were non-Sadducean, but does not identify them uniquely as Pharisees.
  • The Essene and Qumran-Adjacent Hypotheses: André Dupont-Sommer (1973) proposed that the psalms originated among the Essenes, a hypothesis further refined by P. N. Franklyn (1987), who posited a previously unrecorded branch of the Essene movement. However, no copies or fragments of the Psalms of Solomon have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the references to fleeing into the wilderness (PsSol 17:16) reflect temporary flight during siege warfare rather than permanent communal withdrawal to Qumran.
  • The Zadokite Displacement Model: Advanced by Heerak Christian Kim (Zadokite Propaganda in the Late Second Temple Period, 2014), this theory links the collection with displaced Oniad/Zadokite priests who were ousted from the Temple cult by the Hasmoneans and who produced polemical psalms protesting their disenfranchisement and calling for cultic restoration.
  • The Modern Consensus: Unknown Jerusalem Pietists: The dominant contemporary perspective, articulated by Kenneth Atkinson (I Cried to the Lord, 2004) and endorsed by E. P. Sanders, concludes that the authors cannot be identified with any known historical sect (Pharisees, Sadducees, or Essenes). Rather, the psalms were composed by an unknown, pietistic Jerusalem circle—self-designated as "the assemblies of the devout" (συναγωγαὶ ὁσίων, PsSol 17:16)—rooted in traditional Hasidic piety (Büchler 1922; Flusser 1984; Hann 1988) and maintaining strict covenantal fidelity amid socio-political marginalization.

Original Language and Translation Character

The overwhelming majority of modern scholars (including Ryle and James, G. B. Gray, Emil Schürer, Joseph L. Trafton, and Robert B. Wright) maintain that the Psalms of Solomon was originally composed in Hebrew, and subsequently translated into Greek, from which the Syriac version later derived (or, as Trafton and Grant Ward argue, with both versions reflecting independent access to a common Hebrew Vorlage). The case for a lost Hebrew original rests on several converging lines of philological evidence:

  • Pervasive Semitic Syntax: The Greek text exhibits continuous coordinate clauses linked by καί, construct-state periphrases, rigid Hebrew word order, and idioms that represent word-for-word calques of classical biblical Hebrew poetry.
  • Demonstrable Translation Errors: Several obscure or impossible Greek readings are explicable only as misreadings or graphic confusion of Hebrew consonants. For example, at PsSol 2:25, the translator appears to have misread Hebrew rymhl ("to change/alter") as rm'l ("to say"), producing the ungrammatical Greek phrase τοῦ εἰπεῖν. Similarly, at PsSol 2:26, the description of Pompey's insolence (ἡ ὑπερηφανία αὐτοῦ) likely reflects a graphic confusion of Hebrew g'wtw ("his pride") for gwytw ("his corpse").
  • Intertextual Dependence with Baruch: The undeniable literary relationship between Psalm of Solomon 11 and Baruch 5:5–8 demonstrates that one work drew upon the other. Because PsSol 11 displays superior poetic unity and structural cohesion, scholars widely judge that Baruch translated or adapted a pre-existing Hebrew Vorlage of Psalm 11.
  • The Syriac Evidence: Comprehensive philological analysis by Joseph L. Trafton (1985, 1986) indicates that while the Syriac text shows close affinity with the Greek manuscript family of Group 253, several Syriac readings preserve genuine Semitic idioms or variants that suggest access to a Semitic Vorlage.

A vocal minority (beginning with Hilgenfeld in 1871 and revisited by some contemporary linguists) has argued for direct Greek composition in intentional imitation of the Septuagint. However, as Kenneth Atkinson notes in the NETS commentary, the persistent "lexical stereotyping" (e.g., translating Hebrew hasid uniformly as ὅσιος and hesed as ἔλεος) and syntactical stiffness are standard hallmarks of translation Greek rather than Hellenistic Greek composition.
details.manuscripts:
The Greek Manuscript Tradition

The Greek text of the Psalms of Solomon survives in eleven manuscripts dating from the tenth to the sixteenth century CE. Through the stemmatic analyses of Robert R. Hann (The Manuscript History of the Psalms of Solomon, 1982), Robert B. Wright (The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text, 2007), and Felix Albrecht (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3, 2018), these witnesses are classified into four distinct textual families, alongside ancient indirect witnesses:

Rahlfs No. Siglum Repository and Shelfmark Date Textual Family / Stemmatic Characteristics
253 V Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. gr. 336 (olim 253) 11th–12th c. Group 253: Primary and most reliable witness to the earliest reconstructible archetype. Closely allied to the Greek Vorlage underlying the ancient Syriac translation.
655 o Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ottob. gr. 60 16th c. Group 253: Discovered after Rahlfs (1935); direct descendant and close congener of MS 253.
659 p Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ottob. gr. 384 16th c. Group 253: Discovered after Rahlfs (1935); congener of MS 253 and 655.
260 H (Hauniensis) Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, GkS 6 fol. ("Bible of Niketas") 10th–11th c. Group 260: Oldest surviving complete Greek manuscript; principal representative of the widespread "Bible of Niketas" Byzantine recension.
149 A (Augustanus) Wien, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Theol. gr. 11 (olim 149) 11th c. Group 260: Direct congener and copy of MS 260; basis of David Hoeschel's rediscovery and the 1626 editio princeps.
471 M (Mosquensis) Moscow, State Historical Museum, Syn. gr. 147 (olim Athos, Iviron) 12th–14th c. Group 260: Important secondary witness of the Niketas recension, collated by Oscar von Gebhardt.
606 P (Parisinus) Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, gr. 2991A 14th–15th c. Group 260: Derivative witness of the Niketas textual family.
3004 L (Vossianus) Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Misc. 15 16th c. Group 260: Discovered and collated by W. Baars in 1961. Contains PsSol 17:2b–18:14 and uniquely isolates PsSol 18:10–12 as a separate "nineteenth psalm," partially confirming Ryle and James's nineteenth-century conjecture.
629 C (Casanatensis) Rome, Biblioteca Casanatense, MS 1908 (olim Casanat. 715) 12th–14th c. Group 629: Preserves a mixed textual tradition exhibiting contamination across Groups 253 and 336.
769 B (Benaki) Athens, Benaki Museum, MS 5 (olim Athos, Great Lavra) 12th–14th c. Group 629: Close congener of MS 629, collated on Mount Athos by Gebhardt.
336 R Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. gr. 336 12th–14th c. Group 336: Standalone witness preserving an independent, archaic recension with idiosyncratic readings; historically prominent in early printed editions.

Ancient Indirect Attestation

  • Codex Alexandrinus (MS A, 5th century CE): Listed in the table of contents (Pinax) under disputed books (antilegomena) immediately following 1–2 Clement with the entry ΨΑΛΜΟΙ ΣΟΛΟΜΩΝΤΟΣ ΙΗ ("Eighteen Psalms of Solomon"). The folios containing the text at the very end of the great codex were lost prior to the modern era, but the entry proves its canonical reception in late antique Egypt.
  • Patristic Stichometries: Cited in the pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (early 6th c.) and the Stichometry of Nicephorus (Patriarch of Constantinople, 9th c.), which reckons the work at 2,100 stichoi among the ecclesiastical books.

The Syriac Tradition

The Psalms of Solomon is also preserved in the Syriac tradition across five manuscripts (critical edition by W. Baars, 1972):

  • MS S (7th century CE): A fragmentary marginal text preserved in the margin of a manuscript of the Hymns of Severus of Antioch (British Library, Add. 14538).
  • The Complete Syriac Codices: Manchester, John Rylands Library, Syr. 9 (the celebrated 16th-century "Harris codex"); Birmingham, Selly Oak Colleges, Mingana Syr. 163; Cambridge, University Library, Add. 2012; and Jerusalem, St. Mark's Monastery, Syr. 161.

In the Syriac manuscripts, the eighteen psalms are appended directly to the Odes of Solomon, numbered continuously as Odes 43–60. Philological evaluations by Joseph L. Trafton (1985) demonstrate that the Syriac translation differs from the Greek in only about 62 verses (roughly 10%) and shows an intimate affinity with the Greek archetype of Group 253, while in several passages reflecting independent Semitic idioms.

History of Printed Editions

  • Editio Princeps (1626): First printed by the Jesuit scholar Juan Luis de la Cerda in his Adversaria Sacra (Lyon, 1626), based on a transcript of MS 149 rediscovered in Augsburg by David Hoeschel (1556–1617).
  • Oscar von Gebhardt (1895): Die Psalmen Salomo’s; the foundation of modern stemmatic criticism, expanding the known Greek witnesses from five to eight manuscripts through Mount Athos discoveries.
  • Alfred Rahlfs (1935): Septuaginta; incorporated eight manuscripts, providing the widely adopted standard chapter and verse numbering.
  • Robert B. Wright (2007): The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text; the first complete edition to collate all eleven Greek manuscripts and four Syriac codices with high-resolution digital imaging.
  • Felix Albrecht (2018): Psalmi Salomonis (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3); the definitive monumental edition providing exhaustive stemmatic apparatus, patristic citations, and orthographic documentation.

title: Vitae prophetarum
section: XII PROPHETAE - ISAIAS - JEREMIAS - BARUCH - EZECHIEL

details.intro:
The Lives of the Prophets (Greek: Περὶ τῶν βίων καὶ τῆς τελευτῆς τῶν προφητῶν / Peri tōn biōn kai tēs teleutēs tōn prophētōn; Latin: Vitae prophetarum / De vitis prophetarum; Syriac: Tash'yāthā d-nebīyē) is an ancient Jewish hagiographical and biographical compendium detailing the careers, origins, ancestral tribes, prophetic signs, deaths, martyrdoms, and burial locations of twenty-three biblical prophets. Attributed spuriously in early Christian transmission to Epiphanius of Salamis (Cyprus, 4th c.) or Dorotheus of Tyre, the core document is a product of 1st-century CE Palestinian Judaism, compiled in Greek (or translated very early from Hebrew) prior to the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE.

The work is organized systematically by individual prophetic entries, typically following a rigid fourfold formula:

1. The prophet's hometown, geographical region, and ancestral tribe.

2. Distinctive miraculous deeds, prophetic oracles, and biographical anecdotes unrecorded in the biblical canon.

3. The circumstances of the prophet’s death (frequently violent martyrdom at the hands of wicked rulers or rebellious compatriots).

4. The exact topographical site of the prophet’s tomb and burial shrine, often accompanied by accounts of local pilgrimage, healing waters, or eschatological portents.

Survey of the Twenty-Three Prophetic Lives

A. The Four Major Prophets (chs. 1–4)

1. Isaiah (ch. 1): From Jerusalem; of the tribe of Judah; martyred under King Manasseh by being sawn in two with a wooden saw (priōni xylinō) beneath the Rogel oak tree. Before dying, Isaiah prayed for water, and God miraculously opened the spring of Siloam (Silōam, "Sent"); the spring flowed or ceased according to the prayer of the prophet. Buried near the Tomb of the Kings.

2. Jeremiah (ch. 2): From Anathoth; of the tribe of Levi; stoned to death by his own people at Taphnas (Tahpanhes) in Egypt and buried near Pharaoh’s palace. By prayer, Jeremiah banished the asp-vipers, crocodiles, and water-beasts (kēdoi) of Egypt. Before the fall of Jerusalem, Jeremiah miraculously concealed the Ark of the Covenant, the golden altar of incense, and the tables of stone inside a rock on Mount Nebo, sealing the crevice with his finger; the cloud of glory will not reveal the holy relics until the Lord gathers His dispersed people at the End of Days.

3. Ezekiel (ch. 3): From the land of Sarira; of the priestly order; slain in Chaldea by the leader of the Jewish exiles whom he reproved for practicing idolatry; buried in the double cave (spēlaion diploun) of Arphaxad. Ezekiel parted the waters of the river Chebar so fleeing exiles could escape the Chaldeans, and miraculously multiplied fish in the river during severe famine.

4. Daniel (ch. 4): From Upper Beth-horon; of the tribe of Judah; a man of renowned asceticism whose face shone with celestial beauty because he abstained from meat and wine. Interceded for Nebuchadnezzar during his zoomorphic madness, weeping for the beast-king until his reason returned. Buried in the royal tomb in Babylon.

B. The Twelve Minor Prophets (chs. 5–16)

5. Hosea (ch. 5): From Belemoth of the tribe of Issachar; gave the prophetic sign that the Lord would arrive on earth when the oak at Shiloh divided into twelve parts; buried in his native district.

6. Micah (ch. 6): From Morasthi of the tribe of Ephraim; executed by Joram son of Ahab (thrown from a precipice); buried on his family land near the burial ground of the Enakim.

7. Amos (ch. 7): From Tekoa; assaulted by Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, whose son Amaziah struck Amos’s skull with a club; carried half-dead back to Tekoa where he expired; buried with his ancestors.

8. Joel (ch. 8): From the territory of Reuben (Bethom); died in peace and buried in his home field.

9. Obadiah (ch. 9): From Beth-acharam; identified as the royal steward of Ahab who hid and fed one hundred prophets in a cave (1 Kgs 18:4); became a disciple of Elijah; buried in Samaria.

10. Jonah (ch. 10): From the district of Kariathmaus near Azotus; identified as the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah revived from the dead (1 Kgs 17); after his mission to Nineveh, wandered with his mother to Sour (Tyre) and died; buried in the cave of Kenaz, the first judge.

11. Nahum (ch. 11): From Elkesi; foretold the overthrow of Nineveh by freshwater flood and subterranean fire; buried in his native land.

12. Habakkuk (ch. 12): From Beth-zouchar of the tribe of Simeon; fled to Ostrakine when Nebuchadnezzar advanced; carried by an angel by the hair of his head to Babylon to bring food to Daniel in the lions' den; gave the eschatological sign: "When a light shines in the Temple, they will see the glory of God"; buried in his own field.

13. Zephaniah (ch. 13): From the mountain of Sarabatha of the tribe of Simeon; prophesied concerning the captivity; buried in his field.

14. Haggai (ch. 14): Born in Babylon as a youth; saw the rebuilding of the Second Temple; buried near the tombs of the priests in Jerusalem.

15. Zechariah (ch. 15): Son of Berechiah; returned from Chaldea in extreme old age; blessed Zerubbabel and Josedek; buried beside Haggai.

16. Malachi (ch. 16): From Sopha; of the tribe of Zebulun; a man of exceptional piety and beauty; an angel of God appeared invisible to the multitude, repeating and confirming Malachi's prophecies (whence his name Angelos / Malachi); died young and buried in his ancestral tomb.

C. Prophets from the Historical Books (chs. 17–23)

17. Nathan (ch. 17): From Gaba; of the tribe of Judah; prevented David from building the Temple; died in old age and buried in his home.

18. Ahijah the Shilonite (ch. 18): From Shiloh; foretold the division of the kingdom to Jeroboam; saw a vision of two yoked heifers treading down the sanctuary; buried near the oak of Shiloh.

19. Joad (The Man of God from Judah) (ch. 19): From Samareim; the unnamed prophet of 1 Kings 13 slain by a lion after being deceived by the old prophet of Bethel; buried in Bethel beside his deceiver.

20. Azariah son of Oded (ch. 20): From the district of Subatha; urged Asa to purify Judah from idols; buried in his native field.

21. Elijah the Tishbite (ch. 21): From Thisbe of Gilead; of the priestly line; at his birth, his father Sobacha saw angels wrapping the newborn in bands of fire and feeding him with flames; ascended into heaven in a fiery chariot.

22. Elisha (ch. 22): From Abel-meholah of the tribe of Reuben; at his birth in Gilgal, the golden calf in Bethel bellowed so loudly it was heard throughout Jerusalem; buried in Samaria.

23. Zechariah son of Jehoiada (ch. 23): Slain by King Joash between the Temple altar and the sanctuary; his blood congealed upon the stone paving of the Temple and could not be washed away until the Babylonian invasion; buried in his father’s tomb in Jerusalem.
details.manuscripts:
The Lives of the Prophets was among the most widely circulated hagiographical texts of late antiquity and the Byzantine Middle Ages, preserved across Greek, Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Arabic linguistic streams.

A. The Greek Manuscript Tradition

The Greek text is preserved in dozens of manuscripts exhibiting six major recensional families (classified by T. Schermann, E. Nestle, and J.-C. Haelewyck):

1. Epiphanii Recensio Prior (The Anonymous/Epiphanian Primitive Recension):

  • Preserved in Codex Marchalianus (Vat. gr. 2125) (6th/7th c., margin notes), Codex Parisinus gr. 1115 (dated 1276 CE), and Codex Vaticanus gr. 2024.
  • Considered by Torrey, Hare, and Schwemer to preserve the oldest and purest Jewish textual form.

2. Dorothei Recensio (Pseudo-Dorotheus of Tyre):

  • Found in historical catenae and discipular catalogs (Index discipulorum); characterized by stylistic smoothing and Byzantine chronographic notes.

3. Epiphanii Recensio Altera (Secondary Epiphanian Recension):

  • Represented by Codex Coislinianus 224 (10th/11th c.) and Codex Parisinus gr. 2496.

4. Recensio Anonyma:

  • Independent text form preserved without patristic attribution in Byzantine florilegia.

5. Recensio Scholiis Adiecta:

  • Integrated into the catenae and scholia of medieval Septuagint Bibles.

6. Recensio Liturgica (The Byzantine Synaxaria and Menologia):

  • Prophetic lives adapted into liturgical reading lessons for saints' feast days in the imperial Menologion of Basil II and the Great Synaxarion of Constantinople (ed. F. Halkin, A. Negoitǎ).

B. The Latin Tradition

  • Circulated early in the Western Church under the titles De vita et obitu prophetarum and De ortu et obitu patrum:
  • Isidore of Seville (De ortu et obitu patrum, 7th c., PL 83:129–156): Drew directly upon an early Latin translation of the Vitae.
  • Moses of Bergamo (12th c.): Translated Greek prophetic lives into Latin.
  • Critical studies and text editions by François Dolbeau (1986, 1990, 1994) recovered late antique Latin translations predating Isidore.

C. The Syriac Tradition

  • Widely diffused throughout the East Syrian (Nestorian) and West Syrian (Jacobite) churches:
  • Berlin MS Sachau 131 (fols. 57r–65v): ed. F. Baethgen (1886).
  • Union Theological Seminary MS Syr. 16: cataloged by M. Goshen-Gottstein (1979).
  • Solomon of Basra (The Book of the Bee, 13th c.): Incorporates chapters of the Vitae into chs. 32–33 (ed. E. A. W. Budge, Oxford, 1886, pp. 69–79).
  • Isho‘dad of Merv (9th c.): Extensively quotes the Vitae in his biblical commentaries (ed. C. van den Eynde, CSCO, 1962–1972).
  • Syriac chrestomathies: Eberhard Nestle, Syrische Grammatik (Berlin, 1888, pp. 86–107).

D. Other Ancient Versions

  • Ethiopic (Ge'ez): Translated from Christian Arabic or Greek; ed. J. Bachmann, Aethiopische Lesestücke (Leipzig, 1893); M. A. Knibb, "The Ethiopic Version of the Lives of the Prophets: Ezekiel and Daniel" (1985).
  • Armenian: Preserved in Armenian biblical manuscripts and Menologia; ed. S. Josepheanz (Ankanon girk‘, Venice, 1896, pp. 207–227); trans. J. Issaverdens (Venice, 1901, pp. 141–168).
  • Arabic: Extant in numerous Christian Arabic codices (Sinai Ar. 389, 448); ed. Oscar Löfgren, "An Arabic Version of the 'Vitae prophetarum'" (Orientalia Suecana 25–26 [1976–1977]: 77–105).

title: Apocalypsis Sophoniae
section: XII PROPHETAE - ISAIAS - JEREMIAS - BARUCH - EZECHIEL

details.intro:
The Apocalypse of Zephaniah is an ancient Jewish pseudepigraphic revelation recounting the visionary ascent of the biblical prophet Zephaniah through the heavens, his inspection of post-mortem judgment, and his tour of Hades.

Although original Greek copies have perished, the work is directly quoted in Greek by Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 5.11.77.2–3) in the late 2nd century CE:

> "Does not the spirit also speak similarly in the prophet Zephaniah? 'And the spirit took me up and carried me into the fifth heaven, and I beheld angels who are called lords, and their diadem was set upon them in the Holy Spirit, and the throne of each of them was sevenfold brighter than the light of the rising sun, dwelling in temples of praise and hymning the ineffable, most high God.'"

The bulk of the surviving text is preserved in two Coptic dialectal recensions discovered in Upper Egypt at the end of the 19th century:

1. Akhmimic Coptic Manuscript: Preserves 18 leaves recounting Zephaniah's cosmic vision, the recording of human deeds, the confrontation with the demonic accuser, the crossing of the underworld sea in a heavenly boat, and the intercession of the patriarchs.

2. Sahidic Coptic Fragment: A single leaf detailing a vision of cosmic torment and the punishment of hypocrites.

Thematic Structure and Content

  • The Heavenly Books and Recording Angels: Zephaniah beholds the dual bookkeeping of human existence. The angel Dokiel writes down the righteous deeds of humans, while another recording angel transcribes their sins and omissions.
  • The Accuser and the Angel of the Abyss: The prophet encounters the terrifying angel of Hades, Eremiel ("who is over the abyss and Hades"), whose countenance is terrifying and whose hair sweeps the ground, but who functions as a guide. When the demonic Accuser appears to condemn Zephaniah, the prophet prays and puts on the angelic garment, causing the demon to flee.
  • The Golden Boat and the Underworld Lake: Zephaniah is conveyed across an ethereal body of water into the realm of the righteous in a golden boat piloted by thousands of radiant angels.
  • Patriarchal Intercession for the Damned: Zephaniah witnesses Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob daily entreating the Almighty on behalf of the sinners undergoing torment in Hades—constituting one of the earliest witnesses in Jewish literature to the concept of righteous intercession modifying the post-mortem fate of the wicked (paralleling Testament of Abraham and 4 Ezra).
  • The Eschatological Trumpets: Angelic blasts of the trumpet (shofar) inaugurate distinct stages of cosmic reckoning, culminating in the destruction of the world of flesh and the victory of the Lord.
details.manuscripts:
A. Coptic Manuscripts

1. Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS copt. 135 (Akhmimic):

  • Date: Late 4th or early 5th century CE.
  • Provenance: Discovered at Akhmim (ancient Panopolis), Upper Egypt.
  • Contents: 18 leaves containing the major continuous sections of the Apocalypse of Zephaniah, bound together with the Akhmimic text of the Apocalypse of Elijah.
  • Editions: First transcribed by Urbain Bouriant (1885), critically edited with German translation and glossary by Georg Steindorff (1899).

2. Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS copt. 135, fol. 1 (Sahidic):

  • Date: 4th/5th century CE.
  • Contents: A single folio containing an independent Sahidic version of the visionary ascent and the lake of fire.

3. Naples, Biblioteca Nazionale, Borgia copt. 109:

  • Small supplementary Sahidic fragments closely related to the Paris manuscript.

4. Louvain, Bibliothèque de l'Université, Coptica Lovaniensia MS 12:

  • Date: 5th century CE.
  • Contents: A fragmentary Coptic leaf explicitly preserving the subscript title naming Zephaniah (Tsophanias), published by L. T. Lefort in 1938 (the manuscript itself was unfortunately destroyed during World War II).

B. Patristic Greek Citations

  • Clement of Alexandria, Stromata (Stromateis) 5.11.77.2–3 (quoting Zephaniah's ascent to the fifth heaven and the enthroned lordly angels).

title: Ascensio Isaiae
section: XII PROPHETAE - ISAIAS - JEREMIAS - BARUCH - EZECHIEL

details.intro:
The Ascension of Isaiah (Ascensio Isaiae / Ἀναβατικὸν Ἡσαΐου) is a composite apocalypse combining ancient Jewish haggadic traditions with early Jewish-Christian visionary literature. Redacted in its final form in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE (likely in Roman Syria or Asia Minor), the work consists of three historically and thematically distinct components:

1. The Martyrdom of Isaiah (Asc. Isa. 1:1–3:12; 5:1–16):

  • An ancient Jewish narrative composed in Semitic (Hebrew or Aramaic) during the 1st century BCE or 1st century CE. King Hezekiah instructs his wicked son Manasseh. Upon Manasseh’s accession, the demonic ruler Beliar (Sammael) inspires apostasy and idolatry in Jerusalem. Isaiah flees with his prophetic disciples (including Habakkuk and Joel) to a mountain near Bethlehem. The Samaritan false prophet Belkira (Malkira) denounces Isaiah to Manasseh. Isaiah is arrested and horribly executed by being sawn in two with a wooden saw (serratus sectus est). Throughout the ordeal, Isaiah converses with the Holy Spirit, shedding neither tears nor uttering cries.
  • Ancient External Attestations: Alluded to in the New Testament (Heb 11:37: "they were sawn in two"); Justin Martyr (Dialogus cum Tryphone 120.5); Tertullian (De patientia 14; Scorpiace 8); Origen (Comm. in Mt. 13.57; Epistula ad Africanum 9); and the Babylonian Talmud (b. Yevamot 49b; b. Sanhedrin 103b).

2. The Testament of Hezekiah (Asc. Isa. 3:13–4:22):

  • An independent Christian apocalyptic interpolation dating from the late 1st century CE (ca. 80–100 CE). Isaiah delivers a prospective vision of the descent of the Beloved (Christ), His ministry with the Twelve, His crucifixion, and His resurrection. He foretells the corruption, lawlessness, and greed of the post-apostolic elders and bishops, followed by the descent of the cosmic prince Beliar in the likeness of the matricidal Roman emperor Nero ("a lawless king, the murderer of his mother"). Beliar-Nero works deceptive signs, establishes worldwide imperial worship, and persecutes the faithful for 3 years, 7 months, and 27 days (1335 days), after which the Lord arrives from the seventh heaven with his angelic host to cast Beliar and his armies into Gehenna.

3. The Vision / Ascension of Isaiah (Asc. Isa. 6:1–11:43):

  • An early 2nd-century CE (ca. 110–130 CE) visionary apocalypse originally circulating independently. In the 20th year of Hezekiah, Isaiah falls into an ecstatic trance before the king and prophets. A radiant angel guides him in an ascent through the seven heavens: in the second through fifth heavens, he witnesses the angelic orders praising the divine throne; in the sixth heaven, all praise is directed upward in unison; in the seventh heaven, Isaiah sees the righteous souls clothed in light, with their garments, thrones, and crowns awaiting them.
  • The Cosmic Descensus and Ascensus: God commissions the Beloved to descend through all seven heavens down to the earthly realm and the underworld (Sheol). In His descent, the Beloved conceals His glory, transforming His appearance in each heaven so that the resident archons do not recognize Him. On earth, He is born miraculously of the virgin Mary without labour or pain (11:2–14), lives unrecognized, is crucified by the rulers of the cosmos under the instigation of Beliar, rises on the third day, and ascends back to the seventh heaven in full, dazzling majesty, receiving the adoration of all cosmic powers.
details.manuscripts:
While fragmentary remains survive in Greek, Latin, Coptic, and Slavonic, the complete text of chapters 1–11 is preserved only in classical Ge'ez (Ethiopic):

A. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

The primary witness for the entire work, preserved in nine manuscripts:

  • MS A (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Aeth. d. 13, fols. 95r–115r): 15th-century codex; the base text for Laurence and Dillmann.
  • MS B (London, British Library, MS Or. 501, fols. 62r–69v): 15th century.
  • MS C (London, British Library, MS Or. 503, fols. 57r–62v): 18th century.
  • MS E (EMML 1768, fols. 83r–88v): 15th century.
  • MS F (EMML 3067, fols. 99r–117v): 15th century.
  • MS G (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. Aeth. 263, fols. 85v–104v): 14th/15th century.
  • MS H (Paris, BnF, d'Abbadie 195, fols. 74r–87r): 17th/18th century.
  • MS I (Paris, BnF, d'Abbadie 156, fols. 46r–52v): 18th century.
  • MS L (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod. Aeth. 63): 18th/19th century.

B. Greek Tradition

1. Amherst Papyrus 1 (P. Amherst I.1; London, Pierpont Morgan Library / British Library):

  • 5th-century CE papyrus preserving Greek Asc. Isa. 2:4b–4:4a (the flight of Isaiah and the beginning of the Testament of Hezekiah).
  • Editio princeps: Grenfell, B. P., and A. S. Hunt. The Amherst Papyri. London, 1900, 1:1–22.

2. Patristic Citations:

  • Origen (Comm. in Mt. 13.57; Ep. ad Afr. 9).
  • Didymus the Blind (Comm. in Eccl., P. Tura; ed. D. Lührmann, ZAW 104 [1992]: 231–249 at 233–239).
  • Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 40.2.2–4; 67.3.3).

3. Medieval Greek "Legend of Isaiah":

  • A Byzantine hagiographical adaptation of the Ascension preserved in Paris BnF gr. 1534 (12th cent.) and Vat. Palat. gr. 27 (10th/11th cent.); edited by C. Tischendorf (1866) and B. Flusin in CCSA 8 (1995).

C. Latin Tradition

Two independent partial Latin witnesses:

  • Lat$^1$ (Vatican, BAV, Cod. Vat. Lat. 5750, fols. 278–284): 5th/6th-century palimpsest uncial preserving Asc. Isa. 2:14–3:13 and 7:1–19 (ed. Angelo Mai 1828; C. Leonardi in CCSA 7, 1995).
  • Lat$^2$ (Visio mirabilis Ysaiae Prophetae): 12th-century Latin translation of chapters 6–11 published by Antonius de Fantis in Venice (1517), reprinted by R. H. Charles (1900) and C. Leonardi in CCSA 7 (1995).

D. Coptic Tradition

  • Akhmimic Fragments: Louvain University Library Coptic MS 1 (5th cent., destroyed in WWII); preserved Asc. Isa. 9:35–11:23 (ed. L. T. Lefort, Muséon 1938, 1939).
  • Sahidic Fragments: Paris BnF copte 135 and Cairo Coptic Museum fragments (ed. Pierre Lacau, Muséon 1946; Paolo Bettiolo in CCSA 7, 1995).

E. Slavonic Tradition

  • Preserved in over 20 medieval South Slavic and East Slavic manuscripts (e.g., the 12th-century Uspenskij Sbornik); contains an archaic translation of the Vision of Isaiah (chs. 6–11) translated from an early Greek recension (ed. A. Popov 1879; Alda Giambelluca Kossova in CCSA 7, 1995).

details.intro: 4 Baruch (Paraleipomena Jeremiou) tells of the fall of Jerusalem and the exile. Abimelech sleeps for sixty-six years and wakes to find his figs still fresh; Jeremiah leads the return; and the work ends with Jeremiah's death at the hands of the people.
details.provenance: Most date it in the early 2nd c. CE, after 70 and before the Bar Kokhba revolt. It is a Jewish work with a Christian ending. It survives in Greek, Ethiopic, Armenian and Slavonic.

details.intro: Most scholars conclude the Apocalypse of Baruch (2 Baruch) is a Jewish composition from the regions in or around Judea, written around the end of the first century CE (see discussion below).
details.provenance:
Date

2 Baruch is a pseudepigraphal work written from the perspective of Baruch, the scribe of Jeremiah, and set around the time of the destruction of Solomon's Temple in 586 BCE. However, it is clear that 2 Baruch presupposes the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE (cf. 32.2-4), and that the author was primarily concerned with the theological and pastoral implications of the destruction of the Second Temple. Nickelsburg rightly indicates that the author of 2 Baruch is still "deeply grieved by the events of the year 70" (Jewish Literature, 283).

It is more difficult to determine when, after 70 CE, 2 Baruch was written. The vague reference in 28.2 to the ‘calculation of time in two parts’ pertaining to ‘weeks of seven weeks’ is too vague to be of much value (see L. Gry, “Date de la fin des temps, scion les révélations ou les calcula du Pseudo-Philo et de Baruch [Apocalypse syriaque],” RB 48 [1939]: 337-56). There is also an affinity between 2 Baruch 61.7 and Barnabas 11.9 (written between 117 and 132 CE?), though this may be due to both authors' use of a common source.

Another factor relevant to the dating of 2 Baruch is the document's evidently close relationship with 4 Ezra. Unfortunately, the date of 4 Ezra is itself uncertain (see G. H. Box, “IV Ezra,” APOT 2.553-54). Moreover, while interdependence between the two documents is almost certain, the nature, extent, and order of this interdependence is disputed (Nickelsburg). Although 2 Baruch and 4 Ezra share significant overlaps in content, there are broad thematic differences in their treatment of this common material. Whereas 4 Ezra educes a careful theodicy in response to the tragedy of the temple's destruction, the concerns evident in 2 Baruch are more “pastoral and practical,” addressing matters of consolation and exhortations toward reconstruction (Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283). This ambiguous situation has produced four main suggestions over the past century as to the (inter)relationship of the two apocalypses:

  1. 4 Ezra was dependent on 2 Baruch (see list on Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.26);
  2. 2 Baruch was dependent on 4 Ezra (see list on Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.26; Box, APOT 2:553; Metzger, OTP 2:522);
  3. both were dependent on a common source (Klijn, Arabic Text, 620);
  4. we cannot determine the direction of the dependence (Charles, APOT 2:477; Michael E. Stone, Fourth Ezra [Minneapolis : Fortress Press, 1990], 39).

For a complete, updated discussion, see Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283-85 and see the bibliography below for research between 1999 and 2006.

Some would see this cumulative, though tenuous, evidence to point to a date for 2 Baruch in the first or second decade of the second century CE (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617). Others argue that the document was written toward the end of the first century (Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283), perhaps in 96 CE specifically (Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.294-95; cf. also Nicolae Roddy, “‘Two Parts: Weeks of Seven Weeks’: The End of the Age as Teminus ad Quem for 2 Baruch,” JSP 14 [1996] 3–14).

Locale

2 Baruch was probably written in Judea, Galilee, or a neighbouring region. The original language of the document was most likely Hebrew or Aramaic, and the work shows affinities with later rabbinic literature originating from the land of Israel (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617). The author of 2 Bar. also seems to identify himself with the inhabitants of Palestine who have survived the Roman onslaught, and it is from this standpoint that he exhorts the Jews of the Diaspora in the epistle (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617).

Cultural and Historical Context

According to J. E. Wright, “The overall goal of 2 Baruch is to promote obedience to God’s commandments as the way to survive in difficult times” (“Baruch, Books of,” DNTB, 148-151). The book, somewhat like 4 Ezra, is the author’s attempt both to make theological sense of the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and to exhort Israel to remain faithful to her God in hope of restoration. It is widely agreed that 2 Bar. was originally composed in non-Christian Jewish circles, and the contention that it is instead a Christian composition (Nir, Destruction of Jerusalem, passim) has not found much support. Nonetheless, 2 Bar. is a "Christian text" in the sense that it was adopted and preserved within Christian circles for much of its transmission history.

title: Fragmentum latinum Apocalypsis Baruch syriacae
section: XII PROPHETAE - ISAIAS - JEREMIAS - BARUCH - EZECHIEL

details.intro:
2 Baruch (the Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch) is a premier Jewish apocalypse composed in Judea around the end of the 1st century or early 2nd century CE (ca. 95–110 CE), in the tragic aftermath of the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. Written in a Hebrew or Aramaic original that was translated into Greek, the complete text has survived only in a single Syriac manuscript (along with an Arabic version discovered in 1975).

The work is organized into seven distinct narrative sections structured around fasting, divine dialogues, prayer, and symbolic visions:

1. The Destruction of Jerusalem (Chapters 1–12): God announces the city's destruction; angels bury the sacred Temple vessels in the earth; the Chaldeans/Romans conquer the city.

2. First Dialogue and Fast (Chapters 13–20): Baruch laments the plight of the righteous; God explains the transitoriness of this aeon (‘olam hazzeh) and the glory of the coming age (‘olam habba’).

3. Second Dialogue and the Messianic Woes (Chapters 21–30): Baruch questions the duration of history; God reveals the twelve periods of tribulation and the arrival of the Messiah, characterized by supernatural agricultural fertility.

4. Third Dialogue and the Vision of the Forest, Vine, Cedar, and Fountain (Chapters 31–43): The allegory of the four world empires (Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome); the Roman cedar is uprooted by the Messianic fountain and burned by the Vine.

5. Fourth Dialogue, Consolation, and the Nature of the Resurrection Body (Chapters 44–52): Baruch instructs the elders; God reveals that the dead will rise with their physical bodily defects so they can be recognized, and will subsequently be transformed into starry glory or hideous torment.

6. The Great Vision of the Cloud with Twelve Alternating Black and Bright Waters (Chapters 53–76): An apocalyptic survey of world history from Adam to the eschatological Prince of Peace, interpreted by the angel Ramiel.

7. The Epistle of Baruch to the Nine and a Half Tribes in Exile (Chapters 78–87): Sent by an eagle across the Euphrates, exhorting the diaspora to unyielding fidelity to the Torah until the final judgment.

title: Apocalypsis Baruch graeca

details.intro: 3 Baruch (the Greek Apocalypse of Baruch) describes Baruch, grieving over the destruction of Jerusalem, being led by an angel through five heavens. There he sees the punishment of the tower-builders, the dragon of Hades, the sun and moon, and Michael receiving the prayers of the righteous.
details.provenance: It survives in Greek and Slavonic. A Jewish work of the 1st–2nd c. CE with Christian revision is the common view, though some regard it as Christian.

section: XII PROPHETAE - ISAIAS - JEREMIAS - BARUCH - EZECHIEL

details.intro:
The Apocryphon of Ezekiel is an ancient Jewish pseudepigraphon composed in Greek (or Semitic Vorlage) during the Second Temple period (1st cent. BCE to 1st cent. CE). Josephus refers to Ezekiel having left behind "two books" (Antiquitates Judaicae 10.79), pointing to an extra-canonical book circulated under Ezekiel's name alongside the canonical prophet. Although the complete text has perished, five substantial fragments survive as quotations in patristic, gnostic, and papyrological sources:

1. Fragment 1: The Parable of the Lame and the Blind (apud Epiphanius, Panarion / Adversus Haereses 64.70.5–17):

  • A wealthy king holds a royal wedding banquet for his son and invites everyone except two guards: one blind and one lame. In anger, the two infiltrate the king's garden: the blind man carries the lame man on his shoulders so the lame man can guide him and pluck the fruit. When confronted, each claims physical impossibility. The king places the lame man upon the blind man's shoulders and executes them together.
  • Theological Function: An allegory of the indivisible partnership of the physical body (sōma) and soul (psychē) in human action, establishing their joint resurrection and culpability at the Last Judgment. Directly paralleled in Rabbinic literature: b. Sanhedrin 91a–b (the dialogue between Rabbi Judah the Prince and Antoninus); Leviticus Rabbah 4.5; Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael on Exod 15:1.

2. Fragment 2: The Exhortation to Repentance (apud 1 Clement 8.3; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 1.10.91.2; Quis Dives Salvetur 39.2; Coptic Exegesis on the Soul, NHC II,6, pp. 135.31–136.4):

  • A prophetic call to repentance promising forgiveness even if sins reach from earth to heaven or are redder than scarlet, provided Israel returns with a whole heart and calls God "Father."

3. Fragment 3: The Miraculous Heifer (apud Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 7.16.94; Tertullian, De carne Christi 23; Epiphanius, Panarion 30.30.3; Acts of Peter 24; Gregory of Nyssa, Adversus Judaeos 3):

  • "And the heifer [sterile cow] gave birth, and did not give birth" (καὶ ἔτεκεν ἡ δάμαλις καὶ οὐκ ἔτεκεν). Adopted widely in early Christian apologetics as an ancient prophetic proof-text for the virginal conception of Mary.

4. Fragment 4: Judgment According to the Final State (apud Justin Martyr, Dialogus cum Tryphone 47.5; Clement of Alexandria, Quis Dives Salvetur 40.2; Hippolytus, De consummatione mundi 44; John Climacus, Scala Paradisi 7; Life of St. Anthony 15):

  • "In whatsoever things I find you, in these also will I judge you" (ἐν οἷς ἂν ὑμᾶς καταλάβω, ἐν τούτοις καὶ κρινῶ). A famous agraphon attributed to Ezekiel asserting that judgment falls on a person's ultimate spiritual state at death.

5. Fragment 5: The Good Shepherd and the Flocks (Chester Beatty Papyrus 20 / P. Mich. Inv. 5552):

  • 4th-century CE Greek papyrus leaf containing a poetic lament over an unfaithful, oppressive ruler/shepherd who abuses the weak and fails to seek the lost, contrasting with God's pastoral care; cf. Clement of Alexandria, Paed. 1.9.84.2–4; Origen, Homilies on Jeremiah 18.9; Manichaean Psalm-Book 239.5–6.

details.intro: The Apocryphon of Ezekiel is known only from quotations and fragments. Its best-known passage, preserved by Epiphanius, is the parable of the lame man and the blind man, which illustrates the joint judgment of body and soul.
details.provenance: The work is usually considered Jewish and dated before the end of the 1st c. CE. Early Christian writers quote it under Ezekiel's name.

details.intro: The Byzantine Apocalypse of Daniel (CAVT 197 / CANT 208) is a 9th-century Greek historicized apocalypse recounting Byzantine-Arab conflicts, the rise of the Antichrist, and the final judgment. Edited by F. Macler, L'Apocalypse de Daniel (1895); Klaus Berger (1976); and K. T. Zervos in OTP 1 (1983).
details.provenance: The apocalypse belongs to the Byzantine tradition of Daniel apocalypses that read political history as prophecy. Its account of the end includes a Jewish messiah figure who turns out to be the Antichrist.

details.intro:
4 Ezra (chapters 3–14 of the composite book preserved in the Latin Vulgate as 2 Esdras / 4 Esdras) is a Jewish apocalypse composed in Roman Palestine (Judea) around 95–100 CE, thirty years after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple by Titus in 70 CE (historicized under the pseudonym of "Salathiel who is also Ezra" thirty years after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, 3:1). Written originally in Hebrew or Aramaic, translated early into Greek, and transmitted through multiple ancient versions, the apocalypse is structured into seven visionary episodes:

1. First Episode (3:1–5:20): Ezra laments in Babylon over the desolation of Zion and the prosperity of pagan Rome. The archangel Uriel rebukes him, declaring that human understanding cannot fathom divine ways, that the present age is pregnant with evil because of Adam's "evil heart" (cor malignum), and that the end-time harvest must await the predetermined number of the righteous.

2. Second Episode (5:21–6:34): Ezra questions why God delivered His chosen people to the nations. Uriel reveals that creation has grown old like an aging mother, and explains the transition of cosmic epochs: "Esau is the end of this age, and Jacob is the beginning of the age that follows" (6:9).

3. Third Episode (6:35–9:25): The lengthiest theological dialogue, exploring the fate of souls after death, the intermediate rest in celestial chambers/promptuaries, the 400-year temporal kingdom of the Messiah, the final death of all mortals (including the Messiah) followed by seven days of primeval silence, the universal resurrection, and the irreversible judgment where no intercession is possible for the damned (the famous "Lost Fragment," 7:36–105).

4. Fourth Episode (9:26–10:59): Ezra sees a weeping, disheveled woman mourning the sudden death of her only son on his wedding night. As Ezra consoles her, she is transfigured into a vast, shining, founded city. Uriel explains that the woman is Zion, her thirty barren years represent the period before Solomon, her son is the Temple destroyed by the Romans, and the radiant city is the eschatological heavenly Jerusalem.

5. Fifth Episode: The Eagle Vision (11:1–12:51): An imperial eagle with twelve wings, three heads, and eight contrary winglets arises from the sea, exercising oppressive global dominion. A roaring lion emerges from the forest and pronounces the eagle's annihilation. Uriel identifies the eagle as the fourth kingdom of Daniel 7 (Rome, reigning from Julius Caesar and Augustus through the Flavian emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian), and the lion as the Davidic Messiah who will judge and destroy the empire.

6. Sixth Episode: The Man from the Sea (13:1–58): A cosmic man rises from the depths of the sea, flies with the clouds of heaven, carves out a great mountain (Mount Zion) without hands, incinerates a hostile attacking army with a stream of fire and flaming breath from his mouth, and then gathers a peaceful multitude: the lost Ten Tribes of Israel, who had crossed the Euphrates to the distant, unpolluted land of Arzareth.

7. Seventh Episode: The Voice from the Bush and the Restoration of the Scriptures (14:1–48): God calls Ezra from a thornbush as He did Moses. Ezra drinks a cup of glowing water like fire, receiving divine wisdom for forty days. Assisted by five rapid scribes, he dictates 94 books: 24 exoteric books to be made public for the worthy and unworthy alike (the Hebrew biblical canon), and 70 esoteric books reserved exclusively for the wise.
details.manuscripts:
The original Semitic text is lost, but the text is preserved across eight major ancient language traditions, all translated directly or indirectly from a lost Greek translation:

A. Latin Tradition (Versio Latina)

The Latin version is the primary witness for Western biblical transmission. It falls into two groups depending on the presence of the "Missing Fragment" (7:36–105), which was omitted from the Clementine Vulgate because a single leaf had been deliberately cut out of the primary archetype:

  • MS S (Codex Sangermanensis I; Paris, BnF lat. 11504–11505): Copied at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 821/822 CE. Archetype of all European Vulgate manuscripts lacking 7:36–105.
  • The Eight Independent Latin Manuscripts (preserving the missing section):
  • MS A (Codex Ambianensis; Amiens, Bibliothèque Municipale 10): 9th-century manuscript in which Robert L. Bensly discovered the "Lost Fragment" in 1874.
  • MS C (Codex Complutensis 1; Madrid, Universidad Central 31): 9th/10th century.
  • MS E (Codex Epternacensis; Luxembourg, Bibliothèque Nationale 264): Dated 1051–1081 CE.
  • MS L (Codex Legionensis 2; León, Real Colegiata de San Isidoro I,3): Dated 1162 CE.
  • MS M (Codex Mazarinaeus; Paris, Bibliothèque Mazarine 3–4): 11th/12th century.
  • MS N (Codex Bruxellensis; Brussels, Bibliothèque Royale 9107–9110): 12th century.
  • MS V (Codex Abulensis / Avila; Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional Vitr. 15–1): 12th/13th century.

B. Syriac Tradition (Versio Syra)

  • Preserved complete in the famous 6th/7th-century Peshitta codex: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 Inf. (fols. 267v–276v). Provides the most faithful and reliable oriental translation of the lost Greek text.
  • Critical Editions:
  • Ceriani, Antonio Maria. Liber IV Esdrae syriace. Monumenta Sacra et Profana 5. Milan, 1868, pp. 41–111; and photolithographic edition, MSP 6, 1876.
  • Bidawid, R. J. "4 Esdras." In The Old Testament in Syriac according to the Peshitta Version, Part IV, fasc. 3. Leiden: Brill, 1973.

C. Greek Citations and Fragments

  • Patristic Citations: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.22.149.3 and 3.16.100.3; Apostolic Constitutions 2.14.9 and 8.7.6.
  • Papyrus Fragment: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus VII 1010 (4th cent. CE, containing 4 Ezra 15–16 [= 6 Ezra]).
  • Palimpsest Fragment: Rubinkiewicz, Ryszard. "Un fragment grec du IV$^e$ Livre d’Esdras (chapitres XI et XII)." Le Muséon 89 (1976): 75–89 [Preserves Greek text of the Eagle Vision in codex Marcianus Gr. 498].
  • Denis, Albert-Marie. Fragmenta pseudepigraphorum quae supersunt graeca. PVTG 3. Leiden: Brill, 1970, pp. 130–132.

D. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

  • Preserved in over 20 manuscripts (e.g., Tānāsee 51; Paris BnF éth. 50; British Library Add. 16188).
  • Laurence, Richard. Primi Ezrae libri, qui apud Vulgatam appellatur quartus, versio Aethiopica. Oxford: Parker, 1820 [Editio princeps].
  • Dillmann, August. Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici. V. Libri apocryphi. Berlin: Asher, 1894, pp. 152–193 [Critical edition].

E. Arabic Traditions

Two distinct Arabic translations made from different Vorlagen:

  • Arabic 1 (Arab. 1): Oxford, Bodleian MS Huntington 254 (translated from the Syriac; ed. Ewald 1863).
  • Arabic 2 (Arab. 2): Mount Sinai Arabic MS 589 (9th/10th cent. CE; ed. A. Drint, CSCO 563–564, 1997).

F. Georgian Tradition

  • Preserved in the Jerusalem Georgian MS 43 (11th/12th cent.) and Mount Athos Iviron MS (10th cent.).
  • Edition: Blake, Robert P. "The Georgian Version of Fourth Esdras from the Jerusalem Manuscript." Harvard Theological Review 19 (1926): 299–375; and "from the Athos Manuscript," HTR 22 (1929): 57–105.

G. Armenian Tradition

  • Preserved in 28 biblical manuscripts, representing a highly paraphrastic, interpretive (targumic) recension.
  • Editions:
  • Yovsēp'ianc', Sahak. Ankanon girk' Hin Ktakaranac'. Venice: San Lazzaro, 1896, pp. 251–299.
  • Stone, Michael E. The Armenian Version of IV Ezra. University of Pennsylvania Armenian Texts and Studies 1. Missoula: Scholars Press, 1979.
  • Stone, Michael E. A Textual Commentary on the Armenian Version of IV Ezra. SBLSCS 34. Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1990.

H. Coptic Tradition

  • Sahidic papyrus fragment preserving 4 Ezra 13:29–48.
  • Edition: Leipoldt, Johannes, and Bruno Violet. "Ein saidisches Bruchstück des vierten Esrabuches." Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde 41 (1904): 138–140.

details.intro: The Letter of Aristeas describes how Demetrius of Phalerum persuaded Ptolemy II to have the Jewish law translated into Greek. Seventy-two elders come from Jerusalem, answer the king's questions at banquets, and complete the translation, which the Alexandrian Jewish community then approves.
details.provenance: Written in Greek by an Alexandrian Jew, the letter is generally dated to the 2nd c. BCE. It was transmitted in Greek manuscripts of the catenae on the Octateuch.

details.intro: The Sibylline Oracles are quoted extensively by the church fathers (see Thompson, “Patristic Use of the Sibylline Oracles,” Review of Religion [1952] 115-36). They also influenced Renaissance literature and art.
details.provenance:
Though the Jewish and Christian oracles contained in this collection are the only extant extended versions of the genre to survive, oracles of the Sibyl were extremely popular in Greco-Roman antiquity from the 5th century BCE onward. The Sibyl, characterized as an aged female prophetess whose “raving mouth” (Plutarch, Moralia 397A) almost always forecasted doom, uttered her oracles in Greek hexameter and her oracles usually served purposes of political propaganda. Caesar Augustus is said to have destroyed two thousand prophetic books, including some Sibylline Oracles, because of their subversive nature (Seutonius, Augustus 31:1). The earliest Sibyl was believed to have lived in Erythea in Ionia. Other well known Sibyls are associated with Cumae in Italy and Marpessus in Asia Minor (Collins 1983: 317). The proliferation of Sibyls led to various attempts to enumerate them. The most influential of these lists was that of Varro, who counted ten (Lactantius DivInst.1.6). The prologue of the present collection repeats this list but associates the Persian Sibyl with an otherwise unknown Hebrew Sibyl.

If, as is widely argued (see below), books 3, 4 and 5 can be located in Egypt then these Sibyls significantly enrich our understanding of Egyptian Judaism during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Collins has suggested that book 3 is unique inasmuch as it looks to a Ptolemaic king as savior figure (the “seventh king of Egypt” vs. 193, see also vss. 318, 608). Barclay, however has warned against making too much of this and suggests that both books 3 and 5 can be seen as popular literature of Alexandrian Judaism. As such they attest to the cultural antagonism between Jews and their Gentile surroundings in that locale. This antagonism would later culminate in the Diaspora Revolt of 115-117 CE. Many of the oracles contain a strong polemic against idol worship and homosexuality, which was a common feature in Jewish apologetic.

Provenance of the Individual Oracles

Locating the date and provenance of the individual books within the collection is extremely difficult. Even books which can be confidently assigned to a particular place and time often contain later interpolations.

Books 1 and 2 are likely a unit and consist of a Jewish oracle which has been edited by a later Christian redactor. In the ψ family of manuscripts book 2 contains a lengthy excerpt from Pseudo-Phocylides, the anonymous 1st century Jewish author whose ethical maxims are usually found embedded in the work of the 6th century BCE philosopher. The prominence given to Phrygia in the book indicates that the work originated in Asia Minor. Since Rome alone is singled out for destruction in the tenth generation and Roman power in Asia Minor was consolidated around 30 BCE, the Jewish sections of the book are likely no earlier than this date. Though there is passing reference to the fall of Jerusalem (1.393-400), Collins has suggested that the brevity of this reference and the fact that Rome is not here singled out for recrimination indicates that this section must be part of the Christian interpolation. Thus the Jewish sections of the book can possibly be dated between 30 BCE and 70 CE [Collins 1983: 331]. The reference to the destruction of the Temple sets the earliest date for the Christian redaction. A terminus ante quem is more difficult to establish.

Books 3 and 5 are widely believed to have originated in Egyptian Jewish circles. Because of references to the seventh king of Egypt (vss. 193, 318, 608), the provenance of most of book 3 can likely be located in Ptolemaic Egypt in the second century BCE. Numerous additions (vss.350-80) s eem to have been made in the first century BCE as is suggested by references to Cleopatra and her anticipated triumph over Rome. Line 776 may be a Christian interpolation inasmuch as it notes that “mortals will invoke the son of the great God.” In his reassessment of the provenance of much of the Jewish Pseudepigrapha, Davila does not wholly refute this consensus but notes that while the work speaks of the Jewish law, the content of this law mostly concerns proper worship of God, and is not concerned with food laws, the Sabbath or circumcision. Thus, while the work could have been authored by an assimilated Jew, it could also be the work of “a gentile who was much taken with and influenced by Judaism in the second or first centuries BCE” (Davila 2005: 186). This is plausible.

The earliest possible date for book 5 is 70 CE, since the work makes use of the Nero Redivivus

motif and thus must come after that emperor’s death in 68 CE. Inasmuch as the work contains positive references to Hadrian (vss. 46-50), the book is likely not later than 132 BCE, since it is difficult to imagine that a Jewish author would have spoken favorably of Hadrian after the Bar Kochba revolt (132-135 BCE). There is a strong anti-Roman sentiment in these oracles, and the Sibyl looks to a heavenly savior figure. This savior figure is identified with Jesus in a Christian interpolation in lines 255-59. Davila suggests that is just as possible that the work is entirely that of a Christ-believing Jew (thus eliminating the need to posit interpolation) or that the work is that of devout gentile God-fearer (Davila 2005: 189).

Book 4 is composite. The original oracle (vss. 49-101) is likely from the Hellenistic period, and there is nothing in the work to suggest Jewish authorship. The oracle has been augmented by a Jewish redactor (vss. 1-48; 102-172). References to the destruction of the temple and to the eruption of Vesuvius date this redaction to the late first century CE. The provenance of the redaction is debated (Thomas 1935; Nikiprowetzky 1970). The work contains a rejection of temple worship (this is in sharp contrast to books 3 and 5) and an interest in baptism. This interest suggests a provenance in Syria or the Jordan Valley, where baptismal movements seem to have been common, but this can not be confirmed (Collins 1983: 382).

Book 6 is not internally presented as a Sibylline Oracle at all but as hymn to Christ. The hymn begins with the baptism of Jesus, ends with his death and suggests that the cross itself was taken up to heaven after the crucifixion. The work must have been written before 300 CE, when it is quoted by Lactantius (Collins 1983: 406). Its provenance is not known.

A terminus ante quem f for book 7 is also provided by Lactantius (DivInst 7.16.13). The work is Christian, and portrays Jesus as a Davidic messiah (vs. 31) who will be enthroned above the angels (vss. 31-33). The work evinces an interest in the baptism of Christ (vss. 65-67) which is to be commemorated by a unique ritual in which a dove is prayed over and then released (vss. 76-81). The provenance of the work is not known.

Book 8 is composite. The first section, vss. 1-216, consists of political prophecies, mostly against Rome. Verses 131-38 were clearly written by a different author than the rest of the work, inasmuch as the pro-Hadrian stance of these verses contradicts verses 50-72. It is uncertain whether this section of the book has its origins amongst a Christian group or a non-Christ believing Jewish group but references to the return of Nero during the reign of Marcus Aurelius (65-74) indicates that book was written during the reign of that emperor, roughly around 175 CE. The second section of the book, lines 217-500, is clearly Christian and is primarily concerned with Christology. It is difficult to date precisely but, again, Lactantius provides a terminus ante quem.

Book 9 is comprised of material in from books 1-8. Book 10 repeats the material in book 4. (See Manuscripts, below).

Books 11-14 seem to represent “an ongoing tradition that was repeatedly updated” (Collins 1983: 430). Each book picks up where the previous one left off and each concludes with a prayer of the Sibyl. Book 11 contains a review of history from the flood to the death of Cleopatra. Several references to Egypt and to the foundation of Alexandria (vs. 219) suggests that the book may have originated in Egypt. Collins suggests that references to Joseph, Moses and Solomon (vss. 29; 38-40; 80-103) indicate that the work is Jewish. Davila, however, does not find this to be persuasive evidence and maintains that the work could just as easily be Christian.

Book 12 shows dependency on SibOr 5, indeed the first eleven verses are taken directly from that book. The bulk of the work is probably Jewish but verses 30-34 and 232, which both speak about the coming Christ (“the secret word of the Most High will come/ wearing flesh like mortals”; 32-33) are Christian interpolations. A reference to the death of the emperor Alexander Severus (288) (235 CE) provides a terminus pro quem of 235 CE.

Book 13 contains praise of Odenath of Palmyra (vss. 150-73) who fought for the Romans against the Parthians during the reign of emperor Gallienus (260-68 CE). Since it does not know of the deaths of either of those figures the work can be dated to approximately 265 CE. The importance accorded Odenath could suggest that the work originated in Syria, but references to Egypt and Alexandria (vss. 43-49) could point to an Egyptian origin. A reference to Decius’ persecution of Christians (vss.87-88) could be a Christian interpolation (Collins 1983: 453) or could indicate that the entire work is Christian (Geffcken 1902: 59-63). Collins suggests that references to the Most High (vs. 109) and the polemic against astrology (vss. 69-73) suggest Jewish authorship, though these elements are also congruent with a Christian provenance.

The dating of book 14 is uncertain. There may be a reference to the Arab conquest (vss. 340-49) which would place the book in the 7th century CE. There are also seem to be references to several Roman emperors, but because the text is exceedingly cryptic, it is difficult identify which ones are being alluded to. There are references to Egypt and to Alexandria (vss. 295-296; 320) which suggests that the book originated there. The concluding verses which proclaim that “the holy nation will hold sway over the whole earth/ for all ages, with their mighty children” (vss. 360-361) suggest Jewish authorship.
details.manuscripts: There are three manuscript groups. Both the φ group and the ψ group contain books 1-8, with the former containing also an anonymous prologue. The φ group begins with book 1 and lacks 8.487-500, while the ψ group begins with book eight (some mss also omit 6 and 7). The third manuscript group, Ω, begins with a ninth book, which is comprised of material in from books 1-8; book 6, then a single verse not found in books 1-8, then 8.218-428. Book 10 repeats the material in book 4. Books 11-14 are preserved only in the Ω group.

details.intro:
The Sibylline Oracles (Greek: Χρησμοὶ Σιβυλλιακοί / Chrēsmoi Sibylliakoi; Latin: Oracula Sibyllina) constitute a vast, multifaceted collection of Greek hexameter poems composed by Jewish and early Christian authors between the 2nd century BCE and the 7th century CE. The collection adopts the authoritative literary persona of the Sibyl—the inspired, ecstatic prophetess of ancient pagan Greece and Rome (traditionally associated with Erythrae, Cumae, or Delphi)—to proclaim biblical monotheism, castigate pagan idolatry, prophesy the rise and fall of world empires, and announce impending cosmic judgment, divine conflagration (ekpyrōsis), and the messianic age.

The standard critical corpus comprises fourteen numbered books (Books 1–8 and 11–14; Books 9 and 10 in early numbering represent duplicated material), plus several independent fragments preserved in patristic literature (Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius).

Classification of the Corpus

A. The Major Jewish Sibylline Books

1. Book 3 (The Ptolemaic Jewish Sibyl, ca. 163–145 BCE; with later additions ca. 30 BCE):

  • The oldest, most substantial, and most influential Jewish Sibylline composition, originating in Alexandria, Egypt, during the reign of Ptolemy VI Philometor (180–145 BCE).
  • The Main Core (ll. 97–808):
  • The Tower of Babel and the euhemeristic myth of the Titans (Kronos, Titan, Prometheus, ll. 97–161).
  • Succession of world kingdoms: Solomon, Persians, Macedonians, Greeks, and the menacing rise of the Roman Republic (an empire of many heads).
  • The Seventh King of Egypt (ll. 193, 318, 608): Under the seventh Greek Ptolemaic monarch, the Great King from the Sun (ap' ēelioio) will arrive to usher in divine peace and exalt the Temple of Jerusalem.
  • Oracles of doom against pagan nations (Babylon, Egypt, Greece, Libya) for their idolatry, sexual perversions, and plundering of the holy sanctuary.
  • The final eschatological crisis: Kings of the earth unite to assault Mount Zion; God intervenes with fiery swords, torrential brimstone, and cosmic earthquakes; the righteous dwell in eternal safety around the radiant Temple, feasting on honey, milk, and wine.
  • The Augustan Addition (ll. 1–96, ca. 30 BCE):
  • Allusions to the Second Triumvirate, Cleopatra VII (a female reign over Rome), and the arrival of Beliar from the Sebastoi (ek Sebastēnōn), who will perform signs and deceptions until consumed by heavenly fire.

2. Book 4 (The Post-70 CE Hellenistic Jewish Sibyl, ca. 80 CE):

  • Composed in Judea, Syria, or Asia Minor shortly after the volcanic destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum by Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE (an air-borne fire bursting from a fissure in Italy, ll. 130–136).
  • Historical outline of four world kingdoms: Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Macedonians, followed by the fifth: Rome.
  • Depicts the sack of Jerusalem and the burning of the Second Temple by a Roman general (Titus, ll. 115–129).
  • Theological Distinctiveness: Complete rejection of animal sacrifice and man-made temples; the author preaches salvation through moral repentance and purification in running streams/rivers (lousasthe potamois, ll. 165–170), reflecting Jewish baptist piety.
  • The Nero Redivivus Legend: Nero's flight across the Euphrates into Parthia and his impending return with a terrifying army to incinerate the West (ll. 119–124, 137–139).
  • Universal physical resurrection: God will reshape human dust and restore flesh and breath to bones for the great judgment in fire (ll. 179–192).

3. Book 5 (The Trajanic/Hadrianic Egyptian Jewish Sibyl, ca. 115–132 CE):

  • Composed in Roman Egypt during or shortly after the catastrophic Diaspora Revolt under Trajan and Hadrian (115–117 CE).
  • Fierce, unmitigated anti-Roman polemic: Rome is reviled as the "impious Babylon," the bloodthirsty harlot that devastated Jerusalem.
  • Chronicle of Roman emperors from Julius Caesar to Hadrian (indicated by gematria / initial letters of names: J=10, A=1, T=300, etc.).
  • Nero depicted as an eschatological cosmic monster and Antichrist returning from the ends of the earth to level cities.
  • The Heavenly Man and the Celestial Temple: A divine redeemer descends from heaven, rebuilding a radiant, indestructible Jerusalem.
  • The Battle of the Stars (ll. 512–531): Cosmic battle of constellations; the zodiac signs tear each other apart and plunge into the abyss.

4. Books 1–2 (Jewish Core ca. 1st c. BCE; Christian Redaction ca. 150 CE):

  • Periodization of world history into Ten Generations (decas).
  • The first through sixth generations recount primeval history: Adam, the Fall, the giants, the wickedness of mankind, and Noah's prophetic preaching before the Deluge.
  • The Christian redactor inserted Christological prophecies and interpolated lines 5–79 of Pseudo-Phocylides into Book 2 (ll. 56–148).
B. The Christian Sibylline Books
  • Books 6–8 (Late 2nd to 3rd c. CE):
  • Book 6: A short, beautiful liturgical hymn to Christ, his baptism in the Jordan, and his crucifixion.
  • Book 7: Apocalyptic prophecies against nations, the destruction of Rome, and the final conflagration.
  • Book 8: Contains the famous 34-line acrostic hymn (ll. 217–250) whose initial Greek letters form the confession: ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΕΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΥΙΟΣ ΣΩΤΗΡ ΣΤΑΥΡΟΣ (Iēsous Chreistos Theou Yios Sōtēr Stauros, "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior, Cross"), forming the sacred anagram ΙΧΘΥΣ (ICHTHYS).
  • Books 11–14 (The Byzantine Historical Sibyls, 4th–7th c. CE):
  • Historical retrospectives in prophetic disguise, tracking imperial rulers from Julius Caesar, through Constantine and Justinian, down to the Arab-Islamic conquest of Egypt and Syria (Book 14).
details.manuscripts:
The complex transmission history of the Sibylline Oracles is classified into three distinct manuscript groups:

A. The Three Recensional Manuscript Families

1. Group $\Phi$ (Codices 1–8):

  • Preserves the anonymous Byzantine Christian Preface/Prologue (summarizing the ancient Sibyls according to Varro) and Books 1–8 (lacking only 8.487–500).
  • Key manuscripts:
  • MS A (Codex Ambrosianus D. 84. inf.): 15th century, Milan.
  • MS B (Codex Vaticanus Graecus 743): 14th century, Rome.
  • MS C (Codex Monacensis Graecus 351): 15th century, Munich.
  • MS P (Codex Parisinus Graecus 2851): 15th century, Paris.

2. Group $\Psi$ (The Phocylides Recension):

  • Preserves Book 8, followed by Books 1–7 (omitting Books 6 and 7 in several witnesses).
  • Distinctive feature: Interpolates Pseudo-Phocylides lines 5–79 as SibOr 2.56–148.
  • Key manuscripts:
  • MS D (Codex Laurentianus plut. XI. 17): 15th century, Florence.
  • MS E (Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1120): 14th century, Rome.
  • MS H (Codex Monacensis Graecus 499): 16th century, Munich.

3. Group $\Omega$ (The Mai Discoveries: Books 11–14):

  • In 1817 and 1828, Cardinal Angelo Mai discovered in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana (Milan) and the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana (Rome) manuscripts containing four previously unknown Sibylline books, published as Books 11–14 (along with alternate recensions of earlier books, numbered 9 and 10).
  • Key manuscripts:
  • MS M (Codex Ambrosianus E. 64. sup.): 15th century, Milan.
  • MS Q (Codex Vaticanus Graecus 744): 16th century, Rome.
  • MS Z (Codex Vaticanus Graecus 2038): 16th century, Rome.

B. Patristic and Classical Testimonies

  • The Sibylline Oracles were extensively quoted by ancient apologists to demonstrate that even pagan prophets attested to monotheism, the incarnation, and the final judgment:
  • Theophilus of Antioch (Ad Autolycum 2.31, 36, 38): Quotes large sections of the Jewish Fragment 1 and Fragment 3 (the Prooemium).
  • Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, Protrepticus).
  • Lactantius (Divinae Institutiones): Quotes hundreds of Sibylline verses in Latin translation, providing invaluable early text-critical evidence.
  • Emperor Constantine: Quoted the Book 8 acrostic in his Oration to the Assembly of the Saints (ch. 18).
  • Saint Augustine (De Civitate Dei 18.23): Translated the 27-line acrostic of Book 8 into Latin hexameters.

title: Demetrius the Chronographer — On the Kings in Judaea

details.intro:
Introduction

Demetrius the Chronographer (late 3rd century BCE, ca. 221-204 BCE) is the earliest datable Jewish author writing in Greek whose works have survived. He composed a work entitled On the Kings in Judaea (Περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ βασιλέων) or On the Jews (Περὶ Ἰουδαίων), preserved primarily through excerpts of Alexander Polyhistor quoted in Eusebius's Praeparatio Evangelica (9.19.4; 9.21.1-19; 9.29.1-3, 15, 16) and Clement of Alexandria's Stromateis (1.21.141.1-2).
details.provenance:
Provenance

Alexandria, Egypt, during the reign of Ptolemy IV Philopator (221-204 BCE), as established by Demetrius's own chronological reckonings down to that monarch.

title: Eupolemus — On the Kings of Judaea

details.intro: Eupolemus wrote a history of the Jewish kings in Greek. The fragments preserved through Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius and Clement deal mainly with Moses as the first sage, David, and Solomon's letters to the kings of Egypt and Tyre about the building of the Temple.
details.provenance: He is often identified with the Eupolemus whom Judas Maccabeus sent to Rome (1 Macc 8:17). If so, he was writing in Judea in the mid-2nd c. BCE.

details.intro: Artapanus wrote a romance-like history of the Jews in Egypt. Fragments preserved through Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius present Abraham, Joseph and especially Moses as founders of Egyptian culture and religion.
details.provenance: He is generally dated to the 3rd–2nd c. BCE, in Egypt.

details.provenance: He wrote before the mid-1st c. BCE, when Alexander Polyhistor quoted him; no more precise date or place can be established.

details.provenance: Neither his date nor whether he was Jewish, Samaritan or a gentile can be settled. He wrote before the mid-1st c. BCE, since Polyhistor cites him.

details.intro: Two anonymous fragments, preserved by Eusebius and once attributed to Eupolemus, connect Abraham with astrology, the giants and the tower of Babel, and with the teaching of the Phoenicians and Egyptians. The first locates Melchizedek at Argarizin (Mount Gerizim).
details.provenance: Because of the Gerizim reference they have often been attributed, following Freudenthal, to an anonymous Samaritan, but R. Doran (OTP 2) argues that the two fragments are too dissimilar to come from one author. They predate the mid-1st c. BCE.

title: Theophilus — On Solomon and Hiram of Tyre

details.intro: The fragment of Theophilus (FGrH 733) is an excerpt from a Hellenistic Jewish historian preserved by Alexander Polyhistor and cited by Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica IX.34.19, recounting Solomon's gift of a golden image to the king of Tyre in exchange for the gilded pillar of the Temple.
details.provenance: Theophilus is otherwise unknown; he is usually dated before the mid-1st century BCE, since Alexander Polyhistor quotes him. Whether he was Jewish or a pagan writer drawing on Jewish tradition is disputed.
details.manuscripts: Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica IX.34.19 (citing Alexander Polyhistor).
