title: Justus of Tiberias — Chronicle of the Kings / Jewish War

details.intro:
Introduction

Justus of Tiberias (fl. late 1st century CE, ca. 66-100 CE) was a Galilean Jewish statesman, historian, and rival of Flavius Josephus. He served as court secretary to King Herod Agrippa II and composed a Chronicle of the Kings of the Jews (Ἰουδαίων βασιλέων τῶν ἐν τοῖς στέμμασιν) extending from Moses to the death of Agrippa II, as well as a contemporary history of the Jewish War against Rome.
details.provenance:
Provenance

Tiberias in Galilee and the court of Agrippa II, composed in Greek in the late first century CE (reign of Domitian/Trajan).

details.intro: The fragments of Thallus the Chronographer (FGrH 256) derive from a universal history in three books written by a Samaritan or Jewish chronographer of the 1st century CE. Syncell. 610) regarding the darkness at the Crucifixion, and by Theophilus of Antioch (Ad Autolycum III.29) on the antiquity of Belus and the Ogygian flood.

title: Philo the Epic Poet — Peri Ta Hierosolyma (On Jerusalem)

details.intro: Philo the Epic Poet wrote a Greek hexameter poem On Jerusalem. Fragments of it are preserved through Alexander Polyhistor in Eusebius and concern Abraham, Joseph and the water supply of Jerusalem. The language is deliberately obscure.
details.provenance: He is usually dated to the 3rd–2nd c. BCE. Whether he wrote in Alexandria or in Jerusalem is uncertain.

title: Aristobulus of Alexandria — Exegesis of the Law of Moses

details.intro: Aristobulus was a Jewish philosopher who addressed a work on the Torah to a Ptolemaic king. The fragments preserved by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius explain the Bible's anthropomorphisms allegorically, claim that Greek poets and philosophers borrowed from Moses, and discuss the Sabbath and the date of Passover.
details.provenance: Aristobulus is usually dated to the mid-2nd c. BCE, at Alexandria, in the reign of Ptolemy VI Philometor.

details.intro: The Sentences of Pseudo-Phocylides (CAVT 182 / CANT 35) is a didactic wisdom poem of 230 dactylic hexameters composed in Hellenistic Jewish circles between 100 BCE and 100 CE, combining Mosaic ethical precepts with traditional Greek gnomic form. Edited by Theodor Bergk, Poetae Lyrici Graeci, 4th ed., Vol. 2 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1882), pp. 361-373.
details.manuscripts: Extant in over 150 Byzantine manuscripts, including Mutinensis (M), Vaticanus (Va), Baroccianus (B), and Parisinus 1603 (P), as well as Sibylline Oracles Book 2 (vv. 56-148).

details.intro: The Testament of Orpheus (Diathēkai / Hieroi Logoi, CAVT 183 / CANT 33) is a Hellenistic Jewish-Orphic poem in dactylic hexameters in which Orpheus recants his former polytheism and instructs Musaeus in the worship of the One True God, explicitly invoking the law of Moses ('the one born of water'). Extant in three recensions: Aristobulus ap. Eusebius (Praep. Evang. XIII.12.5), Pseudo-Justin (Cohortatio ad Graecos 15; De Monarchia 2), and Clement of Alexandria (Stromata V.123-125). Edited by Otto Kern, Orphicorum Fragmenta (Berlin, 1922), frr. 245-248.

title: Hellenistic Synagogal Prayers — 16 Synagogal Prayers in Apostolic Constitutions 7-8

details.intro:
The Hellenistic Synagogal Prayers comprise a collection of sixteen Greek liturgical prayers embedded within the late 4th-century Syrian Christian church order known as the Apostolic Constitutions (Constitutiones Apostolorum, compiled ca. 380 CE in Antioch or Syria, likely by an Arianizing redactor traditionally associated with Pseudo-Ignatius). Originally identified by Kaufmann Kohler (1893, 1924) and demonstrated systematically by Wilhelm Bousset (1915) and Erwin R. Goodenough (1935), these texts are Greek-language synagogue prayers composed between the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE (ca. 150–300 CE) in the Hellenistic Jewish Diaspora of Syria, Asia Minor, or Egypt. The compiler of the Apostolic Constitutions incorporated this existing Jewish liturgical manual into his work, overlaying minimal Christian editorial glosses (typically Christological doxological formulas such as "through Jesus Christ our Lord" at the conclusions):

The Corpus of 16 Prayers (as numbered by Fiensy & Darnell, OTP 2):

1. Prayer 1 (Ap. Const. 7.26.1–3): Thanksgiving after meals (Birkat ha-Mazon), blessing God for nourishment, spiritual life, and knowledge.

2. Prayer 2 (Ap. Const. 7.33.2–7): Morning prayer praising God as almighty King, creator of heaven and earth, and savior of the patriarchs.

3. Prayer 3 (Ap. Const. 7.34.1–8): Cosmic hymn celebrating the order of creation, providence, the elements, and celestial bodies.

4. Prayer 4 (Ap. Const. 7.35.1–10): The Hellenistic Synagogal Qedushah / Sanctus, recounting the praise of the angelic hosts (Seraphim and Cherubim chanting Isa 6:3 and Ezek 3:12).

5. Prayer 5 (Ap. Const. 7.36.1–7): Sabbath liturgy celebrating God’s cosmic rest, the revelation of the Torah, and the Sabbath as a perpetual memorial of creation and the Exodus.

6. Prayer 6 (Ap. Const. 7.37.1–5): Sabbath morning blessing thanking God for the renewal of cosmic light (Yotzer Or).

7. Prayer 7 (Ap. Const. 7.38.1–8): Liturgical memorial reviewing the historical succession of righteous biblical heroes from Abel, Seth, Enoch, and Noah to Abraham, Moses, and the judges.

8. Prayer 8 (Ap. Const. 7.39.2–4): Blessing over proselytes / candidates for initiation, praying for their illumination in the knowledge of the one true God and the abandonment of polytheism.

9. Prayer 9 (Ap. Const. 8.5.1–4): Prayer for the ordination / appointment of leaders (adapted for episcopal ordination from Jewish semikhah traditions).

10. Prayer 10 (Ap. Const. 8.6.5–8): Intercessory petition over penitents and catechumens.

11. Prayer 11 (Ap. Const. 8.9.8–9): Congregational petition for the peace of the world, civil rulers, and the community (Birkat ha-Shalom).

12. Prayer 12 (Ap. Const. 8.12.6–27): The Great Anaphora / Eucharistic Prayer, incorporating an extensive Jewish cosmic and historical review of salvation history from the creation of Adam to the conquest of Canaan.

13. Prayer 13 (Ap. Const. 8.15.7–9): Post-communion thanksgiving prayer.

14. Prayer 14 (Ap. Const. 8.16.3): Dedicatory prayer over the offering of first fruits (Bikkurim).

15. Prayer 15 (Ap. Const. 8.40.2–4): Evening thanksgiving prayer accompanying the lighting of the lamps (Lucernarium / parallel to evening synagogue blessings and Havdalah).

16. Prayer 16 (Ap. Const. 8.41.2–5): Commendation / memorial prayer for the deceased righteous, professing unwavering faith in the bodily resurrection of the dead.

title: Sentences of the Syriac Menander — Syriac Sapiential Florilegium

details.intro:
The Sentences of the Syriac Menander (also known as Pseudo-Menander, Syriac Melle d-Menandros, French La sagesse de Ménandre l’Égyptien, German Die Sprüche des Menanders) is a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom florilegium of moral instruction and practical aphorisms. Pseudepigraphically attributed to Menander—the renowned 4th-century BCE Athenian comic dramatist whose sententious maxims (Gnomai Menandrou / Menandri Sententiae) were standard texts in Greco-Roman school curricula—the work was composed originally in Greek between the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, almost certainly in Roman Egypt.

The Greek original has not survived, but the text was translated into Syriac around the 6th or 7th century CE and is uniquely preserved in two distinct recensions:

1. The Longer Florilegium (approx. 474 lines of text): A comprehensive, loosely organized wisdom collection containing moral maxims, warnings, and prudential advice arranged in short strophic units.

2. The Epitome (approx. 64 lines of text): An abridged, excerpted thematic compendium preserving selected gnomic sayings from the longer text.

Thematic and Structural Organization

The work opens with a brief editorial rubric: "The sentences of Menander the sage: not all of them, but as much as he [the excerptor] could find." While lacking a rigid formal outline, the sayings address the central spheres of everyday Hellenistic and Near Eastern family and civic life:

1. Piety toward God and Acceptance of Divine Providence (ll. 1–32):

  • The primary duty of human existence is to fear God, offer daily prayer, and recognize God as the ultimate Sovereign of life and destiny.
  • Condemnation of boasting, pride, and claiming self-sufficiency; God alone brings wealth or poverty.

2. Family, Parents, and Domestic Ethics (ll. 33–88):

  • Profound filial duty: Honoring father and mother is paramount; the child who abuses or dishonors parents is cursed by God.
  • Care for aged parents; enduring their infirmities with patience.

3. Marriage, Women, and Household Dynamics (ll. 89–165):

  • Pragmatic, frequently misogynistic warnings typical of Hellenistic and Near Eastern sapiential literature (cf. Ben Sira).
  • Praise of the prudent, quiet, industrious wife; warnings against the adulteress, the shrewish wife, and women who practice witchcraft, potions, or illicit cosmetics.

4. The Dangers of Speech, Anger, and Slander (ll. 166–235):

  • Restraint of the tongue: "Keep your mouth closed, and let your words be few"; the silent person is considered wise.
  • Avoidance of rash anger, hot-tempered associates, gossip, and false testimony.

5. Wealth, Poverty, and Generosity (ll. 236–310):

  • Warnings against the deceitfulness of wealth; ill-gotten gains bring swift disaster.
  • Generosity toward the poor: Share bread with the hungry; do not mock the destitute or the afflicted, for Fortune is fickle and God can reverse fortunes overnight.

6. Social Conduct, Friendship, and Civic Prudence (ll. 311–400):

  • Choosing trustworthy friends; testing associates before confiding secrets.
  • Deference to magistrates and civil rulers; avoidance of violent revolts or public brawls.

7. Mortality, Death, and Mourning (ll. 401–474):

  • Remembrance of human frailty: "Man is like dust and ashes"; death is the universal equalizer of kings and beggars.
  • Moderate grief for the dead; excessive lamentation is futile and displeasing to God.
  • God will judge every human deed; the righteous soul departs in peace.
details.manuscripts:
The Sentences of the Syriac Menander has survived in only two ancient Syriac manuscripts, both preserved in the British Library in London:

A. The Longer Florilegium Witness

  • London, British Library, MS Add. 14658 (fols. 136v–141r):
  • Dating: 7th century CE.
  • Provenance: Written on vellum in early Estrangela script; acquired from the famous library of St. Mary Deipara in the Nitrian Desert (Wadi Natrun, Egypt).
  • Catalog: William Wright, Catalogue of the Syriac Manuscripts in the British Museum Acquired Since the Year 1838 (London, 1870–1872), Part 3, No. 987, pp. 1158–1159.
  • Context: Preserved within a celebrated theological and philosophical anthology containing Bardaisan's Book of the Laws of Countries, pseudo-Platonic dialogues, and Plutarchan treatises.
  • Text: Contains the full 474 lines of the longer florilegium.

B. The Epitome Witness

  • London, British Library, MS Add. 14618 (fols. 20v–22v):
  • Dating: 7th or 8th century CE.
  • Provenance: Nitrian collection; vellum codex written in clear Syrian cursive/Estrangela.
  • Catalog: William Wright, Catalogue of the Syriac Manuscripts, Part 2, No. 753, p. 745.
  • Context: Preserved in an ascetical and gnomic florilegium alongside the Sayings of the Holy Fathers.
  • Text: Contains the 64 excerpted aphorisms of the Epitome.

C. Collateral Traditions and Cross-Linguistic Circulation

While the specific Jewish collection survives only in Syriac, related branches of Menandrian gnomic literature circulated widely in the Mediterranean and Near East:

1. The Greek Menandri Sententiae (Gnomai Menandrou):

  • Byzantine schoolbook collections of alphabetical single-line verses (monostichoi); critical edition by Siegfried Jaekel (Leipzig: Teubner, 1964).

2. The Comparatio Menandri et Philistionis:

  • A 4th- to 6th-century CE Greek rhetorical debate/contest in verse between Menander and Philistion; edited by W. Meyer (1891) and G. Studemund (1887).

3. Arabic Gnomic Collections:

  • Sayings of Menander preserved in medieval Arabic wisdom florilegia (e.g., al-Mubashshir ibn Fatik's Mukhtar al-Hikam); studied and edited by Manfred Ullmann (Die arabische Überlieferung der sogenannten Menandersentenzen, Wiesbaden, 1961).

4. Coptic and Old Church Slavonic Witnesses:

  • Coptic and Slavic translations of Greek gnomic sententiae attributed to Menander; analyzed by Moreno Morani (1996).

details.intro: The Apocalypse of Sedrach (CAVT 184 / CANT 207) is an eschatological dialogue in which Sedrach (associated with Ezra / Shadrach) intercedes for mankind and questions divine justice regarding the fall of Adam and the punishment of sinners. Edited from Bodleian MS Miscell. gr. 56 by M. R. James, Apocrypha Anecdota (T&S 2.3; Cambridge, 1893), pp. 130-137.

details.intro: The Vision of Ezra (Visio Beati Esdrae) is a Latin apocalypse in which Ezra is led by angels through the places of punishment, sees the torments of various classes of sinners and intercedes for them, and is then taken to see the righteous in paradise.
details.provenance: The Latin text is known in a shorter form and in a longer form, which P.-M. Bogaert published from the Teano legendary (Barberini lat. 2318). The work is related to the Greek Apocalypse of Ezra and the Apocalypse of Sedrach; its date is disputed.
details.manuscripts:
The original Semitic text is lost, but the text is preserved across eight major ancient language traditions, all translated directly or indirectly from a lost Greek translation:

A. Latin Tradition (Versio Latina)

The Latin version is the primary witness for Western biblical transmission. It falls into two groups depending on the presence of the "Missing Fragment" (7:36–105), which was omitted from the Clementine Vulgate because a single leaf had been deliberately cut out of the primary archetype:

  • MS S (Codex Sangermanensis I; Paris, BnF lat. 11504–11505): Copied at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in 821/822 CE. Archetype of all European Vulgate manuscripts lacking 7:36–105.
  • The Eight Independent Latin Manuscripts (preserving the missing section):
  • MS A (Codex Ambianensis; Amiens, Bibliothèque Municipale 10): 9th-century manuscript in which Robert L. Bensly discovered the "Lost Fragment" in 1874.
  • MS C (Codex Complutensis 1; Madrid, Universidad Central 31): 9th/10th century.
  • MS E (Codex Epternacensis; Luxembourg, Bibliothèque Nationale 264): Dated 1051–1081 CE.
  • MS L (Codex Legionensis 2; León, Real Colegiata de San Isidoro I,3): Dated 1162 CE.
  • MS M (Codex Mazarinaeus; Paris, Bibliothèque Mazarine 3–4): 11th/12th century.
  • MS N (Codex Bruxellensis; Brussels, Bibliothèque Royale 9107–9110): 12th century.
  • MS V (Codex Abulensis / Avila; Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional Vitr. 15–1): 12th/13th century.

B. Syriac Tradition (Versio Syra)

  • Preserved complete in the famous 6th/7th-century Peshitta codex: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS B. 21 Inf. (fols. 267v–276v). Provides the most faithful and reliable oriental translation of the lost Greek text.
  • Critical Editions:
  • Ceriani, Antonio Maria. Liber IV Esdrae syriace. Monumenta Sacra et Profana 5. Milan, 1868, pp. 41–111; and photolithographic edition, MSP 6, 1876.
  • Bidawid, R. J. "4 Esdras." In The Old Testament in Syriac according to the Peshitta Version, Part IV, fasc. 3. Leiden: Brill, 1973.

C. Greek Citations and Fragments

  • Patristic Citations: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.22.149.3 and 3.16.100.3; Apostolic Constitutions 2.14.9 and 8.7.6.
  • Papyrus Fragment: Oxyrhynchus Papyrus VII 1010 (4th cent. CE, containing 4 Ezra 15–16 [= 6 Ezra]).
  • Palimpsest Fragment: Rubinkiewicz, Ryszard. "Un fragment grec du IV$^e$ Livre d’Esdras (chapitres XI et XII)." Le Muséon 89 (1976): 75–89 [Preserves Greek text of the Eagle Vision in codex Marcianus Gr. 498].
  • Denis, Albert-Marie. Fragmenta pseudepigraphorum quae supersunt graeca. PVTG 3. Leiden: Brill, 1970, pp. 130–132.

D. Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Tradition

  • Preserved in over 20 manuscripts (e.g., Tānāsee 51; Paris BnF éth. 50; British Library Add. 16188).
  • Laurence, Richard. Primi Ezrae libri, qui apud Vulgatam appellatur quartus, versio Aethiopica. Oxford: Parker, 1820 [Editio princeps].
  • Dillmann, August. Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici. V. Libri apocryphi. Berlin: Asher, 1894, pp. 152–193 [Critical edition].

E. Arabic Traditions

Two distinct Arabic translations made from different Vorlagen:

  • Arabic 1 (Arab. 1): Oxford, Bodleian MS Huntington 254 (translated from the Syriac; ed. Ewald 1863).
  • Arabic 2 (Arab. 2): Mount Sinai Arabic MS 589 (9th/10th cent. CE; ed. A. Drint, CSCO 563–564, 1997).

F. Georgian Tradition

  • Preserved in the Jerusalem Georgian MS 43 (11th/12th cent.) and Mount Athos Iviron MS (10th cent.).
  • Edition: Blake, Robert P. "The Georgian Version of Fourth Esdras from the Jerusalem Manuscript." Harvard Theological Review 19 (1926): 299–375; and "from the Athos Manuscript," HTR 22 (1929): 57–105.

G. Armenian Tradition

  • Preserved in 28 biblical manuscripts, representing a highly paraphrastic, interpretive (targumic) recension.
